This paper proves that any Zinbiel algebra necessarily has a commutative operation, thereby establishing a connection with the Malcev algebras, and demonstrating that the two algebra types are, in fact, equivalent by defining an isomorphism between them. Additionally, this equivalence in question extends to their respective variants with a distributive law. The paper also provides examples that the distributive Zinbiel-Malcev law leads to a non-trivial extension of the Birkhoff algebra. A database containing multiple views of the same data often employs distinct schema representations. These databases may operate under different data models or include various levels of abstraction. Each database has its own set of defined functional relationships (FDs) to ensure data consistency. However, the presence of null values in tables and incomplete databases can complicate the use of FDs, leading to inconsistent results. Furthermore, differences in data types and schema structure can create integration challenges. This research addresses these issues by developing a method to combine databases in a way that accounts for differing data types, integrates missing values, and accurately handles functional relationships, even in the presence of empty tables. This method enables valid queries to be executed on the integrated database with results that are consistent with each individual database. Additionally, we discuss various optimization problems that arise during the integration process. A preliminary experimental evaluation of our approach is also presented. We develop a time-varying Poisson autoregressive model, capable of handling seasonal fluctuations within data sets. This model's ability to adapt to changing patterns sets it apart from traditional time-invariant models, which can become less effective when underlying structures evolve. A new estimation method for the model's parameters has been created, and our empirical analysis shows that the model excels at capturing complex dynamics and generating accurate forecasts. When compared to leading alternative methods, our model's forecast precision is found to improve significantly, particularly in scenarios where data contains pronounced seasonal variations and non-stationary elements. The introduction of a persistence indicator also enhances the model's ability to forecast persistent data sets accurately. This is demonstrated through additional forecasting applications involving real-world datasets. The model's parameters' rate of change can be seen changing over time, and this change is significant in many cases, as shown in the appendix. The R code for the model and its components, as well as the datasets used in the chapter, are available for public use. The inclusion of this component allows for the modeling of fluctuations within the data itself, making it a true autoregressive model. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that combines internal and external information, enabling robots to perform manipulation tasks based on object categories. NDFs comprise three components: a spatial auto-encoder that represents objects in a category-independent manner, a neural network that predicts external object descriptors, and a regression model that combines both for prediction. We train NDFs to minimize the distance between predicted and actual descriptors, using a combination of contrastive learning and mean squared error. Experimentation on the RealWorld Dataset shows that NDFs outperform baselines in object recognition and manipulation tasks. Additionally, NDFs trained on a smaller dataset demonstrate similar performance to those trained on a larger one, indicating they are capable of generalizing to novel objects. Our method's superiority is further confirmed by analyzing failed attempts with baselines. NDFs are a versatile representation that can be adapted for other tasks, such as object pose estimation and segmentation. We open-source our implementation, along with the training and evaluation code, on GitHub. NDFs trained on a smaller dataset also exhibit the ability to transfer to a larger, more diverse set of objects, demonstrating their ability to capture abstract object descriptors that are independent of specific object instances. We propose a method that adapts NDFs to estimate object poses, and show our results on a publicly available dataset. Similarly, we demonstrate the ease with which NDFs can be modified to perform object segmentation on a different dataset. We believe this versatile representation has the potential to tackle a wide range of manipulation tasks based on object categories. In contrast to other methods that employ graph neural networks or attention mechanisms for object pose estimation, our method is more efficient and requires significantly less data for training. In comparison to other object segmentation methods, our approach offers a notable reduction in memory usage. This classification reveals that the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity, when measured from the equilibrium point, depends on a key parameter and can be determined for all N. In particular, for the simplest case of N=1 (which represents Hermitian matrix models), the edge singularity occurs when the external magnetic field (or the asymmetry parameter) equals half of the broadening of the external field or displacement potential. The accuracy of stellar photometry to assess aerosols has been questioned due to its reliance on outdated assumptions and lack of consideration for modern satellite data. Despite these limitations, this study demonstrates the potential utility of photometry in this context by employing three separate approaches to estimate aerosol properties using different sets of data. While these methods yield mixed results, they indicate that aerosol assessments with photometry are feasible, albeit no better than using alternative techniques. Furthermore, comparisons with modern satellite data reveal the potential benefits of employing more refined models, such as the use of vector irradiance measurements, as well as the importance of accurately calibrating satellite instruments with ground-based photometric data. This study also explores the relationship between aerosols and atmospheric scattering of starlight within the solar spectrum, with the added advantage of this approach in estimating the asymmetry parameter of atmospheric scattering without relying on theoretical assumptions. Ultimately, this work highlights the value of combining photometric and satellite data, as well as the insights gained from analyzing the spectral patterns of starlight, with the potential applications extending to the assessment of aerosol properties in photometric analyses of exoplanetary atmospheres.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or normal vectors instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence points between the 3D object model and the image. This approach is more straightforward, despite requiring a substantial amount of training data, particularly when establishing correspondences. Our proposed framework, DeepHMap++, targets this ease of implementation while addressing two major limitations: projection grouping and correspondence accuracy. Projection grouping is essential to restrict the network to focal regions, thereby preventing the model from scattering correspondences across the image. Our proposed network generates a fully connected, dense grid of correspondences instead of discrete points. To create a dense grid of correspondences, we introduce a novel, differentiable loss function called the Gaussian Field loss, which treats the intensity of correspondences as a continuous, Markov Random Field. This field is parametrized by an autoregressive neural tensor network that builds on top of graph attention networks to create a sophisticated, hierarchical representation of images. This representation enables the network to focus on specific image regions. Our proposed framework, DeepHMap++, is applicable to both category-level and instance-level pose estimation, and our results demonstrate a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art. We present GGLasso, a Python package designed to calculate Generalized Graphical Lasso estimators based on various optimization methods. Generalized Graphical Lasso extends traditional Graphical Lasso by allowing for the inclusion of linear co-variables in addition to inverse dependencies. GGLasso supports several optimization algorithms, including Alternating Projected Quasi-Newton, Conic Viapunkt, and Nesterov's Dual Quasi-Newton, as well as the application of Graphical Lasso to Gaussian Autoregressive models. The package also provides functions for solving Fischer-Burmeister system and Newton's method, and offers a command to generate GAAR models. Furthermore, it contains utilities for GAAR model estimation, model evaluation metrics, and sample datasets. The Python library builds upon existing implementations, particularly the Alternating Projected Quasi-Newton method developed by d'Alché-Buc and Grosse, and the Conic Viapunkt method developed by d'Alché-Buc, as well as the R package mecxPress developed by M. F. Khan. The source code for GGLasso is available on GitHub at https://github.com/abdo22/GGLasso. The package can be installed using pip: pip install python-gglasso. The documentation for the package is available at https://gglasso.readthedocs.io. The authors behind the package are ready to provide support via the GitHub repository. The package is intended for general-purpose use in statistics and machine learning. The efficiency of molecular dynamics simulations is significantly enhanced through the application of precise numerical methods in solving the equations of motion, particularly in the context of configurational sampling. By leveraging precise integrators, such as the velocity Verlet method, the spread of noise during simulations is minimized, thereby reducing crossovers between different molecular configurations and ultimately narrowing the gap between canonical and microcanonical ensembles. However, this approach generates Gaussian distribution of noise rather than Rayleigh distribution in velocities, which could potentially hinder the convergence to thermodynamic equilibrium. In the course of researching efficient configurational sampling strategies, the authors serendipitously discovered the benefits of precise integrators in Langevin dynamics. Due to the built-in thermostat in Langevin dynamics, which generates velocities in Rayleigh distribution, this method is more resistant to temperature fluctuations and dynamics crossovers. Consequently, this method is more suitable for the simulation of complex biological systems, particularly those involving many degrees of freedom, and it outperforms other numerical methods in various benchmarks. Furthermore, this method is more resistant to the negative effects of small time steps, providing accurate results even with time steps that are significantly larger than those required for the accuracy of the numerical integrator used. In the course of researching efficient configurational sampling strategies, the authors also developed a novel algorithm for rewriting the equations of motion in Langevin dynamics in a way that facilitates the application of numerical integrators based on velocity updates. This new algorithm is more versatile and provides greater freedom in the choice of numerical integrators, including those that require the knowledge of high-order derivatives, and it is particularly beneficial for the simulation of many degrees of freedom and complex biological systems. In the course of analysing this algorithm, the authors discovered that it is analogous to the algorithm underlying the Velocity-Verlet Langevin dynamics, which is a well-known and efficient numerical integrator in the context of Langevin dynamics. However, this algorithm had not been reported in the scientific literature prior to the current paper, and it is known by the name 'VV-Langevin' dynamics. The application of VV-Langevin dynamics resulted in the simulation of a Lennard-Jones crystal at a temperature close to its melting point, providing a precise match with the corresponding results obtained through molecular dynamics simulations based on the microcanonical ensemble. The crossovers between different molecular configurations occurred at time steps that were ten times larger than those required for the accuracy of the numerical integrator used in VV-Langevin dynamics, and it outperformed other numerical methods in various benchmarks

In multilayer networks, information can spread across different layers at varying speeds, affecting how nodes are prioritized for tasks like removing influential individuals. Existing methods focusing on optimization problems often result in inconsistent rankings across different layers, due to their exclusive weighting systems. Conversely, our approach uses the prominence of eigenvectors, which consider the significance of each layer and node simultaneously, providing a unified ranking that accounts for interactions across layers. Furthermore, this method enables a dynamic ranking of nodes across layers in response to changes within the network. Our empirical studies on realistic and artificial multilayer networks demonstrate improved accuracy and a more nuanced understanding of network dynamics. This approach has practical applications in utilizing eigenvector-based methods for problems like identifying influential individuals across different social platforms. Our algorithm is available online at https://github.com/AlirezHa/EigenvectorProminenceMLN. Our results are also available at arXiv:2105.02567.

Further discussion is devoted to the implications of code-mixing for various NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, machine translation, and dialogue systems. We conclude by highlighting the importance of incorporating code-mixed data into training models and developing specialized code-mixing models that can leverage the unique characteristics of code-mixed languages. Our work is an attempt to initiate a dialogue that can facilitate a deeper understanding of code-mixed languages and their potential utility in NLP. Our paper is targeted at the NLP research community, specifically researchers and developers working on multilingual NLP systems. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significance as businesses operate globally and user data often spans across different platforms. Despite its importance, this field has several challenges, primarily due to inconsistencies in domain characteristics, limited information available for target domains, and the complexity of user preferences across multiple domains. This paper introduces Hypatia, an interactive tool for resolving conic expressions from a simplified natural syntax into solver-compatible definitions based on standard conic formulations. It offers a character-efficient notation that omits redundant symbols and simplifies the definition of convex sets with affine or convex-over variables. The escalating number of magnetic resonance imaging scans necessitates efficient quality control processes. Radiologic technicians are becoming overburdened, prompting interest in automating this process with artificial neural networks. To achieve this, they must be trained on a mix of data featuring different imaging variables, including varying field strengths, contrast agents, and scan purposes. Furthermore, the networks must be able out-of-sample generalization, being able to accurately assess the quality of scans with combinations of imaging variables not seen during training. In this paper, we investigate the ability of low-dose CT image reconstruction networks to generalize in this multi-factorial manner. To evaluate this ability, we trained multiple types of networks on low-dose CT data from the Minneola dataset and tested their performance on combinations of imaging variables not seen during training. We found that the optimal network depends on the specific imaging variables involved and that the mean absolute error of the networks decreases with increasing training data. Nonetheless, the error remains substantial, and network failure is common. To demonstrate the practical applicability of these networks, we trained the most effective model on a subset of the Minneola dataset and tested it on a subset of the LUNA16 dataset, both of which contain clinical information. The network accurately assigned labels to previously unseen combinations of imaging variables, including combinations involving contrast agents and field strengths. The findings of this study are relevant to the quality assessment of brain MRI scans. To this end, we trained and tested several networks on brain MRI data from the ISIC 19 dataset and found that the optimal network depends on the specific imaging variables involved and that the performance of the networks deteriorates with increasing field strengths. Nonetheless, the networks exhibit low failure rates and are capable of accurately assigning labels to previously unseen combinations of imaging variables, including combinations involving contrast agents and scan purposes. The integration of electric vehicles into the power grid and charging infrastructure is becoming more prominent, with implications for the grid's operational safety and reliability. In this study, a mathematical framework for optimizing individual electric vehicle charging schedules while ensuring the grid's stability is developed. A multi-agent optimization approach is proposed, with each agent representing a distinct entity with its own objectives, such as electric vehicles, charging stations, households, and the power system operator. By applying a hybrid improved artificial fish swarm algorithm and genetic algorithm, the charging schedules that minimize grid instability and reduce charging costs for individual electric vehicles are determined. Computational simulations validate the proposed method's effectiveness. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential for electric vehicles to enhance the grid's resilience during emergency situations. A real-world application in Beijing, China is explored, demonstrating that electric vehicles can contribute to the grid's stability with appropriate management. The research underpins the potential for a'resilience-sharing' mechanism between the power grid and electric vehicles, with implications for how this sharing is optimized. The study's findings also highlight the importance of considering grid resilience when establishing electric vehicle charging infrastructure policies. Reiner, Stevens, and the first author established the Fundamental Coxeter Ensemble (FCE) notion and proved that its members possess an order-isomorphism with the length function. This implies that the FCE is invariant under any ordering defined by the length function. We have now expanded the initial framework to encompass the Bn-type Coxeter groups and demonstrated that the FCE within this setting also exhibits order-invariance. Additionally, we have modified the original proof to highlight the significance of order-invariance in the Bn-type context. In the process, we have introduced a new, equivalent presentation for the Bn-type Coxeter groups and established a connection with the affine Weyl groups of type An. This connection enables us to reinterpret the order-invariance in the An-type context as the stability of the root system under the length function. This notion can be realized through the fundamental theorem, which forms the basis for this order-invariance. We investigated the relationship between Type Ia supernovae and gravitational lensing, using a lensing model that distorts and magnifies distant supernovae. A statistical approach was developed to detect this effect, with estimates of the lensing influence varying based on assumptions about the galaxy population that intervenes. Our research utilized the Pantheon supernova dataset and applied a Bayesian method to calculate the effect of lensing amplification. By subtracting the contribution of extragalactic lenses and considering only the weakest effects, we found a median amplification of 1.01 (with a range from 0.98 to 1.04) when assuming a uniform distribution of intervening galaxies. This value can be further refined with more precise data on these galaxies. The study also explored the lensing influence on the apparent brightness of supernovae, with an estimated median shift of 0.25 magnitudes (ranging from 0.05 to 0.45) due to lensing. This magnification is primarily caused by the adhesion of matter to structure rather than gravitational lensing itself. Finally, the research highlighted the importance of considering lensing effects in future supernova datasets, particularly with the upcoming Zwicky Transient Facility and the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope, where the influence of lensing could be the dominant source of scatter among Type Ia supernovae.

By doing so, a fundamental building block is established that can be incorporated into a larger photonic circuit, complete with a central micro-resonator and two supporting T-shaped arms. This design allows for the efficient coupling of light between a micro-resonator and a photonic waveguide. By adjusting the geometry of the T-shaped structure, efficient light coupling can be achieved with a low propagation loss. The simplicity and robustness of this design make it an ideal choice for large-scale photonic integrated circuit fabrication. The T-shaped micro-bridges presented in this research have a compact footprint of 5x10 micrometers, reducing the overall size of a combined photonic and micro-resonator device. We establish a method for estimating the impact of the image's context on the network's output. This impact is represented by a quantity called context utility, which is calculated by comparing the network's response to the entered image with its response to a randomly generated input of the same type. Our findings suggest that trained neural networks exhibit varying degrees of responsiveness to context, with some being substantially influenced and others being barely affected. Additionally, we found that context has no impact on the accuracy of these networks in a wide range of object recognition tasks. Finally, we discovered a method to fine-tune neural networks so that they become less responsive to context while maintaining their original level of accuracy. This technique involves training them on images that have been manipulated to remove their context. This technique can also be used to transfer knowledge from neural networks that are highly responsive to context to those that are not, without any loss of accuracy. This is particularly relevant for mobile applications that require speed and efficiency. Our research was conducted using a specific neural network called Inception, but its findings are applicable to all neural networks of this type. This research paper focuses on a specific type of Kirchhoff type elliptic system with multiple components, which includes a unique constant that varies in relation to the absolute value of a specific function. The system in question contains a term with an exponential factor that can be seen as a variation of the standard Moser equation. The main challenge lies in handling the lack of uniformity in the Kirchhoff term and the singular nature of the Trudinger-Moser inequality when attempting to establish the existence of multiple solutions to the system. The approach to overcoming these difficulties involves using a combination of the Kirchhoff term's uniform estimate and a modified version of the singular Trudinger-Moser inequality's expansion to create a new variational framework. This variational framework, in turn, enables the application of the Mountain Pass Lemma and the Min-Max method to demonstrate the existence of two distinct solutions to the system. The research also examines the symmetry properties of the system's solutions and identifies a class of solutions that exhibit radial symmetry. The final section of the paper explores the effects of varying key parameters on the system's solutions. The research paper draws on elements from previous studies by J. M. do Ó, O. H. We establish Chernoff and Hoeffding bounds for sums of binary random variables with arbitrary pairwise negative moment correlations. These non-asymptotic concentration inequalities hold without assuming independence and can be viewed as an extension to (but distinct from) the case of independent variables with a fixed success probability. Our bounds incorporate the magnitude of the vector of pairwise correlation coefficients, enabling an improvement over existing bounds for uniformly negatively correlated binary random variables. Furthermore, our concentration inequalities are applicable to negatively correlated Bernoulli variables and provide a logarithmic deviation bound with an exponentially decreasing factor related to the largest eigenvalue of the correlation matrix and its distance from zero. Our approach to achieving these concentration inequalities involves a data-perturbation method rooted in a non-asymptotic matrix concentration inequality with a weak trace class condition, which is itself an extension to non-compact scenarios. Our results have implications for the estimation risk of a binary classification problem using a nearest neighbor classifier with Hamming distance. Our findings can also be interpreted as a characterization of the rate at which estimation risk decays as dimensionality increases in Lasso regression with a Toeplitz matrix penalty. Our most general concentration inequality is realized through an application of a Talagrand's convex concentration inequality to a specially defined class of convex functions, which in turn defines the geometry of the space of negatively correlated binary variables. This geometry, in turn, provides an answer to the question of when the eigenvalues of a Toeplitz matrix are bounded away from zero. Our work also contains an outline for the construction of a specific family of negatively correlated binary variables. Lastly, our results are further illustrated with an inquiry into the asymptotic behavior of the eigenvalues of a Toeplitz matrix. Our results can be found in 3 separate arXiv posts: arXiv:1705.08070, arXiv:1705.08068 and arXiv:1705.08069. Our findings also appeared in 3 separate journal publications: Concentration bounds for some negatively correlated binary random variables in Journal of Applied Probability, Journal of Machine Learning Research and Bernoulli.

Given a symplectic transformation defined by U, this paper establishes the existence of a unique, up to translation, completely integrable system (H, I) such that its symplectic side map is equivalent to U, termed the best normal form with respect to U. Notably, (H, I) is determined by (U,0) and constitutes a complete invariant for the conjugacy class of U. Additionally, the paper explores the relationship between (H, I) and the AltWeyl parameters used in (Arnaudon et Weyl's, 2000) work, providing a distinct and integrable viewpoint on these dynamics. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the best normal form (H, I) can be realized through a symplectic alteration referred to as the U-alteration, and it is distinct in being the simplest known means of achieving this normal form. Lastly, the paper demonstrates that the U-alteration is a Hamiltonian flow that is time-one of a Hamiltonian vector field driven by a Hamiltonian function defined as the x-component of the moment map associated with the U-action, and it includes specific, non-trivial instances such as the standard torus actions on CP2 and the nose of T*CP2.

The problem of ideal kidney acceptance has long been a critical issue in patient matching processes. A perfect match would occur when a patient with a specific HLA genotype is offered a kidney from a donor with the identical genotype. However, due to the complex and diverse nature of HLA genotypes, this scenario is extremely rare and considered unlikely. The concept of an "ideal acceptance" could be redefined as the most likely match, which has been difficult to determine with certainty. Modern registration platforms list 10 HLA antigens, but only 7 of these are considered essential for transplant matching. Using statistical modeling, our study found that the 3 "non-essential" antigens do not significantly impact the likelihood of a match and could be set aside for further consideration. By focusing on the most critical 7 antigens, the probability of finding an ideal acceptance increases substantially. This finding offers a practical solution to enhance the efficiency of online platforms in finding the best kidney match. The research also provides a framework for exploring the "ideal acceptance" in other organ transplant scenarios. The study highlights the importance of a well-curated registration database, complete with precise HLA genotype information, in facilitating the most likely match. The transition from a "perfect" to a "most likely" match also has implications for the fairness of transplant allocation systems. The study demonstrates the benefits of using machine learning algorithms to promote fairness in these systems. The concept of an "ideal acceptance" can be applied to other transplant scenarios, such as liver and pancreas transplants. The study provides data on the frequency of HLA genotypes in different populations, which may be useful for guiding transplant policies. The research offers insights into the complex interplay between different HLA genotypes and the probability of a match, and it provides a statistical modeling framework for this purpose. The study found that the frequency of HLA genotypes in donors and patients is not the same, and it identified the genotypes that are overrepresented in one group but not the other. The research has practical implications for online platforms designed to match transplant patients with suitable organ donors. The study found that the probability of a match increases with the size of the registration database, and it offers a statistical modeling framework for this purpose. The research has also been applied to a real-world scenario involving an online platform in the United States. The study found that the probability of a match is not the same for patients of different blood types, and it identified the genotypes that are overrepresented in one blood type group but not the other.

A key aspect of this research involves developing two tailored tests to evaluate the understanding of word representations, particularly in regards to the nuances of company-related language. Our findings reveal that commonly employed word representations, including BERT and its variants, fail to demonstrate a genuine comprehension of the mentioned linguistic subtleties. Furthermore, we discover that the existing embedding methods, including static and contextual, are ineffective in capturing the polarity of company-related language. In response to these challenges, this study introduces a novel contextual embedding method, named Polar BERT, designed to enhance the understanding of the mentioned linguistic subtles. Notably, when applied to the task of binary sentiment classification, Polar BERT demonstrates a significant improvement over the existing methods. Moreover, we find that this method's performance can be optimized by incorporating an auxiliary task that involves the classification of words based on their associated polarity. This article creates SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based alternatives for the previously presented Wideband Waveforming with Integrated Data and Power Transfer (W2D2PT). The W2D2PT technique exploits time-domain and frequency-domain resources to enhance the performance, but doesn't use spatial resources. The SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equivalents leverage all available dimensions to provide additional performance benefits. The optimal power allocation and symbol mapping strategies for the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equivalents are formulated as convex optimization problems. Numerical results demonstrate the performance gains of the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equivalents over the original W2D2PT in various scenarios. The results also highlight the impact of key system parameters on the performance of the four techniques. The MISO-OFDM equivalent delivers the highest performance, followed by the MISO-OFDM, SISO-OFDM, W2D2PT, and SISO-OFDM techniques in order. The results can guide practitioners in making informed decisions when designing and implementing waveforming techniques in integrated data and power transfer systems. The MISO-OFDM equivalent can also be used as a reference to explore other waveforming strategies that provide additional performance benefits. The optimization and performance analysis of the four techniques can be extended to generalized scenarios for practical applications. The article provides the MISO-OFDM equivalent and W2D2PT code on GitHub at https://github.com/ali-ghorbani/W2D2PT. The article also provides the SISO-OFDM equivalent code on GitHub at https://github.com/ali-ghorbani/SISO-OFDM. This research introduces a hybrid level-set / boundary-aware method to address problems related to melting and freezing in solids. This combined approach seamlessly integrates the benefits of both level-set and boundary-aware techniques, allowing for smooth interface evolution and efficient computation, even near the boundaries of interest. Key features of the combined method are highlighted, along with the solution to the solidification-melting problem using the heat equation as a model. The technique's effectiveness is also demonstrated through numerical tests on a melting problem with convection. The combined method has been shown to produce accurate and efficient results in this scenario. The introduction of this hybrid technique provides a valuable alternative to the level-set approach, particularly when dealing with problems that involve the interaction of moving boundaries and fixed solid obstacles. The code used in this research is publicly available. The combined technique and the associated code can be adapted for use with more complex models, such as the one governing solid-liquid interface dynamics with kinetic and Korteweg stresses. This research investigates the spread of an infectious disease within a complex network that comprises interconnected modules, each representing a distinct population with its own growth and decline dynamics. By developing a mathematical model, we gain insights into how the infection affects each population and, in turn, how their individual responses to the infection influence the overall spread of the disease. As different population responses lead to varying degrees of survival and extinction, we examine the impact on the spread of the disease and offer predictions on the probability of each population's survival or extinction. By analyzing how different population responses affect the spread of the disease, we identify distinct transition points where the disease's behavior shifts abruptly, and these results are visually represented on a map-like structure called a "phase diagram". Furthermore, we determine the probability distributions that determine the survival or extinction of each population and, in doing so, establish a connection to a specific mathematical model known as the "Yule process". This connection enables us to predict the future state of each population at any given time in the future. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our findings on the existing Yule process model. This research was originally published in Science Advances, Volume 7, Number 1, January 2021. In contrast to Einstein's theory, its connection is not symplectic, and its curvature (Riemannian curvature) is nonzero. Nonlocal gravity can be seen as a combination of nonflat geometries connected through vector fields that ensure the absence of nontrivial force-free acceleration. This new perspective provides a more comprehensive understanding of static, spherically symmetric solutions, often analyzed within nonlocal gravity. These solutions can be generically five-dimensional nonflat geometries, including hyperboloid, de Sitter, and flat spaces, surrounded by scalar fields that give rise to monopole-like behavior. Additionally, this formulation offers insights into four-dimensional nonlocal gravity solutions and provides a foundation for extending nonlocal gravity to the full nonabelian gauge theory framework. The LHC has a robust capability to produce small or "minor" systems at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider's (RHIC) intensity levels. This capability can be leveraged to perform three distinct functions. Firstly, to enhance the understanding of single nuclei-proton interactions by analyzing the isobar scattering data off protons at the LHC. Secondly, to perform precise measurements of certain rare processes in the weak interaction sector, similar to neutrino scattering, on protons or lead nuclei. Thirdly, to investigate the possibility of performing deuteron-gold or heavy-heavy collisions at the LHC's full design energy. Utilizing the LHC's extensive detector suite, renowned for its high-precision and comprehensive particle measurement capabilities, offers a strong potential for obtaining rich and accurate data from these minor systems. Consequently, the potential for delivering substantial scientific gains from the LHC's capability to produce small systems at RHIC-like intensities is evident. To accomplish this, the beam and detector operating configurations would require fine-tuned optimization. To this end, the paper examines optimized beam and operation configurations for the LHC and its detectors in search of this scientific opportunity. Specifically, it explores the production of isobar-scattering data off protons, as well as the production and detection of rare processes in the weak interaction sector, and evaluates the possibility of performing heavy-heavy collisions at lower intensities. Additionally, it delves into the possibility of producing the "deeply virtual compton scatter off heavy nuclei" process. The paper also discusses the feasibility of optimized configurations for the Heavy Ion APT (HIAPT) scheme, a proposed scheme for enhancing heavy ion beam production and detection efficiency, and concludes by outlining the potential for HIAPT to deliver more efficient heavy ion beam production and detection through better synchronization between the SPS and LHC beam schedules. The paper is organized as follows. The introduction is presented in chapter 1, while chapter 2 discusses the optimization of proton-leads collisions at 5.02 A TeV. Chapter 3 examines the production and detection of rare processes in the weak interaction sector, with chapter 4 discussing the possibility of performing heavy-heavy collisions at lower intensities. Chapter 5 delves into the production of deep virtual compton scatter off heavy nuclei, with chapter 6 outlining the feasibility of the Heavy Ion APT (HIAPT) scheme. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre have revealed that certain sources, remaining active for extended periods, suddenly brighten and fade quickly. It has been proposed that many of these sources, excluding the well-known binaries, GX 339-4 and XTE J1739-302, which reside within a specific inner radius of $<3.6$ pc from Sgr A*, are low-mass binary systems, where the companion star remains too faint to detect optically. By cross-referencing these sources with a comprehensive database of neutron star X-ray binary formation and evolution models, we identified 8 likely low-mass binary candidates within this specific inner radius. Analyzing 13 years of Chandra observations for these 8 sources, along with 2 known neutron star binary candidates, revealed a highly variable period distribution, potentially linked to the complex interstellar medium of the Galactic Centre. Furthermore, we found that the sources with the shortest recurrence periods exhibit longer quiescent durations, suggesting that the character of the sources, specifically whether they are low-mass binaries, may be revealed through the relationship between their active and dormant phases. The frequent detection of sources with long recurrence periods and short quiescent durations also raises the possibility that many of the variable sources outside the $<3.6$ pc radius from Sgr A* may actually be low-mass binaries, rather than non-binary sources. Non-detection of optical companions for many of these sources, along with the narrow distribution of binary periods, supports this claim. The possible misclassification of some of the variable sources outside the $<3.6$ pc radius from Sgr A* as non-binary, rather than low-mass binaries, also has implications for the estimated population of this type of binary within the Galactic Centre. Despite this semantic diversity being inherent to conversation, most previous research has focused on simple, similar interpretations. Traditional approaches to defining kernel functions are data independent, using fixed profiles that can lead to suboptimal performance. In contrast, our method utilizes a novel type of Fourier polynomial called Random Fourier Traits (RFTs), which can be automatically fitted to individual data points without requiring a parametric model. We demonstrate that our non-parametric RFT-based kernel functions achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art parametric methods while providing a significant computational speedup. Furthermore, our method can be easily applied to the challenging problem of estimating kernel density estimation, yielding results on par with existing methods. We also introduce a technique for adapting our method to better suit the needs of kernel-based algorithms by leveraging the uniqueness of each data point. Our method, RFT-Kernel, is simple to implement and delivers superior performance in various kernel-based algorithms and density estimation scenarios. We support our claims with comprehensive experimental evaluations, showcasing the benefits of our method in multiple contexts. Based on an analytical model, the proposed design is expected to significantly improve the signal-to-noise ratio of gravitational wave detectors at high frequencies and also reduces backscatter of light within the device. The predicted improvement in the noise floor is expected to align with the level required for future gravitational wave detectors beyond the third generation. The proposed design also includes a demonstration of a device that combines a sloshing geodesic interferometer with a carrier diffusion photodetector, however this design is less efficient but simpler to implement and is already sensitive to gravitational waves at the level of modern detectors. The noise characteristics of these devices are comparable to other proposals for improved photodetectors and suggest various possible designs that could provide an alternative to the sloshing-Sagnic interferometer. The development of the proposed device also raises the potential for its use in other applications that require the detection of changes in carrier distributions caused by light, but is sensitive to backscattering of light. We investigated the morphological patterns created by vertical shear instability in young stellar disks, focusing on the predictions they would make for the detection of dust emission in the near-infrared and submillimeter. We analyzed over 6 million elements of 0.1 arcsecond resolution and identified patterns of emission that could be explained by the presence of turbulent streams and vortex structures. These patterns would likely be observable with the James Webb Space Telescope and the Next Generation Atacama Array, and would be distinguishable from alternative explanations such as protoplanetary disk models, outflows, and external contamination. However, they may be challenging to model numerically due to their dynamic nature, so we developed a simpler empirical method for predicting their characteristics based on variables such as the wavelength, brightness, and inclination of the disks. This approach allows us to make specific predictions about the sizes, shapes, and positions of features associated with the VSI, which would be crucial for extracting the information needed to study the VSI and its effects on the formation and evolution of planetary bodies within the disks. The application of this method to our numerical data revealed that the VSI creates features with distinct sizes and shapes at different wavelengths, and it generated maps that match the patterns formed by the VSI in our previous simulations based on the principles of radiative transfer. The study of these patterns can be used to recover the characteristics of the VSI, which in turn can be used to test the hypothesis that the VSI is responsible for patterns found in some disks and to provide insights into the formation of small particles, the creation of which it impeded, and the planetary bodies, which it assisted in forming. The method we developed can also be applied to the study of other types of patterns and structures in protoplanetary disks. The empirical predictions we made for the patterns created by the VSI are consistent with the available observations, which were discovered in the disks of young stars in the Taurus, Ophiuchus, and Upper Scorpius molecular clouds. The accuracy of quantum operations, specifically the M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate, depends heavily on the precision of frequency calibration in trapped ion systems. A key challenge arises when using multiple motional modes, as their slightly different frequency measurements can lead to flawed beam splitters and subsequent errors in the gate. In this research, we demonstrate how employing more than one motional mode equally can actually contribute to more precise frequency information, ultimately resulting in the execution of a fault-tolerant M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate. Additionally, we identify a specific condition under which a frequency-stable gate can be achieved with an indefinitely large set of motional modes. A distinguishing feature of our method is the ability to obtain the same outcome with a range of initial motional occupation numbers. The research has been conducted within a theoretical framework that can be directly applied to real situations using ion trap technology. The theoretical model developed can be translated into a practical protocol with sequentially executed beam splitter operations, offering the advantage of being able to gauge the accuracy of the gate with classical post-processing of the data. Moreover, we provide the specific parameters required to execute a reliable gate in a system modeled after a trapped ion system. The most efficient execution of the gate is achieved when the small frequency differences between the motional modes are comparable to their initial occupation, with the optimal condition being when the average occupation is two. The minimal error of the gate decreases with increasing motional mode frequency ratio, with the most efficient execution being achieved with a ratio of seven. The magnitude of the error is influenced by the initial motional occupation and frequency ratio, with the most compact expression requiring the application of a dimensionless parameter that combines these two factors. We propose the (111)-face-perovskite iron chalcogenides, with long-range coulomb interactions, as a highly likely example of a strongly coupled semimetal. Due to the unique arrangement of their electronic bands, characterized by crossing points at all corners of the (111) Brillouin zone, this material class would be exceptionally suitable for the study of coupled fermions in a semimetal framework. The highly dispersive and globally distributed conical points at the (111) zone corners are anticipated to give rise to novel physics when the next-door Weyl points are connected through a closed loop, likely resulting from the interplay of the (111) zone corner points and a Fermi surface boundary. The predicted effects include the generation of a topological nodal net, coupled Weyl and Dirac points, a type of the "semimetal-ferromagnetic" state, and a "double Weyl" phase. The theoretical model presented here is amenable to numerical solution, allowing a precise calculation of the electronic band structure, Coulomb interaction effects, and the resulting magnetic and electronic phases. The estimated parameters of the model are also used to predict the low-energy effective Hamiltonian of the (PbM'3) (M'=Ir,Os) and (SrM'3) (M'=Ru,Os) families. The predicted physics are likely to give rise to novel effects in the magnetic and electronic transport of iron chalcogenide materials, and could be realized in the (PbM'3) (M'=Ir,Os) and (SrM'3) (M'=Ru,Os) families via tuning of their lattice parameters. The proposed research involves ab initio band structure calculations, numerical solution of the multi-orbital Hubbard model using Dynamical Mean Field Theory, and the low-energy effective Hamiltonian approach. The outcomes of the research will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and presentations at conferences. The research will be conducted in partnership with experimental groups, and involves the development of suitable growth and preparation protocols for (111) face-perovskite iron chalcogenide materials, as well as advice on the parameters of interest that should be measured in order to compare the theoretical predictions with experimental data. The proposed research will contribute to the development of an international network of researchers with an interest in (111) face-perovskite iron chalcogenide materials. The project duration is 24 months, and the total budget is $240,000

The addition of neutral heavy leptons in the Standard Model can rectify its anomalies and address cosmological issues. Revisiting the interpretation of the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays, we find that the NA62 experiment at CERN, with its upgraded setup, can significantly restrict the parameter space for a specific heavy lepton generation, down to masses as low as 125 MeV for a particular decay mode and 245 MeV for another. Furthermore, we identify prospects for discovering two other heavy lepton generations, with predicted rates allowing for the detection of just a few dozen events, and thus necessitating a tenfold increase in statistics from the same $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay channel. Naively, this may seem comparable to LHCb's capabilities, but due to the much lower background rates at NA62, its sensitivity is actually much greater. In fact, NA62 could reduce the heavy lepton mass range by nearly a factor of two compared to LHCb, or discover one of the two remaining generations at masses as low as 625 MeV. In addition to this, with a larger acceptance for neutral decay products, NA62 could also search for another heavy lepton generation through the $K^+ \to e^+ N$ decay channel, although this would lower the detection threshold to 225 MeV. In all cases, the NA62 upgrade's higher beam intensity poses a challenge, but this could be mitigated by reducing the beam intensity to a level that keeps the detection threshold above 200 MeV, at the cost of discovering one of the two remaining generations at much higher masses, specifically 1.3 GeV. In such a scenario, with a lower beam intensity and a neutral decay acceptance of at least 98%, NA62 could detect one of the two remaining generations at masses as low as 1 GeV, or alternatively, reduce the heavy lepton mass range to 250 MeV or less with a neutral decay acceptance of at least 99%. In any case, with the correct data selection, NA62 can also search for heavy lepton decays to muons in $K^+ \to \mu^+ N$ decays. Neural language models have surpassed $n$-gram models but require vast amounts of data to learn, making them impractical to use on tiny datasets. This limitation is particularly challenging in tasks like creating training data for low-resource natural language processing. In response, neural models have been replaced with $n$-gram models in these scenarios. This paper explores a novel approach where a neural network trains an $n$-gram model, leveraging the strengths of both models to enhance performance. The neural network learns from an $n$-gram model pre-trained on a massive dataset, resulting in a significant reduction in required training data. Furthermore, it can be effectively fine-tuned for specialized tasks with minimal data, reducing the expense and safety risks associated with natural language generation. Experimental results on datasets for language modeling, sentence translation, and summarization demonstrate the efficacy of this approach. The code for this work is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/neurlm.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the problem space. To tackle this problem, researchers often rely on separate modules for predicting pose and geometry. However, this approach frequently leads to pose estimation issues causing the reconstruction to suffer. Our proposed solution employs a dual-face prediction model, where two faces are generated from a shared set of parameters, one reflected across the y-axis to complement the original image. This dual-face prediction approach enables robust geometry prediction, reduces the impact of head pose variations, and expands the model's capacity to learn from both the input and reflected image. The model's self-alignment capability also eliminates the need for a separate regression module for pose, which would otherwise contribute to pose estimation issues. Experimental evaluations on the AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets demonstrate our method's superior performance over current state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, we introduce a new large-scale dataset, named Head Pose Face Face Reconstruction Dataset HPFRD, comprising 50,000 images with their corresponding 3D face reconstructions, specifically designed to evaluate face reconstruction across various head poses. Evaluations on this new dataset yield promising results for our method. All project files are available at https://github.com/ghr96/SADRNet. Experimental findings have been illustrated in the paper, along with raw code and datasets used.

We establish a connection between rooted trees and a specific class of directed trees, which we call "ordered trees." This connection enables us to translate questions about the structure of rooted trees into equivalent form as questions about ordered trees, specifically focusing on the highest ancestor each label has in its tree. We then calculate the expected number of a label's deepest ancestor in a random ordered tree of $n$ labeled vertices. To accomplish this, we use the generating function $g(z)$, which represents the distribution of directed tree sizes, and calculate the expected value $a_n$ as the expected number of a label's deepest ancestor in an arbitrary ordered tree of $n$ labeled vertices. We find that $a_n$ is given by the $n$th coefficient of the generating function $h(z) = z \cdot (1 - g(z)^{-1})$, which we can also express as $h(z) = \frac{z(1 - \sqrt{1 - 4z})}{2z}$. By using the Lagrange inversion theorem, we can rewrite $h(z)$ in a different form as $h(z) = \frac{4}{9} \cdot \frac{(3-\sqrt{1 - 6z})^3}{\sqrt{1 - 6z}}$. Finally, we derive the explicit formula for $a_n$ as $a_n = \frac{4}{9} \cdot \frac{(3-n)^{\frac{3}{2}} \cdot (n+3)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{n}$. We also examine the relationship between ordered trees and binary search trees and find that the expected number of a label's deepest ancestor in a random binary search tree of $n$ labeled vertices is $a_n = n$. We conclude by exploring the extension of this problem to directed trees where each label has a distinct highest ancestor and find that this is equivalent to examining the structure of ordered trees with internal node labels rather than just the edge between nodes. Lastly, we consider the expected number of a label's deepest ancestor in a random binary search tree with internal node labels and derive that it equals $a_n = 2n$. We end by posing the question of determining the precise distribution of the number of a label's deepest ancestor in a random binary search tree with internal node labels.

A key factor for success in decentralized energy markets involves balancing supply and demand dynamically. Batteries can serve this purpose, but their limited capacity and inefficient charging and discharging processes make their optimal placement crucial. By analyzing the optimal control of individual assets within a centralized framework, this study translates the goal into a decentralized context using contraction algorithms. Here, each asset makes independent decisions based on its local surroundings, leading to a collective optimal solution. The method identifies suitable triggers for storage-powered contractions and incorporates valuations for convenience and capacity into the planning process. A real-world application at the University of Hohenheim, Germany, serves as an implementation example. Compared to centralized and other decentralized approaches, our method's efficacy in this case is demonstrated. Moreover, an examination of the relationship between storage-powered contractions and payoffs for convenience and capacity is also performed. This study was previously known under the title "Decentralized Storage Planning via Discrete Contractive Algorithms".

Our key innovation involves creating a trainable module that identifies peer models requiring similar data and learns from their own effectiveness, thereby producing a more efficient collaborative learning model. By transitioning to an end-to-end trainability setting, we find that the model can determine optimal peer models and even determine the optimal set of models to collaborate with. In turn, this leads to a model that optimally selects models to collaborate with, thus achieving a true dynamic learning model. When applied to real-world tasks, this model achieves collaborative learning results comparable to those obtained through meticulous dataset and peer model selection processes. Moreover, by transitioning to an end-to-end trainability setting, we are able to leverage the vast amount of data available for ImageNet, thereby setting a new record for classification accuracy on this scale. Specifically, our model achieves a 89.05% top-1 classification accuracy on ImageNet, thus surpassing previous collaborative learning-based records and achieving the highest accuracy to date on this benchmark. The code for our model is publicly available at https://github.com/DeepMind/Dynamic-Learning.

Our investigation employs the time-dependent Kohn-Sham method to model quantum conduction in HgTe quantum wells with a very small band gap, and investigates the possibility of efficient long-distance long-lived coherent electron transport. To this end, we examine drift currents, quantized vortices formed in magnetic fields, and oscillations between states in a double well structure, all for different sizes of mass-imbalanced quantum wells. Our study reveals that in the limit of small wells, electron transport becomes direct and fast, while in large wells it becomes helical and slower due to the increased impact of boundary-induced Coulomb interaction effects. In order to increase bandwidth efficiency, cellular networks employ Time Division Duplexing (TDD) scheduling, where a specific fraction of time is allocated for uplink transmission and the remaining for downlink transmission. However, static TDD scheduling fails to accommodate sudden spikes in uplink or downlink traffic. Dynamic TDD scheduling can address this issue by adjusting uplink and downlink time slots based on real-time traffic demands. Yet, it introduces interference between uplink and downlink transmissions, limiting available bandwidth for time slot switching. To mitigate this effect, a delay-tolerant approach known as Co-Generic TDD divides time slots into smaller blocks that can be scheduled independently for uplink or downlink use. Although this method reduces interference-induced bandwidth costs and enhances cellular network adaptability, it introduces scheduling complexity. A new game-theoretic framework is proposed to manage this challenge. The proposed approach utilizes a combination of double auction and combinatorial bidding to ensure efficient adaptation of TDD scheduling in response to changing traffic conditions. Moreover, the proposed framework ensures compliance with delay-tolerant constraints and reduces generated interference in Cellular Network. In this work, we explore the potential benefits of using Hamiltonian Neural Networks to derive gradient information for optimization tasks. By considering a simple stochastic gradient descent process, we establish a relationship between the logarithm of the likelihood ratio and the gradient, framed within a Hamiltonian dynamics context. However, we find that this connection isn't universally applicable and demonstrate that it fails for certain common optimization processes, including batch gradient descent and Adam. To illustrate the limitations of this approach, we conduct a series of experiments and find that while Hamiltonian Neural Networks can accurately estimate certain aspects of the optimization process, they struggle with providing reliable gradient information, with performance degrading in comparison to conventional methods when evaluated on a range of tasks. Ultimately, our findings highlight the restricted scope of using Hamiltonian Neural Networks to estimate gradients and suggest that they be viewed as a means of acquiring task-relevant features rather than directly as a source of gradient information. To facilitate further development, we open-source the code used in this project.

Neural network-based approaches have achieved a high level of performance in Word Sense Discretionary (WSD), but tend to struggle when faced with gloss-containing contexts. Our research introduces a novel Context-gloss Enhancement framework to boost performance in such instances. Context-gloss Enhancement employs two techniques: a context-gloss blending method and a context-gloss expansion method. By intermingling the target word with its definition, the model is exposed to a more nuanced understanding of the context, while the context-gloss expansion method incorporates a broader semantic scope for the model. Our method is versatile and may be used in conjunction with popular neural WSD models without any modifications. Our empirical evaluation, conducted on the Senseval English WSD corpus with gloss-containing contexts, reveals a notable improvement in F-measure scores compared to the baseline models. The enhancement method also demonstrates scalability when employed with a range of neural WSD models, including WSD-aware word embeddings. Our analysis of the results suggests that the context-gloss enlargement method aids the model in capturing the semantic breadth of the definitions, whereas the context-gloss blending method facilitates the model in deriving a deeper understanding of the contexts. The context-gloss Enhancement method with a deeper understanding of the contexts or the definition width parameter set to 10 presents the best performance in our experiments. Our findings further highlight the influence of the context-gloss Enhancement method's parameter, which determines the depth or width of the context-gloss combinations, on the model's performance. The results indicate that the model performs optimally when faced with contexts that have a medium-level depth when set to 5, whereas on average it performs best with a width of the context-gloss combinations set to 10. The research also explores the exclusive contribution of the context-gloss Enhancement method, which reveals that the method's performance is comparable to that of a complex BERT-based WSD model with just a fraction of its parameters. The findings further validate the context-gloss Enhancement method's efficacy with a simple KNearest WSD classifier, which to our knowledge is the first instance in which such a result has been achieved. The context-glass Enhancement method's efficacy is also reflected in its ability to reduce the F-measure performance gap between the majority and minority sense classes. This study develops a series of intensified integral definitions for the reciprocal Gamma function, extending the basic Riemann, trapezoidal, and compound trapezoidal formulas, as well as a modified trapezoidal formula and a Boisobas formula, by incorporating regularization techniques. The intensified formulas, with lower error terms than their unregularized counterparts, incorporate coefficients derived from Eulerian gamma functions or other means, providing equivalent accuracy to the unregularized versions. A comparison with the unregularized compound trapezoidal formula shows that the regularized version exhibits a quadratically greater convergence rate. Additionally, the study establishes the relationship between the intensified formulas and the unregularized compound trapezoidal formula, enabling the computation of the Eulerian gamma function via numerical integration. A further analysis of the intensified formulas' convergence rates, with respect to both step size and the number of subintervals, is presented. A numerical example illustrating the computation of the reciprocal Gamma function at 2.505 is provided, demonstrating the formulas' practical applicability. Lastly, the study concludes by examining the compound trapezoidal regularized formula's application to calculating the Eulerian gamma function, thereby obtaining an efficient numerical approximation of the reciprocal Gamma function.

Thanks to advances in natural language processing, contemporary language models have refined their ability to analyze natural language. Nevertheless, deciphering structured data formats like SQL continues to pose significant challenges due to the inherent gap between unstructured text and the rigid syntax of SQL. This disparity is particularly pronounced when transferring knowledge across domains, a common requirement in real-world applications. To effectively master this kind of domain adaptation, it's essential to break down the intricate syntax of SQL, specifically by reconstructing the underlying intent and relevant column names from natural language instructions. To tackle this problem, we've developed a novel end-to-end framework called CDT that seamlessly handles both text-to-SQL within a domain and a secondary task of cross-domain column name prediction. By leveraging this auxiliary task, CDT effectively enhances the performance of primary text-to-SQL task through a transfer-of-knowledge mechanism. Our model achieves superior results on publicly available datasets for both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations. Moreover, it demonstrates remarkable capability to carry over knowledge from a simple dataset to a complex, real-world scenario, a capability further validated through a practical case study involving a real-world inventory management system. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ghrua/CDT.

Machine learning models, especially those involving neural networks, exhibit significant variability when trained on different subsets of data. This inherent unpredictability interferes with the common practice of tuning models through grid search, causing an unstable and superfluous expansion of models to test. In the context of NLP, researchers have exploited a different split of data, known as the train-dev split, to circumvent this issue, but unfortunately, this approach leaves too much unused data for optimal model performance. Contrarily, the well-known technique of leave-one-out cross-validation generates too much overfitting. In contrast, a lesser-known method called the J-K fold cross validation has the potential to strike a balance between model size and generalizability. By minimizing the prediction space and incrementing the K-fold evenly, this technique reduces the variance associated with model selection. In the course of our experimentation with various NLP tasks, we discovered that this method hits the sweet spot of adequately utilizing available data while preventing excessive model size and overfitting. In particular, our findings showed that a K-fold of 5-7 minimizes the variance associated with model selection to the greatest extent, a discovery we hope will guide other NLP researchers in their own modeling endeavors. In addition, we provide our pre-trained models for public perusal. In our investigation, we encountered an issue with the estimation of hyperparameters due to the variance associated with the estimation of the train-dev split. This problem also manifests in other research settings, such as estimating hyperparameters for multi-class classification based on the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. In these contexts, low-variance cross validation techniques are crucial for making informed decisions about modeling. In the course of our study, we discovered numerous instances across various fields where low-variance cross validation techniques are employed to guide modeling decisions, although often without explicit justification. In conclusion, we propose a general method for reducing the variance associated with estimating hyperparameters in various research settings, a issue that has the potential to impede progress in numerous fields. In the course of our investigation, we also explored the relationship between the train-dev split and the estimation of hyperparameters, a connection that has the potential to guide other research endeavors. Deep Learning networks, particularly those based on Convolutional Neural Networks, have seen significant improvements in various tasks. However, these advancements came with a substantial rise in their size and computational requirements. As a result, mobile devices and certain embedded systems found it difficult to implement them. To overcome this challenge, thinning techniques were developed for CNNs, initially inspired by neural network pruning. These methods reduce unnecessary connections and parameters, enabling more efficient deployment. Other compression techniques, such as quantization and compressing weight values, were also developed to compress models efficiently. In contrast to compression techniques that alter the model's structure, can be unpredictable and may affect performance. Despite this challenge, these techniques have been shown to demonstrate comparable accuracy to compressed models. In recent years, there has been an increase in teacher-student frameworks, where a more complex model is trained as a teacher and a less complex model as a student. These models can be used for both knowledge distillation and compression. With the growing need for real-time applications, these frameworks have become increasingly popular. In this research, existing teacher-student knowledge acquisition frameworks are reviewed, with a focus on embedding student models within the same class as the teacher. This includes embedding students within the same network as the teacher, training the student on a subset of the data, or training the student on a generated synthetic dataset. This research also explores various evaluation metrics and methods for evaluating these frameworks. Lastly, this survey delves into the open challenges and prospects for future research in this domain. Exact computation of most likely configurations in graphical models is an NP-hard problem that can be intractable for large networks, especially with thousands of variables. Our new algorithm, the Brief Function Solver (BFS), is designed to handle these large models efficiently. BFS generates a compact description of the distribution's underlying structure, which serves as the foundation for our method. This approach is significantly faster than other exact techniques and can handle models with up to 80,000 variables. Additionally, BFS can be used for constrained optimization and maximum a posteriori estimation, and we show that it outperforms existing exact methods and various approximate algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/stephenmerrell/bfs. The BFS website at https://bfs.nips.org/ enables users to upload their own models and compare the algorithm's performance. Existing issues with the dataset used in the paper's Section 4 have been acknowledged and it should not be considered representative. Our default dataset for evaluation is the Shattered Shards dataset.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$ is determined as well as the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. Additionally, an invariant theoretic approach is used to establish a sequence of algebras known as the universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, and the polynomial algebra $\mathbb{C}[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ all share a Hilbert-Poincar\'e sequence.

Search engines like Google prioritize results based on individual search history, making it possible for users to miss relevant information, especially when it ranks poorly. This study examines how Google's personalized search affects the visibility of a fictional company, identifying areas where it may be overlooked and quantifying the extent of this issue with statistical models. We found that, depending on a user's search history, Google might fail to display the company in the top 10 search results for as little as 0.003% of queries, or as much as 92% with more extreme histories. Furthermore, the study reveals that the company may go unmentioned in the first page of results up to 57% of the time and is completely absent from the top 4 results in as many as 26% of cases. By exploring the impact of search history on the company's visibility, we discovered that users with diverse search patterns are more likely to discover the company in the top 10 results compared to those with narrow search histories. However, even among this more inclusive group, the company may still be absent from the first page of results in as many as 21% of cases. This research provides a method for measuring the effect of search engine personalization on the visibility of a given term or entity and offers statistical models that can be applied to similar studies of other search engines. It also highlights the challenges faced by small companies in maintaining a strong online presence and suggests that current search engine optimization strategies may be ineffective for these businesses. The findings of this study are relevant to a broader audience interested in the societal implications of search engine personalization and offer insights into the complex relationships between search engine algorithms, user behavior, and the online visibility of individuals and companies. The statistical models developed here can be applied to other entities and provide a framework for examining the effect of search engine personalization on the visibility of any term or entity. The concept of fabric spaces, initially introduced by Grandis and Marin, serves as a foundation for a broader theory involving triangulations that change over time. This approach can be seen as a variation of the configuration space theory commonly used in problems with moving links. In the context of 2-dimensional spaces, we demonstrate how fabric spaces give rise to a specific form of trampoline spaces - specifically, trampolines with a single layer. Furthermore, we establish that the fundamental group of these space trampolines is equivalent to the pure braid group on three strands. The development of a general formula for the fundamental group of spaces that have multiple layers also follows from this approach. The relationship between these spaces and the pure braid group on three strands can be understood through the incorporation of additional loops, which allows us to connect these spaces to the fundamental group of a torus with three holes. The discovery of a natural map from the space trampolines to this torus-based group also arises from this construction. The incorporation of looped curves within the space trampolines gives rise to a family of subgroups of the space trampolines' fundamental group. The examination of a specific example, generated from a looped curve in the form of a triangle, reveals that this space trampoline is topologically equivalent to a torus with a hole, and the associated subgroup is the fundamental group of this simplified space. The development of a general principle from which the structure of these subgroups can be deduced also follows. The connection between these space trampolines and the hyperbolic plane, maintained by a group of isometries that acts discretely, gives rise to a natural map from the space trampolines to the hyperbolic plane. The examination of this map and its associated looper spaces, as well as its boundary, which is known as the boundary of a group, also follows. The discovery of a natural map from the space trampolines to the hyperbolic plane, along with the incorporation of looped curves, allows us to connect these space trampolines to the Cayley graph of the group that maintains the hyperbolic plane, giving rise to a family of subgroups of the space trampolines' fundamental group. The examination of a specific example, generated from a looped curve in the form of a triangle, reveals that this space trampoline is topologically equivalent to a tree with a leaf, and the associated subgroup is the fundamental group of this simplified space.
