Our research was conducted using high-resolution imaging and a combination of small and large particle sizes in the granular layer. With the camera, we accurately measured the object's position and the behavior of individual grains surrounding it. By analyzing the movement of each grain, we were able to determine the forces exerted on the object and the granules, and how they varied with the speed at which the object was moved. Furthermore, we computed the drag force experienced by the object, taking into account the angle at which the force acts in relation to its long axis. Surprisingly, we found that this angle is significantly greater when moving through a layer of small particles than one composed of large particles. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically focusing on triangular flow in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at various speeds. By conducting a separate over 4-8 GeV in center-of-mass energy, we discovered that the anisotropic initial geometry exhibited triangular symmetry, which was consistent across both collision types. Furthermore, we found that the anisotropic initial geometry and subsequent triangular flow exhibited similar dependence on transverse momentum density, in contrast to oval-shaped anisotropic initial geometry observed in LHC collisions. Additionally, we extracted freeze-out surfaces from our simulations and verified that the anisotropic initial geometry underlying triangular flow was genuine, not a result of surface effects. Our findings are consistent with the idea that high-speed collisions frequently generate irregular, tri-angular patterns of quark gluon matter, and that the same underlying physics applies to Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. However, within the range of speeds we studied, we did not observe significant dependence on nucleon-nucleon pair collisions. Our research also highlights potential for tri-angular flow in lower-speed collisions, such as proton-proton collisions, and emphasizes the importance of distinguishing between oval-shaped and tri-angular patterns of anisotropic initial geometry. Finally, we outline possible paths for further investigation into this phenomenon.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have developed compatible discretization techniques that maintain conserved quantities during the computational process. However, solving the resulting large linear systems obtained after these spatial and temporal discretizations using traditional iterative methods can lead to a loss of preserved properties. This study addresses this challenge by examining compatible numerical schemes paired with iterative methods that preserve inherent properties of the originals equations. Specifically, compatible schemes in conjunction with the implicit Euler temporal discretization and finite difference spatial discretization are considered. Additionally, compatible schemes with the implicit Euler temporal and finite element spatial discretization methods are also examined. The focus then shifts to employing Krylov-based methods within compatible numerical schemes, highlighting the preservation of the underlying properties when using these methods. The paper also presents theoretical support for preserving inherent properties when employing Krylov-based methods within compatible numerical schemes. Furthermore, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the preservation of the underlying properties when employing Krylov-based methods within these schemes. The results obtained from these experiments are compared with those obtained using traditional iterative methods. Understanding the human brain's anatomical structure can be complex due to its irregular three-dimensional nature. Neuroscientists use computational models to analyze the brain's mechanical properties and simulate its behavior under different loads, but these models require precise alignment with MRI data, a time-consuming and challenging process. Our research addresses this issue by developing a biomechanical model that can be aligned with ease in two dimensions while automatically accounting for the one-dimensional variations in different brain vessels, glands, and other features. This model's versatility makes it suitable for various brain analysis tasks, and our results demonstrate its effectiveness compared to traditional one-to-one volume-to-surface registration methods. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for each point in an image by comparing two images taken at different times. Unlike single-image computations like surface normal and depth estimation, no straightforward way exists to use SOTR (Single-Image Time-Series Regression) models for this task. We propose a novel framework called SFNet, which employs a self-guided approach using only a single image by defining a custom loss function that compares each point's past-to-present motion to its local spatial counterparts. This self-referential assessment ensures that the model prioritizes motion coherence over geometric coherence. SFNet demonstrates superior performance on real-world datasets DF and KITTI, surpassing existing scene flow benchmarks by significant margins. Additionally, a design on the NFNet v2 architecture, NFNet v2 SF, shows that modifying SOTR models to accommodate temporal data does not necessarily improve performance. SFNet's efficacy is further illustrated by demonstrating that using neighbor points actually hinders the model's performance. SFNet's code is available at https://github.com/ghr95/SceneFlowNet.

This research investigates the temperature-dependent structure of spin-aligned strange quark stars within a specific framework that includes a strong magnetic field. The model in question, based on the MIT bag model, takes into account the quarks' interaction with the electromagnetic field and facilitates the alignment of strange quark matter's spin. Furthermore, our study revealed that a strong magnetic field compresses spin-aligned stars and accelerates their mass collapse gravity. Additionally, the critical mass of spin-aligned stars was found to be substantially lower than that of their non-spin-aligned counterparts. By examining these features, our study provides a deeper understanding of spin-aligned stars and highlights the importance of considering their unique properties when modeling their behavior. Moreover, our findings suggest that a strong magnetic field and the alignment of quark matter's spin could potentially stabilize strange stars at higher masses, offering a possible explanation for the observed phenomenon of neutron stars with extremely high masses. Lastly, our analysis includes the calculation of the charged Toller's mass-radius equation in a simplified form, which facilitates quicker and more precise computations of spin-aligned stars' masses and radii.

In soccer, the critical moment of a match can significantly influence the outcome, making tactical decisions even more complex and sensitive to their surroundings. Current soccer research focuses mainly on standard game situations, with an overemphasis on attacking strategies. In contrast, our investigation concentrates on high-stakes soccer situations, exploring the interplay between defensive and offensive approaches. We discovered that the most effective strategy in such scenarios is often a balanced, middle-ground tactic that strikes a delicate equilibrium between defending and attacking. To excel in these intense moments, it's essential to adopt a mid-parking, mid-shooting approach. Our findings provide valuable insights for soccer coaches on how to guide their players in similar situations. Moreover, our discovery of a dynamic, fluctuating optimal policy despite the lack of external change in the game environment highlights a prevalent phenomenon in soccer known as "momentum." We hope this concept will be useful in analyzing other temporary, shifting phenomena across various domains. In the course of our research, we created a deep reinforcement learning model capable of simulating the complex, unpredictable nature of soccer. To accommodate the vast, open-ended soccer ecosystem, we developed a novel, memory-based approach that enables efficient reinforcement learning in the face of limitless external variability. This innovative technique, known as Progressive Policy Iteration, leverages the insights gained from a limited sample of the environment to guide its exploration and evaluation. By doing so, it focuses its attention on the most critical aspects of the environment and prioritizes the development of a robust, generalizable policy. The resulting deep reinforcement learning model LeRF (Light Reinforcement Learning Framework) is designed to handle complex, open-ended domains and is capable of producing highly realistic soccer scenarios. Seismic source waveform and wavefield inversion aim to recover the accurate characteristics of source wavefields and earth media through multiple recordings of seismic data. Source waveform inversion determines the source wavefield, whereas wavefield inversion determines the earth media, and both types of inversion problem face non-unique solutions and speed limitations. Traditional full waveform inversion is computationally expensive and slow, but we propose an approach called amplified source waveform inversion, which recovers the source wavefield via an indirect method using additional information about the source wavefield. This recovery process can be done using a range of optimization methods, including quasi-Newton and deep learning techniques. By determining an optimal approximation of the source wavefield, we use it to guide an efficient wavefield inversion algorithm, such as the reduced rank version of the iterative singular value decomposition method, to recover the accurate source wavefield. This proposal can significantly accelerate source waveform inversion and, in turn, wavefield inversion, while producing comparable-quality images of the earth media. Although this proposal has theoretical advantages, it has yet to be tested on real data. In this paper, we outline the theory behind this proposal and provide a preliminary numerical experiment testing this proposal on synthetic data. The results indicate that this proposal can recover the source wavefield and, in turn, accelerate and improve wavefield inversion results. The next step is to apply this proposal to real data. A distinctive neural cell division method called interkinetic nuclear migration occurs in developing vertebrate brains. It involves the alternating migration of cell nuclei towards the surface or the interior of the developing tissue as new neurons are generated on the surface and neural tissue is formed in the interior. Until now, research has focused on complex patterns created by this phenomenon, with little attention paid to its fundamental nature. Using high-resolution imaging and advanced analysis tools, we have investigated the underlying mechanisms of this pattern in the developing zebrafish retina. Our findings suggest that this pattern results from random movement of cell nuclei rather than directed movement, and it can be explained by a simple diffusion model. This model matches the observed movement of nuclei and could be a universal principle underlying this cellular phenomenon, potentially applicable to other developing tissues. It also implies that this pattern is unstable and prone to randomness, and it requires continuous neuronal addition to maintain its structure. The retinal pattern transitions from a linear to a parabolic pattern as it develops, which can be attributed to increased speed of nucleus movement as it develops. The relationship between the distance of nucleus migration and the thickness of the developing retina also supports this idea. The ongoing movement of nuclei even after the completion of brain development adds another layer of complexity to this pattern. The widespread occurrence of this phenomenon in developing vertebrate brains suggests that it could also result from random movement of nuclei in other situations. It may be influenced by the constraints of the developing brain structure, but further research is needed to fully understand it. The term "dynamical template" has been used to describe the relationship between the distribution of nuclei and the developing brain structure, and it could be a useful concept for studying this phenomenon in other developing tissues. The movement of nuclei in the zebrafish retina also exhibits unique characteristics that distinguish it from random movement, and it may provide a model for studying the interaction between the extracellular environment and cells during development. The discovery that the pattern created by this phenomenon is unstable and prone to randomness could also provide a framework for understanding the development of the brain and the retina. The finding that the movement of nuclei in the zebrafish retina results from random movement rather than directed movement may also provide a contrast to the similar phenomenon in the developing mouse neocortex. As a result, the rotation velocity of these asteroids gradually changes over time, and in some cases, it can lead to rotational breakup or even a stable rotation state with a short rotation period. The predicted timeframes for possible rotational disruptions or a stable rotation state in the two most vulnerable asteroids are also calculated in this research. The YORP effect's strength in this case is estimated to be around 1 to 10 degrees per century squared, and it further solidifies the YORP effect's position as a key driver in the rotational evolution of small asteroids. The research also highlights the potential risks posed by artificial perturbations from spacecraft, and it emphasizes the importance of mitigating such impacts in the future to avoid similar effects on other small asteroids. A dynamic fluid's response to deformation can be understood by analyzing dynamics near equilibrium. Research has shown that the majority of non-Newtonian fluids exhibit either Newtonian-like or opposite behavior when subjected to shear and normal stresses (known as 'extensional flow'). The normal stress phenomenon exhibits two opposing phenomena: 'friction' or 'pulling', where fluids reduce friction when stretched and move further apart when compressed, or 'pushing', where they move closer when stretched and move further apart when compressed. The classification of fluids' behavior under shear and normal stresses remains an open problem. A dynamic fluid's classification requires knowledge of its normal stress response in an unknown state of deformation. Once the sign of the deformation is known, we can classify a dynamic fluid that exhibits normal stress response in an unknown deformation as 'pushing' or 'pulling'. This classification holds for any dynamic fluid, even those that behave differently in response to changing deformations. This refinement enables us to define quantum procedures that can produce sets with specified characteristics based on input predicates, using a predicate and a measure of the quality of that predicate. We then demonstrate how this measure-based predicate can be used to calculate the expected cost of a quantum procedure. Additionally, we explore the relationship between this expected cost and a more general property, validity, which is certain in the context of reliable procedures. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases during public gatherings has long been a pressing concern. Historically, events like the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic's military camp outbreaks and the 2020 NFL pro-football spread have highlighted the extreme contagiousness of some individuals. We introduce a mathematical model that accounts for these super-spreader incidents in its epidemic transmission dynamics. Our analysis examines how these incidents affect the spread of a disease during an event, including how they influence the transmission of the disease among a larger population. Our results also provide critical thresholds for mitigating measures that lower transmission risks in public settings. Ultimately, our model offers insights into the complex interplay between individual transmission risks and the massive spread caused by a single highly contagious individual. By exploring these dynamics, our model equips us with the tools to make data-driven decisions about public safety protocols in various settings. We demonstrate this by calculating the optimal ticket sales cap that prevents an event from turning into a massive spreader event. Our research provides a framework that can be applied to a broader range of epidemics involving super-spreader incidents. It does so by utilizing a recently developed mathematical model that incorporates the extreme transmission caused by these incidents. This model takes the form of a nonlinear integral equation that has been well-studied in the context of a single, closed population system but less so in an open system similar to that found in public gatherings. Our results show that events with a large, crowded audience are particularly vulnerable to super-spreader incidents. This is because they have a higher potential for massive transmission caused by a single highly contagious individual. This risk is exacerbated by events with frequent guest arrivals and departures, providing opportunities for the disease to spread to and from the external environment. This is in contrast to a closed population system where the transmission caused by a single individual has a more limited impact. This distinction is critical as it influences the public safety protocols required to prevent the transmission of the disease during an event. It also dictates the optimal ticket sales cap needed to prevent an event from turning into a massive spreader event. This cap is directly related to the transmission risk associated with each individual attendee and is calculated by analyzing the distribution of the model's parameter that determines transmission risk. This distribution can be derived from data on the crowd's composition, including the demographics of the attendees. This is made possible by employing a contrastive loss function within a contrastive loss function-based framework, which compares the model's outputs with an output model pre-trained on the target task, using a set of latent representations as the medium of comparison. Furthermore, we facilitate the method's practical utility by exploring a simple yet efficient way to map the model's outputs into the same latent space as the target task's output, thus eliminating the necessity for a vast amount of comparative data. The method's efficiency and efficacy are substantiated through the successful deployment of retrieval augmentation on multiple cross-task scenarios, including but not limited to natural language processing and computer vision tasks. We applied an advanced model that explains the behavior of 37,040 stars in the solar neighborhood by combining two stellar populations, and evaluated its effectiveness to determine the composition of 140,000 stars observed in the APOGEE database. The model's ability to accurately predict chemical characteristics for each star, coupled with its insight into underlying trends and patterns, has been demonstrated. However, small amounts of heavy-element data remain unaccounted for by the model, suggesting the presence of 9 residual elements that were likely present in the sun in its early stages but are now scarce in the solar neighborhood. The model also revealed a discrepancy in the predicted frequency of barium in the sun, offering a potential explanation for the solar anomalies in the form of variable stellar nucleosynthesis. The application of the model to the APOGEE data spanning the galaxy's center and outer regions revealed a uniform heavy-element distribution, with no noticeable difference in elements synthesized through the rapid proton-proton chain but an excess of elements produced in the carbon-nitrogen cycle in the galaxy's bulge. The model's prediction of a variable solar abundance of barium due to asymptotic giant branch stars in the galaxy's vicinity also provided an alternative explanation for the solar anomalies, arising from variable stellar nucleosynthesis rather than cometary impacts. The model's capacity to break down the heavy-element distribution within the galaxy into distinct communities shaped by its structure and evolution, coupled with its ability to account for the sun's anomalies, gives it value as a tool for understanding the formation and chemical evolution of the galaxy. The full analysis of the model's results, along with the remaining unresolved quantities within the data, is also presented. The COVID-19 pandemic spread rapidly across the globe in early 2020, leading to severe consequences and immense public interest. In China, online rumors about COVID-19 intensified during the peak period of the outbreak, necessitating the government to intervene swiftly to control their spread. To comprehend the situation, we conducted an in-depth analysis of online COVID-19 rumors in China, focusing on Weibo posts from January 7th to February 29th, 2020. Our study identified an estimated 4,500 new COVID-19 rumors daily, with over half being spread through word of mouth. We discovered that both fake news and online rumors primarily originated in the initial stages of the outbreak but saw a decline in later stages, whereas medical and conspiracy-themed rumors persisted throughout. Furthermore, our findings revealed that the primary sources of these rumors were often low-ranking healthcare officials, indicating potential security breaches in the healthcare sector. We also identified key factors contributing to the duration of these rumors' lifespan. In response to these rumors, the Chinese government implemented various measures, including deploying big data technology, offering financial incentives for tip-offs, and conducting investigations into healthcare officials. Our research highlights the importance of these measures in controlling the spread of online COVID-19 rumors in China but also notes the persistence of certain medical and conspiracy-themed rumors, suggesting that alternative strategies are necessary to address their root causes. Ultimately, our study provides valuable insights for the Chinese government on effectively managing similar situations in the future and highlights the significance of identifying and addressing the underlying sources of online rumors in the healthcare sector. Additionally, our research has implications for mitigating the impact of online COVID-19 rumors in other countries and highlights the importance of global cooperation in this regard. Lastly, our study sheds light on the enduring nature of certain medical and conspiracy-themed rumors in China during the COVID-19 outbreak and encourages further inquiry into this phenomenon.

Every day, hospitals around the world generate countless streams of patient data, incorporating over 100 different data streams from various sources, exceeding 10 Gigabytes in total. Processors powering visualisation systems, particularly those used in medical imaging, also produce extensive streams of data. Existing stream processing engines, designed to handle high-speed, time-sensitive data streams, have fallen short in addressing periodic flows efficiently. Current solutions, prioritizing real-time analysis for event-driven data, lack optimal handling for recurring, time-stamped records. This paper introduces LifeStream, a state-of-the-art stream processing engine specifically engineered to handle periodic data streams at scale. This efficiency is realized through LifeStream's novel design, characterized by the integration of multiple concurrent instances of streams within a single engine, combined with the engine's ability to utilize vast amounts of memory effectively. This design enables LifeStream to achieve remarkable performance in processing large data streams, outperforming leading stream processing engines and widely used database management systems in tests. This capacity to handle enormous data streams in excess of one terabyte in size indicates LifeStream's capability to handle complex biomedical applications involving extensive genetic data streams. Traditional coherent CPM detection requires a precise knowledge of the carrier phase, making it susceptible to phase ambiguities. This issue can be mitigated by non-coherent differential CPM detection methods. Despite the phase robustness, the detection experiences a performance degradation due to its reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection. This paper explores ways to increase the delay of non-coherent differential CPM detection by employing diverse pulse shapes and considering even-order differentials. It is demonstrated that with BPSK and QAM constellations, and specifically for 4QAM, it is possible to enhance the detection delay to over 10dB while maintaining a symbol error rate of 10^-3. The optimal even-order differential detection that minimizes the error rate for a given delay is also determined. The results can be applied to diverse environments where the delay constraint is violated, or to situations where increased delay becomes a design criterion. The paper also highlights the specific conditions under which the detection delay exceeds 10dB, a critical value for some wireless applications. The term 'delay enhancement' in this context refers to a performance milestone where the detection error rate remains under 10^-3 for 10dB or more excess delay. The paper further explores the particular design criterion of 10dB delay, the results of diverse pulse shapes including rectangular, raised cosine, and Gaussian ones, as well as the optimal even-order differential detection required to achieve this performance in various scenarios. The research indicates that both the diversity and pulse shapes have a minor impact on the 10dB delay criterion, whereas the 4QAM constellations exhibit the best delay performance among the examined ones. The 4QAM case achieves a symbol error rate of 10^-3 with a delay of 10dB or more when employing a 4th-order differentially encoded detection method. The concept of spacetime incompleteness, also referred to as quantum gravity's capability, is a fundamental requirement that arises from combining the principles of general relativity and quantum mechanics. This capability indicates that there is a limit to how low the density of vacuum can drop before it becomes impossible to define coordinates within a specific region of spacetime. In the context of a specific model that incorporates thermal fluctuations, we determine the precise threshold for this capability and demonstrate how it varies depending on both the size of the region in question and its internal temperature. Furthermore, we show that this capability is directly related to a particular type of curvature, specifically extrinsic curvature, rather than overall gravitational acceleration. In the process, we also clarify the relationship between this scenario and the principles of holographic theory. Additionally, we provide an alternative interpretation of this scenario in terms of holographic theory alone. In the process of analyzing this model, we encounter an issue with the holographic theory, describing it as "compressibility." This compressibility can be observed in the way the theory responds to an influx of matter, resulting in the formation of distinct, self-contained, and independently expanding "thermal zones" of spacetime. This phenomenon is analogous to the kind of compressibility seen in materials that changes in response to pressure applied. Creating machines that excel at human-level intelligence requires addressing the gap between superficially entered commands and underlying factual knowledge. For a machine to accurately answer a question, it must possess a foundation of general knowledge that goes beyond the specific question being asked, yet this knowledge cannot be inferred solely from the question itself. To tackle this challenge, we developed the ATOMIC database, a comprehensive atlas of fundamental knowledge consisting of over 180,000 implicit reasoning rules that connect various entities, attributes, and relationships in a network of 600,000 connections. This atlas of machine common knowledge, which underlies the majority of our Internet Annotated Knowledge (iANK) dataset of 1.5 million annotated web pages, serves as a tool for evaluating and benchmarking natural language processing systems that excel at if-then reasoning and related tasks. By leveraging this database, our results demonstrate substantial improvements in tasks such as zero-shot rule-based question answering and the challenging TextWorld game. The ATOMIC database is publicly accessible at www.atomicdataset.com. The iANK dataset used in our experiments is also publicly available at www.iankdataset.com. The code for our system is available at github.com/deanmatis/textwise.

This article investigates the asymptotic behavior of the set of natural numbers that can serve as initial positions in a horizontal line to form parking functions according to the standard recursive rule. We define a function $f_n$ as the number of parking functions that can be constructed using $n$ applications of the recursive rule, and demonstrate that $f_n$ follows an additive pattern similar to Pascal's triangle. By examining the asymptotic distribution of initial positions in parking functions formed using the recursive rule in an arbitrary horizontal line, we establish their equivalence to a uniform distribution on the interval $[0, n]$. Additionally, we provide an alternative analysis based on the recursive rule's equivalence to uniform distributions on the interval $[0, k]$ for $k$ equal to $n, n+1, \dots, n^2$ with a calculated probability, and compare our findings to existing research on uniform distributions on the interval $[0, n]$ with calculated probabilities. Lastly, we explore the asymptotic behavior of initial positions in parking functions formed using the recursive rule in a vertical line, and determine their distribution as a sum of unit steps with a calculated probability. Lastly, we offer an open problem on the asymptotic behavior of parking functions formed using the recursive rule in a diagonal line. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a gate-voltage-dependent critical thickness for coherent quantum phase slips in the bulk of the material. This phenomenon can manifest as the conductance vanishes or fluctuates between discrete levels below a certain thickness, attributed to either coherent quantum phase slips or Coulomb obstruction. Here, we propose an explanation for the observed behavior based on the occurrence of coherent quantum phase slips at the ends of the nanowires, specifically within the 1-10 nm junctions at their termini. We calculate the conductance thickness scales and fluctuation levels due to coherent quantum phase slips in these junctions and find they match our experimental findings. Consequently, our analysis eliminates the need for the previously proposed Coulomb obstruction explanation. Additionally, we provide a framework for calculating the conductance thickness distributions associated with the junctions, offering a means to differentiate between this coherent quantum phase slip scenario and Coulomb obstruction based solely on thickness measurements. This approach is applicable not only to NbN nanowires but also to superconducting carbon and silicon nanowires with similar junction structures. Further research may involve modifying the nanowire fabrication process to reduce the size of the junctions and thus potentially eliminate the conductance fluctuations and thin-layer behavior.

In applications such as video surveillance, view changes often occur, changing the visible perspective of what is observable in a video sequence. Video prediction research focuses mainly on forecasting subsequent frames from a given frame without considering view transformations. In contrast, we present an approach that simultaneously anticipates both the visual perspective and upcoming frames in a video sequence, taking into account possible view changes. A novel dual representation framework, comprising an independent past and future network, effectively captures the distinction between past and future frames. This framework generates both the upcoming frames and predicts the future viewing perspective based on the current frame, considering the possibility of a view change. A dual attention mechanism in the past network identifies distinct patterns in past and future frames, while a temporal transition module in the future network models the temporal evolution of the frame sequence. The transmission of diseases during public transportation poses an significant problem, particularly in densely populated cities with limited ventilation systems in buses. Since urban buses frequently stop and change passengers, a crucial factor affecting the spread of illness within this environment is the mixing pattern of air. Some researchers suggest that a well-mixed model adequately captures air dynamics during bus travel, while others propose a plug flow model as a more accurate representation. This study investigates the validity of these mixing models by examining how different bus ventilation scenarios, including open and closed windows, influence the spread of a disease among passengers. It also explores the implications for public health policies aimed at controlling the transmission of diseases during bus travel. By analyzing existing experimental airflow data and numerically simulated models of bus ventilation systems, our research finds that the dynamics of air mixing vary significantly, ultimately supporting the use of the plug flow model over the well-mixed framework. Consequently, reducing the maximum allowed distance between individuals on a bus by one meter can decrease the transmission rate by at least 50%. Given that urban buses generally operate at high transmission rate limits due to their compact design, this finding has practical implications for public health officials tasked with mitigating the spread of diseases during bus travel. It also highlights the importance of improving bus ventilation systems to prevent the transmission of diseases. The spin-orbit proximity effect in layered structures composed of a non-magnetic material surrounded by a ferromagnetic layer has been successfully utilized to create a gradient of spin-orbit torque magnitude. However, the actual degree to which the spin-orbit torque is influenced by the proximity effect near the interface, as well as the effect of the interface on the spin-orbit torque, particularly for a interface between bulk bismuth and cobalt layers, remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the spin-orbit torque and other possible effects caused by the interface on the bulk Bi layers. By comparing the resistance, magnetization, and the spin-orbit torque-induced voltage in structures with a Bi/Co interface and those without any interface, we found that the influence of the interface on the bulk Bi layers is minimal. Additionally, we analyzed the theoretical spin-orbit torque and scattering-induced spin-orbit coupling in these structures, which includes the influence of the interface on the Bi layers' crystal structure, surface Rashba effect, and the bulk Bi layers' spin-orbit coupling. Our results suggest that the Bi layers' crystal structure and spin-orbit coupling have a negligible effect, whereas the surface Rashba effect plays a crucial role. This is consistent with our experimental findings showing that the spin-orbit torque-induced voltage and the magnetization's oscillation amplitude in the Bi/Co multilayer are explained by a surface Rashba effect rather than the spin-orbit proximity effect. Which implies that this structure can be utilized as a source of the surface Rashba effect, allowing for the demonstration of a spin-orbit torque-induced magnetization oscillation in pure bulk Bi layers. This paper investigates a higher-dimensional time-invariant fractional Schrödinger equation within a generalised Mie-like potential framework. Initially, a specific generalised Mie-like potential is defined, and then the fractional Schrödinger equation is formulated using the Jumarie type fractional derivative. By applying this derivative, the fractional Schrödinger equation can be rewritten in a form that is analogous to the Einstein-Schrödinger equation, allowing for the identification of a potential that satisfies the Einstein-Schrödinger equation when inserted into the fractional Schrödinger equation. Furthermore, this potential is found to be solvable in one-dimensional and higher-dimensional settings, with the ground state and first excited state energy levels determined for both cases. Additionally, the paper examines the ground and first excited state energy levels for a class of generalised Mie-like potentials in one and higher dimensions. The results indicate that the ground state energy levels conform to the $(-\alpha)\text{-dependent}$ power law, whereas the first excited state energy levels follow the $\text{hyperbolic}$ law. The solvability of the fractional Schrödinger equation is also compared with the corresponding complex fractional differential equation, demonstrating that the derivative type significantly influences the solvability of the equation. The paper concludes by highlighting the importance of distinguishing between different derivative types and their impact on the fractional differential equations. The results obtained in this study are applicable to a broad class of generalised Mie-like potentials in one and higher dimensions. The paper is concluded by outlining an open problem related to the ground state energy levels for the fractional Schrödinger equation within the generalised Mie-like potential framework. We're exploring the utilization of low-dose PET for patient imaging, with the aim of significantly decreasing the administered radiation while preserving image quality. To this end, we're developing a novel neural network, capable of operating in uncertain environments with varying levels of radiation doses. This network, built using two distinct components, leverages both low-dose and matched MRI data to generate PET images. The heart of the coreference resolution task lies in identifying expressions with the same meaning within a text, considering their relationship to a central reference point. Known as the "center" of each chain, determining these centers is a critical step in this process. Although a well-established framework called Centering Theory (CT) was developed to analyze such relationships, its relevance to modern neural-based coreference resolution systems is unclear. This study investigates the connection between CT and these systems by examining if incorporating CT's principles improves their performance. Our analysis takes place within the PyCoref framework, which provides pre-trained models that can be augmented with features derived from CT. By testing various combinations of these features, our study uncovers the relationship between CT and the systems it aims to enhance. Furthermore, it offers valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of these systems. Originally proposed in the 1990s, CT's ability to effectively guide modern neural-based coreference resolution systems provides these ancient ideas with new significance. This study's findings also highlight potential avenues for developing more effective neural networks, specifically by utilizing features related to the "periphery" of each chain, which were found to contribute significantly to the systems' performance. Our discovery of a subset of chains referred to as "self-chains" with distinct characteristics offers another valuable insight into the workings of these systems. Ultimately, this research on the intersection of CT and neural-based coreference resolution systems opens the door to exploring other connections between older linguistic theories and modern neural networks. Recently, wireless networks have seen significant growth, enabling widespread use of devices with location awareness. Machine learning models, particularly those based on artificial neural networks, have become popular in estimating the physical distance between devices using WiFi signals. However, training these models requires a large amount of data, making them less practical for many real-world applications. In this study, we propose a novel method for calculating the distance between devices using WiFi signals, relying on an unsupervised artificial neural network known as an autoencoder. Since this model doesn't need data on distance labels during training, it can be more easily implemented in many contexts. Moreover, we developed a separate model to predict the desired distance output, using the information encoded by the autoencoder, with satisfactory results according to our testing. This approach allows for a significant reduction in the data needed for training and improves the generalizability of the model. Furthermore, we discovered that using a single output autoencoder model provides a more accurate prediction than using a traditional supervised model. This method, along with its code, has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ali-ghorbani/WiFi-Range-Estimation-Autoencoder. Moreover, pre-trained models are available for download at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/?fuser=true&uid=104844798449528449983&usp=drive_web&tab=gd&authuser=0. Lastly, this research was conducted within the framework of the university project number 99/97245.

The phenomenon is particularly problematic when multiple beams interact within a ring. The beam disruption instability can lead to the creation of a performance barrier in particle accelerators designed for high-power applications. The source of this instability lies in the electrical current generated by an incoming beam as it travels through the ring. This induced current then causes an oscillation in the charge of a stored beam, resulting in the beam disruption instability. The degree to which this instability affects a particular beam depends on multiple factors, including the configuration of the ring, the characteristics of the incoming beam, and the filling pattern of the ring. The beam disruption instability can either shift the performance limit upwards or downwards, or even remain neutral in response to changes in the ring configuration or beam characteristics. The task of eliminating this performance barrier in Energy Recovery Linacs is complicated by the fact that there are an infinite number of beam configurations that could potentially be employed, further exacerbating the difficulty. This calculation involves a Lorentzian analysis of the self-energy correction and relies on a Lorentzian metric, with the resulting vertex expression being a function of the Mandelstam variables $s$, $t$, and $u$. We also examine the relationship between the central-emission vertex and the three-gluon vertex, with the two being distinct due to different spacetime metric implications. Furthermore, we explore the implications of conformal symmetry on the vertex expression, with the resulting coefficient being directly linked to the free field theory contribution. Additionally, we provide a comparison with the equivalent QCD calculation, with the two being distinct due to massless versus massive particle behavior. Lastly, we discuss the extension of this calculation to include two colorless fermions.

The dynamics of polymers in good solvents are significantly influenced by their architecture, and researchers have long recognized the importance of considering the local geometry of a polymer chain when analyzing its dynamics. Specifically, the rate at which a polymer end point moves in a good solvent has been found to vary inversely with the local curvature of the chain's architecture. This phenomenon is particularly evident in branched polymers, where the rate of end-point motion is slowed in regions of high curvature, such as the vertices of a dendrimer. In this study, we introduce a mathematical framework that applies this principle to polymers with complex shapes, using a statistical approach to model the distribution of end-point motion within a freely draining branched polymer. By contrast to previous models based on precise, regular geometries, our approach allows us to account for the inherent disorder in many real polymer systems. We derive explicit expressions for the rate of end-point motion at various positions within a polymer, even in the presence of tight, inaccessible regions. Additionally, we demonstrate how our approach can be applied to predict the dynamics of a polymer with a deliberately constructed "hole" or restricted area, providing a blueprint for creating polymers with tailored, asymmetrical dynamics. This research builds on previous work by eliminating the requirement for a flat interface between the polymer and the surrounding solution, and instead uses the principles of strong stretching to describe the motion of a polymer bristle. We believe this model to be more representative of reality, given the compressive forces that likely act on the interface between the solution and the polymer. Furthermore, we anticipate that this model will be particularly relevant to dynamic comb polymers, given their propensity for stretching and asymmetry. The metric dimension of a graph measures the minimum number of markers required to uniquely identify vertices based on distance information. This paper introduces a new concept, called the shortened metric dimension, which determines the minimum number of markers needed to identify vertices by considering the smallest possible distance from each marker. We examine the shortened metric dimension in various types of graphs, establishing its equivalence to the metric dimension in some cases, while also discovering distinct characteristics in others. Furthermore, we provide lower and upper bounds for the shortened metric dimension and investigate its relationship with the metric dimension and other graph parameters. Additionally, we offer guidelines for constructing minimal-sized graphs achieving a specified shortened metric dimension and analyze the complexity of this construction problem. Lastly, we discuss the connection between the shortened metric dimension and other unique identifying dimensions.

In a sequence of independent first-price auctions, each auction is contested by the same set of symmetric and privately informed bidders. We compare the expected revenue from holding a single auction to repeating the same auction in a circular manner, where the same set of bidders contest each auction in the sequence. Interestingly, implementing a cycle over a single first-price auction with private values generates the same expected revenue as if each bidder were alone in the standalone auction. Furthermore, this cycle phenomenon even yields the same expected revenue when considering non-identical and non-private value bidders. Notably, this particular cycle structure also yields the maximum possible expected revenue across all possible sequences of first-price auctions. Lastly, when considering non-private values, the cycle structure generates the highest expected revenue among all possible sequences of first-price auctions. Moreover, when bidders have non-private values, implementing the cycle structure with truth-telling as the bidding strategy achieves the same expected revenue as the optimal mechanism achievable through Bayesian mechanism design. The expected revenue gained from this cycle over a standalone auction can be substantial, especially when the number of bidders is large and their valuations are closely distributed. The underlying mechanism applies broadly, spanning various applications, including auctions for wireless communication spectra, sales of exclusive broadcasting rights, and property auctions. The cycle mechanism also offers valuable insights into the behavior of repeated games with imperfect public goods, such as the aforementioned sequence of auctions, where each auction represents an independent action within the game. The public good in question here is the collective knowledge of the existing sequence of auctions, which provides valuable information for informing decisions in each individual auction. The fact that the cycle mechanism generates the maximum possible expected revenue in such a setting with an exclusive good suggests that it may be more challenging to devise better mechanisms for this class of models than it may initially seem. The underlying theory includes the special case of the sequence of auctions, often referred to as the "chain-store" game, but with a significant distinction arising from the presence of public knowledge within the sequence of actions. We designed two distinct approaches to pinpoint binary asteroids within the solar system by utilizing archival images from the Pan-STARRS1 telescope. The first method involved contrasting the observed orbits of near-Earth asteroids (NEAs) with potential binaries, likely formed as a result of asteroid capture by the Earth due to gravitational influences. This would be evident by discovering NEAs that share nearly identical orbits with a larger asteroid population, and have a smaller companion detected within the Pan-STARRS1 images. The second approach targeted binary asteroids among main-belt and Jupiter trojan asteroids by searching for closely paired objects within the Pan-STARRS1 images, with a focus on discovering pairs that could have originated from the solar nebula but are now bound together. By applying a machine learning-based algorithm, we were able to identify 26 binary candidates among NEAs, with orbits that match 25 known asteroids, as well as 13 potential binaries among main-belt and Jupiter trojan asteroids. Verification of these findings necessitates additional observations from radar or spectroscopy. The most promising binary NEA candidate is (16) Psyche, with a companion diameter estimated at approximately 200 km. The largest binary main-belt asteroid candidate is (121) Hermia, with a companion diameter estimated at approximately 140 km. The most promising binary Jupiter trojan candidate is (4507) 1990 SV, with a companion diameter estimated at approximately 100 km. The existence of these binary asteroids provides valuable insights into their formation mechanisms. The largest known asteroid with a diameter over 10 km without a detected companion is also reported. The data and findings presented here are derived from the PS1 Science Archive and are subject to the embargo dates listed, with additional restrictions applicable to certain datasets. The discovery of these binary asteroids becomes particularly significant in the context of NASA's Dragonfly mission to Saturn's moon Titan, with a focus on searching for life, with (16) Psyche now identified as a potentially fascinating target for further study. The findings reported here are also relevant to the NASA's OSIRIS-ARPHEMER and DART missions, with (16) Psyche and Didymos being notable examples. The approach employed in this research is applicable to similar searches within the Pan-STARRS1 images for other small bodies within the solar system, with potential targets including comets and asteroid satellites. We introduce the "AI Dungeon Master's Handbook" challenge, a groundbreaking initiative that brings together two cutting-edge areas in artificial intelligence: interactive dialogue and theory-of-mind. Based on the popular Dungeons and Dragons group activity, this challenge involves a computer-Generated Dungeon Master (DM) engaging in a conversation with multiple players. Unlike traditional dialogue systems, the DM's primary goal is not simply to respond to individual queries, but rather to guide multiple independent participants towards a shared objective by presenting them with distinct challenges and misleading information. In this version of the challenge, the DM's intentions and individual players' knowledge and misconceptions about each other's thoughts are critical factors in determining success. We outline two versions of the "AI Dungeon Master's Handbook" challenge: one with a focus on learning intentions from data, and a more complex version that also considers the theory-of-mind aspects of the players' knowledge and misconceptions about each other. To solve both versions of the challenge, we rely on deep learning techniques, specifically policy-based methods, reinforcement learning, and graph attention networks. Our results show that with sufficient training data and adequate models, it is possible to successfully complete both versions of the "AI Dungeon Master's Handbook" challenge. We believe this challenge has far-reaching implications for creating more sophisticated artificial intelligence in various areas, and we make all the necessary code and data available for use by others. We also propose two variants of the challenge that could be used as platforms for hosting artificial intelligence development competitions. The "AI Dungeon Master's Handbook" challenge is a groundbreaking step in the field of artificial intelligence, and we anticipate it will give rise to a wide range of related research opportunities. We encourage other researchers to explore this challenge and related problems in their own work. The term "handbook" in "AI Dungeon Master's Handbook" refers to the comprehensive guide that is necessary for the DM to successfully complete the challenge, but we stress that this term in no way implies that the challenges posed are routine or commonplace. On the contrary, the challenges we have defined are exceptionally difficult, and we believe they are among the most complex problems yet proposed in the field of artificial intelligence. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their functional flexibility is an area that researchers are still trying to fully understand. Recent studies have shown that the spatial arrangement of knotted proteins is linked to specific bending patterns, but more analysis is needed to uncover these patterns and shed light on the relationship between knot structure and protein dynamics. In this study, we used magnetic resonance and mass spectrometry to map the conformation and chemistry of six knotted proteins and applied topological analysis to identify distinct bending pathways associated with their native states. By integrating these results with existing data on linear proteins, our findings reveal a distinct grouping of knotted proteins based on their bending patterns and chemistry, and demonstrate how topological methods can be used to select specific bending pathways from a complex and disordered population of protein states. This research paves the way for a deeper understanding of how protein knots influence their flexibility and provides a novel approach for using topological methods to explore the complex geometry of disordered populations. This approach can be applied to other biomolecular assemblies that are knotted, as well as other fields that involve the analysis of complex, embedded spaces. This study is also accompanied by an interactive three-dimensional visualization of the knotted proteins discussed in this research. This visualization was created using the tool, Coevolve. While counterfactual knowledge has been successfully demonstrated for binary decisions, numerous real-world choices involve categorizations rather than binary options. Additionally, most existing methods focus primarily on individual data points, without accounting for the counterfactual nature of nearby observations. This paper introduces the term "phrasal counterfactual" to describe statements like "If I were living in New York," and explores their potential to capture nuanced, contextual differences. We've developed a dataset comprising 10 diverse sets of counterfactual statements regarding categorizations, along with their corresponding non-counterfactual contexts. This dataset serves multiple purposes: it's the first to contain counterfactual statements about categorizations, it encompasses a range of domain types, and it includes both individual and contextual counterfactuals. We've also introduced several evaluation metrics to assess the effectiveness of counterfactual models within both individual and contextual frameworks. By leveraging the T0 large language model, we've demonstrated a significant improvement in performance when evaluating contextual counterfactual models. Furthermore, we discovered that contextual models accurately captured the magnitude of counterfactual differences, while individual models prefer binary counterfactual decisions. The data and model evaluations are available for public use.

The unique epitaxial relationships in Heusler thin films are utilized in the development of spin-orbit coupled materials and half-Heusler thermoelectric semiconductors. Graphene substrates offer an intriguing opportunity to create epitaxial relationships via van der Waals bonding, in addition to remote and pinhole epitaxy. The equilibrium between these epitaxial modes is influenced by surface free energy, strain, and lattice mismatch. It is proposed that controlling surface free energy, via the introduction of defects in the Heusler films or the graphene substrate, can produce a genuine multiepitaxial mode of growth. It is further suggested that this mode of growth can be managed to favor specific epitaxial relationships. A theoretical analysis of the epitaxial modes of Heusler films on graphene substrates is conducted, with the aim of guiding experimental design to achieve desired epitaxial relationships. It is demonstrated that both half-Heusler and full-Heusler compounds can exhibit unique epitaxial relationships on graphene substrates. It is proposed that the use of hydrogen terminated graphene substrates can prevent oxidation of the Heusler films and facilitate the formation of epitaxial relationships via van der Waals bonding. It is further proposed that the use of small Heusler crystal domains can prevent misfit dislocations and facilitate the formation of epitaxial relationships via van der Waals bonding and remote epitaxy. It is demonstrated that Co2Cr0.5Fe0.5Heusler films exhibit unique epitaxial relationships on graphene substrates, with the possibility of realizing spin-orbit coupled materials and the potential for thermoelectric applications. It is further demonstrated that Co2Cr0.5Fe0.5Heusler films exhibit an in-plane anisotropy of the lattice parameter, which can influence the epitaxial relationships with the graphene substrates. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in addressing imbalanced data sets. Nonetheless, training these models is notoriously challenging due to the instability of the backpropagation of gradients through the inverse of the latent space. We propose a novel technique based on a latent space redefinition that significantly reduces the magnitude of the gradient required for updating the discriminator, thereby substantially easing the difficulties associated with training conditional GANs. Our innovative method becomes particularly effective when employed with the binary cross-entropy loss function, enabling us to successfully train a conditional GAN even when the latent space has a vast discrepancy in scale. We have tested our method on three diverse data sets and the results show that it outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods. The emergence of powerful gamma-ray detectors has allowed the identification of gamma-ray emission from nearly all types of active galaxies. While their jets can produce high-energy radiation, only a small fraction of jets exhibit gamma-rays with energies above 1024 MeV, a range that is particularly challenging to explain due to the overwhelming cosmic background. In this paper, we propose an explanation for this phenomenon based on the alignment of magnetic fields within nearby galaxies and investigate three specific examples - NGC 1068, NGC 253, and IC 310 - each characterized by a unique magnetic field structure that is capable of converting low-frequency gamma-rays into polarized high-energy ones. By simulating the interaction between aligned magnetic fields and electrons within their disks, we found a viable pathway for producing MeV-to-GeV gamma-rays from capture disks in nearby galaxies. This theory is supported by existing observational data on the polarization of low-frequency gamma-rays and can be further tested by future telescopes with higher sensitivity to polarized signals. Moreover, this model also predicts the occurrence of high-energy neutrinos in the range of ~100 TeV in certain scenarios. This research highlights the significance of low-frequency gamma-ray monitoring in detecting high-energy radiation and the importance of magnetic field studies in understanding the physics of these phenomena. This work also paves the way for exploring the connection between high-energy radiation and the characteristics of magnetic fields within the Milky Way. This model can be applied to nearby active galaxies with strong magnetic fields, and it suggests that the known gamma-ray blazar within 2 kpc, the blazar PKS 1510-069, which exhibits a massive black hole with a small bulge, might be harboring a weak magnetic field similar to IC 310. This finding is consistent with the observation that massive black hole bulge-less galaxies exhibit weak magnetic fields. The proliferation of wearable devices for health monitoring allows the collection of biometric data without restraint. However, training a classifier on this data is complicated by data privacy concerns limiting feasible data transfer. In addition, these devices are often used in different environments by various individuals, resulting in transferred data having highly disparate contexts that can significantly compromise the effectiveness of a trained classifier. We address these challenges by developing an efficient framework called FedHealth, capable of accommodating classifiers trained on data from diverse contexts with minimal loss of performance. This framework leverages a fusion technique to combine local classifiers by weighting them proportionally to how well each classifier performs on a particular dataset, thereby accounting for differences in data quality and context. We also introduce an iterative procedure called Adaptive Bias Learning (AdBL) to gradually reduce contextual disparities during the federated learning process. Experiments conducted using real-world data from the PhysioNet20x and CardioNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FedHealth, showing it outperforms existing methods particularly in scenarios with extreme contextual variations. The code for FedHealth is available at https://github.com/ChengningYang/FedHealth.

The rapid spread of the COVID-19 epidemic has underscored the significance of mathematical modeling in informing public health policy. This paper provides an overview of prominent modeling frameworks used to analyze epidemiological data, focusing on basic reproduction numbers and compartmental models. We discuss the underlying assumptions of these models, including their ability to account for variable infection periods, the inclusion of asymptomatic cases in transmission models, and the incorporation of non-uniform mixing patterns among populations. Although these models have been successful in historical context, such as in analyzing the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic, they have also been associated with notable errors, like underestimating the severity of the Ebola outbreak in West Africa or overpredicting the speed of smallpox extinction. By examining these limitations, we highlight the need for caution when applying these models to interpret current and past epidemiological data. Additionally, we outline the importance of incorporating diverse data types, including but not limited to, genomic sequencing, into modeling efforts. The COVID-19 epidemic poses unique challenges, but also presents an opportunity to innovate and improve modeling techniques. The paper concludes by discussing the potential risks and benefits of using more advanced mathematical modeling methods, such as using machine learning to model individual behavior and complex network analysis, though such methods may lack the simplicity needed to inform rapid policy decisions. Ultimately, the most effective models will be those that strike a balance between complexity and ease of interpretation, and provide accurate predictions that account for the uncertain and ever-changing nature of real-world epidemics. Such models will be critical in helping us prepare for and respond to not only the current SARS-CoV-2 epidemic but also future outbreaks and the ongoing challenge of managing infectious disease in complex, dynamic populations. This encoding approach ensures a balance between achieving a minimal length of 6-bit nodes and an optimal distribution of data across 3 segments of the DNA strands. To enhance data durability, HDSA includes error-correcting codes in the encoding process. Furthermore, HDSA offers two strategies for updating the stored data: one that minimizes insertions and deletions of 69-base DNA fragments and another more efficient method with a lower fragmentation size of 25-base DNA fragments, but requiring more insertions and deletions of the DNA fragments. We demonstrated the effectiveness of HDSA by encoding real-world hierarchical data, including the protein structure database, and compared its performance to existing DNA storage methods in terms of data compression, encoding and decoding efficiency, and update and repair costs. The results showed that HDSA outperforms these existing methods across all metrics examined. Additionally, we applied HDSA to a real-world DNA storage use case, successfully retrieving original data from recovered DNA strands that had undergone degradation over time. The HDSA code has been made available publicly for download. The proposed 25-base fragment repair method and the encoding of the repair information added an extra 2 kilobase to the Sabanci SAKI 1000 DNA storage capacity. The reduced 6-bit node encoding method, on the other hand, resulted in a more compact encoding of approximately 1.5 kilobases. The recovered protein sequences from the repaired DNA storage matched 100% with the original sequences submitted to GenBank. A distinct DNN is trained for each reach, allowing for flexible application to varying river configurations, and it produces predictions over a limited distance range. Ultimately, our technique is designed to be used in conjunction with a traditional solver, with the DNN providing an initial, approximate answer that serves as the starting point for a series of successive, increasingly precise calculations. This note represents an initial attempt to incorporate the b-principle, a concept originating from flexible algebraic geometry, into the realm of geometric topology. A particular aspect of flexible algebraic geometry, known as the Mumford Conjecture or more specifically the Weak Mumford Conjecture, is explored in this context. By combining the b-principle with techniques from the theory of pseudocycles, we are able to prove the Weak Mumford Conjecture. This conjecture's equivalence to another statement, the Strong Mumford Conjecture, which also implies Hilbert's 16th Problem, is also demonstrated. Additionally, the note includes a discussion on the relationship between these geometric and analytic problems. Finally, it concludes with the identification of the Weak Mumford Conjecture as a principle that falls within the b-principle category, the b-principle being a broader geometric paradigm that encompasses a variety of other principles, including the additivity principle, the extension principle, the folding principle, the contraction principle, the sliding principle, the combination principle, the Whitney trick, and the extension of the Whitehead and homotopy extension principles. A key factor in these tests is the presence of highly contrasting spatial scales, which significantly impact the speed and precision of the models. In the context of a multigrid solver, the creation of a multilevel linear system involves constructing a hierarchical structure comprising multiple discrete time-stepping solutions, each defined on a progressively smaller spatial domain. However, determining the precision of this system and the time-stepping scheme requires evaluating the condition number of the system, a computationally demanding task that can be performed using various scalable methods to assess the models' accuracy and efficiency. We evaluated multiple methods for calculating the condition number of a multilevel system in different large-scale simulations, ranging from simple cardiac electrophysiology to combined cardiac mechanics and electrophysiology models, as well as models incorporating fluid dynamics and mechanics. We present a comprehensive theoretical framework for describing both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between geometric patterns formed within optical resonators and waveguides. This framework, built upon a universal mathematical platform, allows us to explore coupled phenomena in a broad spectrum of configurations, from a single pattern to intricate over-lapping multi-pattern scenarios, across a wide range of dimensions. By integrating a novel dimensionless group, we can map the behavior of these interactions across all spatial scales and any type of geometric configuration. Through this integrated approach, we uncover fundamental patterns of dynamics and stability in both linear and Kerr nonlinear systems, revealing how their overall behavior is influenced by the specific geometric arrangement and the intensity of their interactions. Furthermore, we identify a critical threshold above which patterns enter a chaotic state of instability. By eliminating the dimensionless group, we can map the dimensionless systems' behavior onto their original form, thereby providing a 'blueprint' for any individual optical resonator or waveguide. This includes examples such as micro-rings, nan-fibers, and Bragg micro-resonators, allowing them to be precisely engineered for a desired outcome. With this theoretical framework, we are also able to explore the boundary between which patterns can stably coexist and those that will instead become unstable and chaotic with the introduction of a defect or change in the geometric arrangement. This theoretical model can be applied across a broad spectrum of optical configurations and provides a precise guideline for engineering any desired pattern of behavior within these systems. This includes the creation of optical memory cells, pattern generators, and even systems capable of displaying self-organization and complex chaotic dynamics. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. In response to these challenges, a new evaluation framework, Lifelong Exploration Assessment Tool (L2Explorer), is introduced to assess lifelong reinforcement learning capabilities across constantly shifting landscapes. L2Explorer is comprised of 12 benchmark evaluation tasks that incorporate varied introduction schedules for new elements and provide comprehensive metrics, including cumulative rewards and an information-theoretic measure of task discovery. By exploring a dynamic set of tasks that incorporate both intrinsic motivations and external rewards, L2Explorer offers valuable insights into effective lifelong strategies and reveals the distinct challenges posed by dynamic introduction of new tasks. Existing state-of-the-art lifelong methods are demonstrated to exhibit limitations in L2Explorer, underscoring the need to develop more robust lifelong techniques that can address the pervasive issue of new task introductions. L2Explorer is designed to facilitate meaningful evaluations and rigorous comparison of lifelong methods, as well as provide actionable feedback for their development. The framework and individual evaluation tasks are available at https://github.com/google-research/l2explorer. The framework has been utilized to create the Lifelong Learning Challenge at NeurIPS 2020. The challenge involves selecting optimal methods for sequential, rule-based maze navigation problems characterized by their own distinct structures, designs, and patterns. The most effective methods for this particular challenge are determined through a rigorous comparison of prominent lifelong techniques. The results, along with the underlying code and challenge data, have been made publicly accessible at https://github.com/google-research/l2explorer. The code and data for the challenge include a suite of tools designed to create, validate, and evaluate the methods through intense simulation trials. The most distinguished method for this particular challenge will receive a cash prize of $25,000. The challenge is open to commercial participants. Active learning and exploration are crucial for overcoming information barriers when executing declarative processes, particularly in scenarios where accessing the full state of the world is impractical due to its size or the costs of each individual piece of information. We introduce a novel approach that efficiently identifies the most beneficial new information to acquire, either through interaction with an uncertain environment or by paying for more detailed observations of the world. This approach is suitable for a broad range of domains, including those described by uncertain logic programs and unknown state in grid worlds. We have tested our approach on both synthetic and real-world data, demonstrating its superiority to alternative methods. Additionally, our approach is computationally lightweight and easily integrable into various process frameworks. It can be used within various process frameworks, including those featuring dynamic changes to the underlying process. We have made our approach publicly available as an open-source Python package.

Determining the precise factors driving the deviation from a linear correlation between galactic stellar masses and star formation rates at high mass scales poses a persistent challenge in astrophysics. We suggest that the distinction between central bulges and disk star-forming regions, which are integral to galaxy structure, may be responsible for this phenomenon. Using a morphological star formation rate classification, we analyzed a significant $K_s$-band far-infrared data set consisting of 2129 galaxies across 0.1 < z < 2.5. By comparing unsubceted and seeded bulge-dominated galaxies, we found that the transition to a nonlinear mass-star formation rate relation occurs at lower mass scales (log(Mstar) ~ 10.4) during the distant past but at higher masses (log(Mstar) ~ 11.3) in the present day. This discrepancy may be attributed to the increased prevalence of bulge-dominated galaxies in the distant past but requires further verification. Additionally, we found that the turnover point shifts to higher mass scales with bulge growth but remains independent of dust opacity. Not all bulge-less galaxies are able to exceed this mass scale in the distant past or in the present day. The role of bulge formation in governing the nonlinear mass-star formation rate relation is likely influenced by the interplay between major mergers, gas supply, and quenching, which may vary with redshift. Systematic variations in the turnover point with galaxy population, star formation morphology, and redshift require the development of a more sophisticated model that considers the complex interplay between major mergers, star formation, and gas supply and takes the form of an analytic function that accurately captures these dynamics.
