X-ray images contain implicit information that can be used to forecast patients with COVID-19 who will require intensive care unit (ICU) admission. While radiologic assessments are often inconclusive, experts now agree they hold value in clinical decision making. We suggest examining specific features in lung infected areas that correlate with the likelihood of a patient needing ICU care. Quantifying these characteristics through machine learning analysis of x-ray images can provide a numerical ICU admission risk assessment for an individual patient. Our proposed method involves training a convolutional neural network (CNN) on a dataset that includes x-ray images with corresponding ICU admission outcomes for patients. Utilizing optimized features extracted from the CNN, we employ gradient boosting decision trees to generate a numerical ICU admission risk score from image data, enabling the direct assessment of ICU admission risk for patients with COVID-19. Our results demonstrate that both CNN and gradient boosting features contribute significantly to predicting ICU admission in patients with COVID-19, and that the proposed method outperforms existing multi-classification approaches in terms of area under receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). Furthermore, our findings indicate that the proposed method can distinguish between low and high-risk patients with an AUC-ROC of 0.85, with an estimated 85% confidence interval of 0.78-0.92. Our research highlights that the proposed method, in conjunction with laboratory and clinical data, can predict ICU admission in patients with COVID-19, and that the derived risk score correlates with existing severity assessment tools. Moreover, our findings suggest that the proposed method can differentiate between patients with mild, moderate, and severe COVID-19, with an AUC-ROC of 0.81, with an estimated 85% confidence interval of 0.75-0.87. Our proposed method comprises a risk assessment tool for healthcare professionals to utilize in conjunction with their expertise and existing severity assessment protocols. Our code is available at https://github.com/medimachinelearning/COVID-19-ICU-Risk-Score.

The concept of a global simplicial bundle can be defined using the universal property of the nerve functor, providing a straightforward and intuitive framework. Within this context, the notion of a global simplicial group can also be defined as a simplicial set equipped with specified face maps that satisfy certain compatibility conditions. We then establish that a global simplicial set is equivalent to a simplicial set equipped with face maps that form a group structure, specifically when defined using the nerve functor and natural transformations. Alternatively, this equivalence can be achieved by imposing the condition of functoriality on the nerve functor. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the global simplicial group defined using natural transformations is equivalent to a simplicial group defined using the nerve functor, providing both an internal and an external characterization of the global simplicial group property. Additionally, we derive the result that the global simplicial group is topological when considered under the weak equivalences and homotopy injections criterion. Moreover, we establish that the global simplicial group is topologically equivalent to a higher group defined using the inner automorphism functor, specifically the inner automorphism functor from the category of simplicial sets to the category of simplicial operations. Furthermore, we identify the fundamental group of a simplicial set as the global simplicial group formed using natural transformations, providing an internal characterization that implies the simplicial set is path-connected when the fundamental group is trivial. Lastly, we establish that the fundamental group of a simplicial set is topologically equivalent to the higher group defined using the inner automorphism functor, specifically it is topologically trivial when the simplicial set is path-connected. This research was influenced by the work of Grandis and Lurcat.

This paper delves into the problem of erroneous positive relationships in VRD tasks being overpredicted. We discovered that current approaches overestimate relationships due to overfitting, especially when modeling pair interactions. To overcome this, we developed a dual-path network, initially identifying potential relationships before confirming them. This prior step helps reduce pair interaction overfitting. Additionally, we introduced an external background region to model pair-specific context, further reducing false positives. Recently published research indicates that solar proton events can be decomposed into individual neutrons detected from Earth, a concept that contradicts the long-standing belief that all protons must originate directly from the sun. Our study focuses on analyzing four specific solar proton events, including one notable occurrence on November 7, 2004, when a massive solar flare produced an exceptionally strong neutron flux that penetrated the Earth's atmosphere to an altitude of approximately 70 km, resulting in the detection of cosmic rays 100 times more intense than typical background levels, primarily composed of protons rather than heavy ions. By utilizing detailed recordings from neutron monitors and air shower detectors, along with mathematical modeling, we were able to accurately determine the energy and composition of solar neutrons and derive essential parameters for the sun's cosmic ray generating processes. The research has significant implications for reevaluating the sun's capability to produce high-energy neutrons and the effectiveness of the sun's magnetic shield in containing escaped particles. Modern large-scale complex systems, particularly those seen in natural phenomena and cutting-edge technological applications, comprise intricate interactions among numerous interconnected elements. The non-linear dynamics of these systems, depending on the interactions, can lead to diverse, often unpredictable outcomes, rendering them complex. In this paper, we introduce a new approach that employs Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to analyze and understand the intricate interactions and resulting dynamics in complex systems. By treating interactions as graph edges and elements as nodes, we employ GNNs to model the interactions and, in conjunction with ordinary differential equations, to capture the dynamics. In order to investigate the dynamics, we propose a method that utilizes reverse engineering, starting from the dynamics and interactions to recover the underlying parameters. This approach serves as a foundation for exploring the intricate interactions and resulting dynamics in complex systems through GNNs. We demonstrate the practical utility of this approach by applying it to a real-world technological problem, namely in modeling and analyzing peer-to-peer network dynamics. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the accuracy of the parameter recovery in conjunction with a specific GNN. In addition, we outline a data-driven methodology for constructing a simplified model of a complex system, featuring a reduced number of interactions, as well as a corresponding task to identify whether a given system is stable or unstable. This research was presented at the 2022 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR).

We establish a connection between divisions of polynomial ideals and a specific type of map that can be integrated from the unit circle into the complex plane. This relationship is demonstrated to encompass polynomial factorization, algebraic functions, and algebraic curves. It also provides a framework for analyzing the compositions of two maps, one of which integrates the circle into the complex plane and another of which integrates a finite number of Riemann spheres. This framework enables us to define a set of compositions that are equivalent under a specific relation and, as a result, we can utilize it to address the combinatorial challenge of counting these compositions. This challenge is resolved using the principles of rooted tree structures and the combinatorial formula obtained can be used to determine the number of compositions that integrate a specific polynomial ideal and, in turn, determine the number of roots of that ideal. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this enumeration is related to the formula for the number of roots and, in the special case where the ideal consists of the polynomial x^n, we derive the formula for the number of roots and the number of compositions that integrate the ideal as the (n-1)th Catalan number. This enumeration also has implications for the study of the circle as a level set within the complex plane and it provides an alternative proof for the conjecture regarding the number of roots of the ideal defined by the polynomial x^n. Lastly, this enumeration remains applicable to the study of the circle as a level set within the n-dimensional space and it remains available as a framework for addressing the combinatorial challenge of counting the compositions of the Riemann spheres in the n-dimensional space. This framework in its current form does not, however, extend to the level of the (n-1)th Catalan number in the n-dimensional space. This paper is dedicated to the memory of our friend and colleague, Hans-Herrmann Stappler. It was written based on the notes that he had prepared for a lecture on this subject but was unable to deliver due to his untimely passing. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for problem representation, featuring a clear and intuitive syntax. However, determining the precise meaning of GP 2 expressions can be challenging due to their rich structure and varied concepts. GP 2 expressions comprise interconnected graphs of variables, constants, logical operators, and function applications, including recursive definitions. In contrast, the standard approach to handling GP 2 expresses them as terms in a first-order logic with function symbols and their corresponding sorts. Yet, this method overlooks crucial aspects of the GP 2 syntax, including commas in function signatures and the distinction between infix and prefix operators. As a result, multiple GP 2 expressions can map to the same term, complicating tasks like evaluating expressions, solving for unknown variables, and checking the validity of formulas against GP 2 theories. To address these difficulties, we developed the GP 2 compiler, a tool that translates GP 2 expressions into a more explicit and standardized form called the internal format. This format retains all the details from the original GP 2 expressions, and we provide algorithms for performing tasks like variable substitution and checking formula validity against GP 2 theories on this internal representation. Additionally, the GP 2 compiler includes a feature to enhance GP 2 expressions by adding implicit parentheses and distinguishing prefixes from infixes, making it a valuable resource for developers working with GP 2. The GP 2 compiler is now an open-source tool available under the permissive Apache License 2.0. The internal format it uses and the algorithms for performing tasks on this format are also part of the public domain. The compiler can be used directly through the command line or integrated into other programs using the C API it provides. Working with nominal data poses specific challenges when performing dimensionality reduction, particularly under sparse group assumptions. Standard methods such as Group Lasso aren't effective due to its least-squares nature and tendency to force at least one continuous predictor to zero. Furthermore, conventional Group Lasso implementations fail to account for the structure of nominal data correctly. To address these limitations, we develop a new Group Lasso formulation that properly handles categorical variables and ensures that the sparsity is induced among the continuous predictors only. This formulation is then linked to an equivalent equivalent convex optimization problem that can be solved using a dual block coordinate ascent strategy. Asymptotic performance of the estimator is evaluated through theoretical analysis, revealing that under certain conditions the estimator's risk converges at a rate of n^{-1/5) under mild restrictions on the design and the true parameter. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of our method by applying it to real-world datasets. The algorithm and methodology proposed have been implemented in R in a package called nomG for easy access.

In multi-channel speech processing, having more than one microphone can significantly reduce noise and boost speech quality. However, in single-microphone scenarios, which are the most common case, available techniques leverage techniques that were developed for multi-channel speech, including ICA and BSS, to enhance speech by exploiting the characteristics of different frequency channels. In this paper, we propose the DPCRN, a dual-path convolution recurrent network that applies both spatial and shallow temporal processing to improve speech in individual frequency channels. We also introduce a deep neural network that serves as a fusion module to combine the predictions from different frequency channels. In contrast to conventional techniques such as ICA and BSS, DPCRN requires minimal prior knowledge and can be trained end-to-end for optimal performance. When benchmarked against conventional techniques including UMAN and GANS-Joint, DPCRN demonstrated superior results in terms of both objective and subjective speech quality measures. Moreover, DPCRN outperformed state-of-the-art models including Dual-Stream and Locally Connected CRN in noise-free conditions. Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A step forward in this direction requires testing these models on fundamental convection scenarios. This study applies a simple column model to mimic two-fluid advection-diffusion equations, incorporating buoyancy force and mass flux interaction, and incorporates a quasi-1D implementation of the Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection scenario. Initial assessments with air as the single fluid yield realistic, self-similar solution profiles. As the two-fluid simulation includes mass flux interaction, it results in a shift in the onset of roll formation. Nevertheless, without proper boundary treatment, the model fails to replicate the correct roll structure in both horizontal dimensions. The study highlights the fundamental challenges in replicating the correct roll structure in the two-fluid scenario and emphasizes the necessity for further testing of any multi-fluid convection model. The column model used in this study is straightforward and does not incorporate sophisticated features like wall function treatments or high-resolution numerical schemes. The model has the potential for application in large-scale convection simulations, but it requires significant enhancement to accurately replicate the roll structure in the two-fluid scenario. The failure of the two-fluid scenario in replicating the roll structure also raises implications for the underlying theory of the model. The study demonstrates that the curvature of the S-shaped branch in low-Prandtl Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection results from the two-fluid dynamics rather than the inherent properties of convection alone. The findings of the study are significant contributions to the multi-fluid convection scenario and provide actionable improvement suggestions for the model. The study also highlights the potential of the column model as a building block for more complex multi-fluid models, incorporating features like the mass flux interaction, wall function treatments, and proper boundary treatments, is crucial for refining weather and climate simulations. The study further demonstrates the potential of the column model as a tool for exploring the fundamental dynamics of the Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection scenario in the context of two-fluid dynamics. The study provides an open invitation to researchers with expertise in the field of convection to explore and develop the model further. The numerical implementation and parameters of the model, as well as the results obtained, are made freely available to facilitate this progress. The findings of the study are relevant to researchers with an interest in the development of multi-fluid convection models and the fundamental dynamics of the Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection scenario. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated particles, while the third system has uncorrelated particles. By combining the uncorrelated system with either of the two correlated systems, we determine the conditions under which authentic Bell-state entanglement between the two uncorrelated systems can form. Our analysis shows that genuine entanglement emerges when the uncorrelated system is coupled to one of the correlated systems with a specific parameter value. Additionally, we identify a transition where a concurrence peak indicates a Bell-state-like entanglement phenomenon. Moreover, a non-zero area under the concurrence curve indicates that the uncorrelated system may become entangled with the other system even if the Jaynes-Cummings interaction is not optimal. We also examine the effect of a phase shift and find that it disrupts the symmetry of the concurrence curves. Furthermore, we find that the authentic Bell-state-like entanglement is robust against a phase shift when the Jaynes-Cummings parameter satisfies a particular condition. Moreover, our analysis demonstrates that the genuine Bell-state-like entanglement may extend to the case where the uncorrelated system is coupled to two separate, identically prepared, correlated systems, provided that the systems have the same Jaynes-Cummings parameter and the phase shift is less than π/2. We also investigate the authentic Bell-state-like entanglement formation when the uncorrelated system is coupled to two separate, identically prepared, correlated systems with different Jaynes-Cummings parameters, and our analysis shows that this scenario may lead to the formation of a Bell-state-like entanglement between the two uncorrelated systems, with the corresponding concurrence curves displaying a peak at specific phase shift values. We term this phenomenon "inter-system entanglement switching". We further analyze the relationship between the average photon number and the genuine Bell-state-like entanglement, and our findings indicate that the authentic Bell-state-like entanglement formation is associated with the disappearance of the non-zero area under the curve that describes the relationship between the average photon number and the Jaynes-Cummings parameter. Twitter has grown into a significant source of public sentiment towards prominent entities such as politicians, sports teams, and famous individuals. Accurate sentiment analysis on Twitter can provide valuable insights for various purposes including political campaign analysis and sports team popularity measurement. In this project, we gathered a large dataset comprising publicly observable Twitter posts about ten renowned individuals from ten different domains. Each dataset contains 10,000 historical tweets along with the accompanying sentiment ratings from 1 to 5. We preprocessed the data by converting all usernames and hashtags into a neutral form and implemented an LSTM-based classification model to determine the sentiment of each tweet. Using a 70-30 split ratio, we trained the model on 7,000 tweets and tested it on the remaining 3,000 tweets. The results showed an average precision of 0.78, average recall of 0.76, and an F-score of 0.77 for each individual. Additionally, we compared the model's performance with a conventional machine learning approach and found that the LSTM-based model yielded a 12% improvement in F-score. The dynamic Wigner function, represented by a complex-valued function, provides a comprehensive view of a quantum system's dynamics. However, calculating dynamic Wigner functions is challenging due to their extensive requirements for computational resources. In contrast, the dynamic tomogram, a 3D representation derived from the dynamic Wigner function, can be efficiently computed and offers valuable insights into the spatiotemporal evolution of the system. Notably, the dynamic tomogram's capability to exhibit non-equilibrium conditions such as the onset of synchronization in a scenario with two mutually coupled oscillators has been demonstrated by our group in a recent study. Furthermore, we have developed a quantitative metric based on the dynamic tomogram to assess the level of non-equilibrium entanglement in a pair of coupled Bose-Hubbard systems. This measure enables distinction between the onset of entanglement, superfluidity and synchronization induced by a driving field. The developed framework is not limited to these specific scenarios and can be applied to the study of other, non-equilibrium quantum states. The introduced quantitative measures of non-equilibrium entanglement and tomographic complexity hold promise for their experimental verification using techniques such as time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. The proposed approach has the potential to provide a deeper understanding of open quantum systems and may serve as a foundation for the development of novel control strategies for the onset of non-equilibrium conditions in the system. The introduced framework is compatible with the quantum acousto-optic disclosure technique that is currently being advanced and could enable the direct measurement of the dynamic tomogram. The introduction of a parabolic approximation allows for the reduction of the dimensionality of the dynamic tomogram from 3D to 2D, facilitating further analysis and providing valuable insights into the underlying dynamics with only a minor compromise in the level of detail. The developed 2D tomogram exhibits distinct patterns for each non-equilibrium scenario and thus serves as a faithful indicator of the system's dynamics. The introduced 2D tomogram shows promise for use in the study of other, open quantum systems and may serve as a foundation for the development of novel control strategies for these systems. Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized to model and compute complex many-body systems by approximating the target state using a network of moderate size. However, constructing precise tensors for every individual site poses a challenge, especially when incorporating time-dependent information. Our approach develops a method to directly construct a network consisting of precise tensors for any many-body system, incorporating both temperature and time-dependent information, by approximating the target state at a specific site rather than the overall system. This technique offers significant advantages over conventional methods, allowing for the precise calculation of physical properties at specific sites rather than system-wide averages, and effortlessly incorporates time-dependent information without destroying the entanglement renormalization network structure. By striking a balance between approximating site-dependent relationships and preserving the precision of site-independent relationships, our method proves particularly effective in efficiently calculating the thermal and time-dependent behavior of lattice systems near half-filling. Moreover, by integrating the time-dependent network structure directly into the network, our approach avoids the necessity for additional time-dependent extrapolation methods, and can be implemented using a range of approximate digital compactifications, including the truncated density matrix renormalization group. We demonstrate the applicability and efficiency of this method by calculating the thermal and time-dependent behavior of a Heisenberg chain. The digital compactifications employed in this research can be varied to strike a balance between computational speed and precision, and are capable of handling small site-dependent relationships in larger systems. The digital compactifications employed in this research include the NESSI platform, specifically the digital compactifications known as "Digital Compactification 1" and "Digital Compactification 2". These compactifications are characterized by having approximately 100 site-dependent relationship angles in "Digital Compactification 1" and approximately 500 site-dependent relationship angles in "Digital Compactification 2". The research employed cameras and microphones provided by the Logitech Group, Rode NT-USB, and Zoom F4. The concept of decoupling is a method for disentangling the behavior of a physical system by separating a central region from its surroundings. In the context of quantum field theory, decoupling a field $\phi$ from a physical system $S$ involves developing an approximation that allows $\phi$'s behavior to be predicted with accuracy, while ignoring the direct coupling between $\phi$ and $S$. A key consideration in this process is the field's efficacy, defined as the strength of its interaction with the environment. In general, the decoupling approximation's effectiveness depends on the distance from the system to the region where the field is efficacious. However, when the field's efficacy has a complex structure, determining the optimal decoupling strategy becomes more challenging. This paper addresses this issue by introducing a scale-oriented approach to predicting the decoupling approximation's behavior in response to variations in the distance from the system to the region where the field is efficacious. By applying this method to a specific, analytically resolvable scenario - a massless scalar field in a de Sitter spacetime - we demonstrate how the decoupling approximation changes with distance and identify the specific scale where the approximation switches from being accurate to unreliable. Additionally, this scale-oriented analysis reveals that the decoupling approximation becomes progressively less reliable as it fails to account for the field's efficacious region correctly. As a result, this approach can be used to guide the development of more sophisticated decoupling strategies for more complex, harder-to-resolve spacetime configurations. This research was presented at the 13th conference on quantum field theory under the influence of external fields in Zakopane, Poland. The intersection of magnetism, optics, and photonic technology holds great promise for creating sophisticated, non-linear optical elements with inherent memory. To achieve this, researchers are drawn to surfaces etched with periodic patterns, known as photonic surfaces or photonic lattices, which exhibit localized, high-sensitivity optical resonance and can be engineered to operate at specific wavelengths. Although research has demonstrated the individual control of magnetic properties and optical resonance within these lattices, orienting the magnetic properties in relation to the lattice structure while maintaining individual control over the magnetic properties at each site has not been possible. In our work, we successfully created a magnetic surface with a 2D photonic lattice structure, where the orientation of the magnetic anisotropy of individual sites is synchronized with the electric field direction of the optical resonance. This configuration enables site-selective, as well as optically-induced, manipulation of the magnetic interactions between sites. As a result, we observed an anomalous optical response when the magnetic interactions switched from being antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic. This breakthrough paves the way for complex, dynamic control of magnetic interactions through light, and our findings are relevant to the development of multifunctional, photonic magnetic memory elements. To create such devices, we propose a strategy for controlling the magnetic interactions in a wide range of photonic lattice structures. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, we designed a more intricate lattice structure with both circular and linear sites, where the magnetic interactions can switch between being confined to specific sites or spreading across the entire surface in response to light. This novel, orientation-sensitive magnetophotonic surface lattice structure, with a unique combination of magnetic and optical properties that can be controlled with light, holds great promise for the development of advanced magnetic memory elements with a wide range of applications. To create functional devices from this technology, we propose integrating it with a range of lattice structures and novel interfaces that can be engineered to operate in multiple wavelengths and dimensions. To achieve this, we developed a flexible design framework known as "Magnetophotonics by Design", which enables the individual control of magnetic interactions, as well as their response to light, across a wide range of photonic lattice structures and surfaces etched with various patterns. Unfortunately, many models are susceptible to these types of attacks and can be easily deceived by them. A solution to this problem is a function called CleanNet, which can determine the level of cleanliness of input data without the need to know the underlying distribution. This information can then be utilized to make informed decisions about the data, such as classifying it or choosing a sample. In this study, we improve the functionality of CleanNet by creating a more sophisticated algorithm that enables a 'black box' model to generate a label from any given class without requiring access to the original training data. This capability allows us to transfer knowledge to a target model from a source model without the need for retraining. The rising popularity of autonomous decision-making in critical situations necessitates the use of neural networks that can observe and decide for themselves. However, deploying these networks requires significant computational resources and substantial sums of money, leading to the need to reduce them to a form that includes a single, trained expert network making observations and a second, trained network that makes decisions based on those observations. This is analogous to a common problem in reinforcement learning where one agent observes and another makes decisions. In this research, we develop a training method for this type of setup, known as Co-Observation Learning, where one network learns to make observations that benefit both itself and the other network. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to an over-observation reduction task in reinforcement learning and an observation learning task in navigation. The results show that Co-Observation Learning reduces the observation loss and leads to decision-making networks that excel in real-world situations. The method also results in networks that are comparable in size to those without the co-observation setup but with a significantly smaller memory footprint. This paper proposes a metric called the "effective pairwise and quadriplets distance" that distinguishes one code from another, surpassing the distinction provided by pairwise and quadriplets distance. We also establish an inequality linking this new metric with codeword distance and identify which codes achieve the minimum distance under this new standard. Furthermore, this new metric offers a basis for defining a coding error and calculates the probability of this error for specific coding scenarios. Lastly, our research reveals that, for large letter sets, the best codes under this new standard are identical to those identified as optimal in previous research.

Evaluating the best action sequence in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) amounts to a long-term optimization problem. Since the set of possible actions in the source string is vast, using the full set as a search space is computationally infeasible. Our solution exploits the observation that competent NMT models typically generate word sequences that adhere to the constraints of the source string. We therefore propose a direct method of evaluating the next action in the sequence, drawing inspiration from policy-based reinforcement learning. By focusing on the upcoming actions, our model prioritizes the easier parts of the translation task, such as expanding existing phrases, rather than attempting difficult aspects like synthesizing the beginning of the sequence. We develop a comprehensive theoretical model to describe a quantum bit that is part of a larger system in a non-equilibrium steady state, driven by periodic energy exchange. Based on this model, we demonstrate the same non-equilibrium steady state can be achieved through multiple driving mechanisms, ultimately leading to the same quantum state in the bit. A key aspect of this state is that it differs significantly from an equilibrium state, even when the driving becomes weak. Moreover, we find that the bit's dynamics can be effectively described by a rotating frame model, although this is only exact when the driving is symmetric. Nonetheless, even in asymmetric situations, this model provides a good approximation, with the bit's steady state deviating only minimally from the driven frame. Notably, the magnitude of this deviation is directly related to the magnitude of the asymmetric driving. We also investigate the impact of asymmetric driving on the quantum state, discovering that it gives rise to the emergence of a quasiperiodic modulation of the steady state. A key feature of this modulation is that it is harmonically locked to the driving cycle, with its very small amplitude offering a potentially measurable indicator of the driving's asymmetry. To demonstrate the practical feasibility of this measurement, we consider a specific scenario based on a superconducting quantum bit, with realistic parameters that could be achieved through available technology. In this scenario, with driving asymmetry of just 1%, the magnitude of the modulation would be approximately 0.1%, offering a measurable quantity that could be derived from the wave function, specifically the expectation value of the quantum state's phase. To carry out this measurement on a single, isolated qubit, we propose a method that could be realized using a variety of different quantum systems, with the specific implementation depending on the particular system in question. We further analyze the theoretical model in depth, with a focus on the driven Jaynes-Cummings model, as well as exploring the applicability of this model to a wider range of harmonic potentials. Additionally, we discuss its potential analogy to atomic systems in cavity quantum electrodynamics. Finally, we outline the scope for future research, with the aim of exploring the driven Jaynes-Cummings model in a broader context, as well as investigating the driven Bose-Josephson system.

Given a rational number p/q, we say a set A is p/q-identifiable if it can be distinguished from the empty set using p true statements about Q and q false statements about Q, where each statement about Q is true for some multiple fraction within a given interval and false for another interval. Our main observation shows that when the denominator of p/q is two, being p/q-identifiable is the same as being decidable. Additionally, we find p/q-identifiable sets for all even denominators greater than two and demonstrate that there are rationally identifiable sets for every odd denominator greater than one. Finally, we establish that being p/q-identifiable is equivalent to being (p,g) or (g,p)-identifiable for any rational number p/g.

MongoDB is a widely used NoSQL document-oriented database that adheres to a transactional protocol to ensure data consistency. Despite the absence of a formal specification, researchers have deduced the underlying transactional model of MongoDB, specifically the commit-two-phase protocol it follows. However, the validation of MongoDB's transactionality relied on inaccurate assumptions regarding the commit protocol. To address this, we corrected the assumed protocol based on a precise examination of MongoDB's source code. Furthermore, we discovered that MongoDB's commit protocol deviates from the standard two-phase commit model, effectively making it a variant of the "blind commit" protocol. Moreover, we established that MongoDB's transactionality is safeguarded by ensuring that the commit protocol successfully completes within a localized context, thus precluding the need for a robust rollback mechanism. Additionally, we found that MongoDB's commit protocol allows for the execution of write operations during the commit process, enabling greater concurrency but also increasing the risk of partial commits. Lastly, we discovered that MongoDB lacks a feature for handling network partition tolerance by implementing a robust rollback mechanism for failed commits, which could lead to the situation known as "split-brain." These deviations from standard transactional behavior necessitate a reevaluation of the transactional integrity of MongoDB, specifically its isolation property and commit protocol. Moreover, we examined the implications of these deviations for MongoDB's document store and proposed a design for a variant called "distributed MongoDB" that addresses the issue with network partition tolerance. Additionally, we identified the challenges associated with determining the transactionality of NoSQL databases in general.

Research on intricate networks with diverse connections has proliferated across fields, and our in-depth analysis provides a novel perspective combining concealed geometry and dynamics. We developed an advanced approach to investigate complex networks with varied interactions, including triangular relationships, by representing them as combined systems of independent components connected through interacting modules. This methodology allows us to explore dynamics within these networks using non-equilibrium statistical methods. Non-linear dynamics emerge due to the interplay between different types of connections, leading to sudden, dramatic events. We discovered that this approach is particularly effective for uncovering hidden geometric information and can be applied to investigate dynamic phenomena in intricate networks. Our research provides a versatile tool for analyzing diverse networks, from triangularly connected magnetic nanoassemblies to biological networks with complex connections, and can be used to investigate phenomena such as magnetic spin changes and protein aggregation. Further development of this method, in our vision, involves incorporating external influences and refining the approach to better capture real-world networks. Our research code is publicly available on GitHub at: https://github.com/AmirHoseinGhasemi/CEmethod.

We analyzed data from the Solar Wind Electromagnetic Investigation suite on board the Parker Solar Probe and found that the solar wind's convective energy flow has a specific pattern inside the heliosphere. Counter to expectations, the energy flow speed does not decrease at the same rate as the distance from the sun, but rather its gradient lessens as it approaches the sun's edge. This reduction in the energy flow's rate of decline occurs when the solar wind's distance from the sun's edge falls below approximately 0.5 AU and may be linked to solar wind acceleration or the energy distribution within the solar atmosphere. Additionally, we observed similar patterns during a coronal mass ejection event, suggesting that the energy flow's behavior is a default aspect of the solar wind system rather than an abnormal phenomenon. Further study is needed to comprehend the underlying causes of this pattern of the solar wind. The solar wind's energy distribution also exhibits an alteration in the inner heliosphere in line with a previous detection in the outer heliosphere but with distinct differences between them. The inner heliospheric wind's energy distribution has a more even pattern, with a more pronounced gradient in the solar wind's speed across a wider range of distances from the sun's edge compared to the outer heliosphere. The disparate patterns between the inner and outer heliospheres may be attributed to various factors including the presence of high-speed solar winds closer to the sun's edge and the influence of solar magnetic cycles on the solar wind's behavior. The data collected by the Parker Solar Probe over the course of its first seven close approaches to the sun provides valuable insights into the solar wind's energy distribution within the inner heliosphere. The findings from this analysis have implications for the modeling of the solar wind acceleration within the inner heliosphere and highlight the significance of continued data collection by the Parker Solar Probe in furthering our understanding of the solar wind's behavior. Thanks to the growing interest in human-machine interaction and conversational AI, speech-emotion recognition (SER) is becoming a vital technology. Although deep learning-based models have achieved high accuracy in laboratory settings with limited speech data, they struggle when adapted for use with natural speech from a variety of sources, including different languages and with different machines. This issue is compounded by the lack of labeled training data available for transfer learning. This research addresses these challenges by introducing a domain adaptation technique that simultaneously tackles model adaptation for both the task and the environment. The results of our experiments, conducted with a range of speech emotions and different environments, show significant improvements over the current state of the art. The developed method was then integrated into a working voice assistant, Amazon Alexa, enabling it to recognize speech emotions in a natural, hands-free format. The source code for the domain adaptation technique is available at https://github.com/ghulamabid/DA-DRL-SER. The developed Alexa application can be found at https://www.amazon.com/Guide-Sentiment-Emotion-Analysis-with-Alexa/dp/B09D43T1V9. The code and application are compatible with Linux-based systems, specifically Ubuntu 18 and later versions. The model's efficiency was further assessed in a real-world scenario at the CONVERSATIONS 2022 conference held in Barcelona, Spain. The technology has numerous practical uses, including but not limited to enhancing user experience with more personalized responses from machines, real-time performance feedback for call center employees, and intelligent video game companions. The development of the model is relatively straightforward for experienced programmers, requiring basic knowledge of Python, TensorFlow, and the Alexa Skills Kit. The model's capacity to learn from limited data and adapt to different speech emotions and environments makes it an valuable resource for individuals and organizations with limited resources. We examine an idealised model where an intense shock is formed in the homogeneous expansion of the cosmos, with a spherical cavity at the shock's centre. The speed of the shock's edge is found to be maximally distant from one, specifically being less than one when the cavity's size is small and increasing towards one as the cavity grows in size. The shock's temperature in this scenario is found to be directly proportional to the square of the cavity's size, while the emission spectrum will be affected by the changing optical depth as the shell expands. The light curves from different post-shock adiabatic expansions will also exhibit a distinguishing double-exponential decay pattern. The presence of a cavity will influence the peak time of light curves in relation to the Hubble time, also providing a possible explanation for observed deviations from one-world peaking times in certain supernovae types. The conditions required for a Type II SN explosion to result from collapsing rotating massive stars, with a significant angular momentum, are found to be stringent, with even near-breakup rotation rates failing to produce a SN due to the direct formation of millisecond black holes instead. The light curves from such black hole formations will appear as SNe with abnormally slow peak times. The SN 2004ET, with a particularly long peak time, is cited as an example of such a case. The same model can also explain the massive star SN explosions within the dwarf galaxies with low stellar masses. The same physics driving the SN formation in such situations also inhibits massive star formation within these same galaxies. The same analysis can be applied to the globular cluster SN formations, which also occur within low-metallicity environments that cannot form massive stars. The same principles can be used to search for SN formed within the low-metallicity environments outside of the galaxies and the Milky Way. This paper investigates the shape of the $B_s^0$ meson decaying into $D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ using data from the LHCb experiment. Since the $D_s^{*-}$ wave function contains both form factors and a contribution from the $D_s^-$ pole, determining this wave function is essential. We extracted the $D_s^-$ pole contribution's magnitude, which is 0.54 $\pm$ 0.01 $\pm$ 0.03, with assumptions that the $D_s^-/D_s^{*-}$ branching fraction lies between 0.1 and 0.5. Additionally, we calculated the $D_s^{*-}\gamma$ helicity amplitude, finding it to be 0.683 $\pm$ 0.043 $\pm$ 0.030. The extracted parameters are applicable to both scalar and vector $D_s^{*-}$ components and remain valid across the $q^2$ range studied. The results were compared to findings from earlier studies and interventions were suggested to improve the accuracy of similar analyses in the future. The research utilized data from 2010 to 2012, with integrated luminosities ranging from 0.46 to 1.0 pb^-1 for different $B_s^0$ energy modes. The most effective strategy for enhancing the analysis, with the largest impact being +10% in 2015, would involve utilizing forward acceptance requirements on the muon final state. The current understanding of heavy light meson wave functions was updated with the results of this study. The same research group had previously explored the $D^0$ and $D^{*0}$ form factors, with the same approach applicable to heavy strange mesons. The paper concluded by highlighting the importance of precisely calculating heavy light meson form factors with the aid of lattice QCD. The associated errors with the lattice predictions could be significantly reduced with the development of more sophisticated lattice methods, such as using quasi-0-form quasi-0 fermion fields, close to achieving 3% accuracy. The optimal strategy for minimizing the charm quark mass's impact on form factor predictions was also discussed, with the goal of reducing this effect to less than 2%. The research was published in the Journal of High Energy Physics for the year 2022. The same topic was also presented at the 2021 European Physical Society Conference on High Energy Physics. The rhythmic cracking sound produced when an adhesive tape is unrolled, a phenomenon known as "Tape Sound", undergoes a transition from a highly disordered state to a highly ordered state as the roll gets smaller. This transition is accompanied by a shift in the frequency distribution of the cracking sounds emitted. Our investigation reveals that the peak frequency of these sounds directly correlates with the angular velocity of the unrolling process. Furthermore, by analyzing the unrolling dynamics, we establish that the most frequent sound pattern is an exact replica of the unrolling dynamics, with each sound corresponding to a specific angular interval. This pattern persists even after the unrolling process reaches its natural end, continuing as the tape is rolled back up, albeit in reverse. This reversal of the sound pattern is reflected in the frequency distribution of the sounds emitted during this process. The term "Concealed Order in Tape Sound" accurately encapsulates this intricate pattern of sound, a pattern that underlies and is revealed through the complex unrolling and rolling dynamics of the adhesive tape. The "Concealed Order in Tape Sound" phenomenon bears resemblance to the "Concealed Order in Sandpiles", a concept discovered through computational simulations. The presence of this order is sustained as long as the system remains in a stationary state, a condition met when the unrolling process is carried out in a specific, controlled manner. The breakdown of this controlled process is marked by a return to a state of sound disorder. The analogy with the "Concealed Order in Sandpiles" also facilitates an understanding of the tape unrolling dynamics, specifically the role of the stickiness of the adhesive tape, a factor that in this context is analogous to the "activity" present in sandpile models. The study of the tape unrolling dynamics, a dynamic system, provides valuable insights into its behavior over time, a knowledge that can be applied to other similar dynamic systems, including those generating complex sounds in other contexts. To address ultralight dark matter detection challenges, we propose modifying the Lorentz non-abeyance assumption. This non-abeyance assumption can be broken in two ways: either the Lagrangian density contains a term that involves a direct scalar product of two Dirac operators, or the Hamiltonian density contains a similar product. We examine these scenarios, known as DA and HA, in the many-body framework and investigate the HA case further to determine if it can be distinguished from the DA case based on detection data. To accomplish this, we develop a theoretical model consisting of a HA operator, coupled to a massive scalar field, in addition to its interaction with a massive vector field. To keep the calculation manageable, we use a semi-quantum approach and derive the HA operator's expectation value in various scenarios. By analyzing the expectation value of the HA operator in a single particle, we find that its average square is approximately 1.25 times the square of the Lorentz non-abeyance assumption's average. When this value is 1 (less than 1), the HA operator's average is positive (negative). We also examine the HA operator's expectation value in a many-body setting and discover that it varies significantly with temperature but remains relatively constant at finite temperatures. To detect the HA operator, we propose using a non-relativistic neutrino detector located underground, specifically the Boulby deep underground neutrino facility, which is designed to detect dark matter particles moving at the speed of light. To accomplish this, we suggest performing a series of experiments with different detector configurations, including with and without a magnetic field, as well as with and without lead shielding, in addition to detecting neutrinos of all masses moving at the speed of light. This research develops a fundamental approach to analyzing option collateral requirements, taking into account the costs of delta hedging and market volatility fluctuations. Unlike the existing literature, which relies on numerical methods to assess collateral needs, our study constructs an analytical formula based on option payoffs, delta hedging expenses, and volatility effects. This analytical expression, however, requires the solution to a specific parabolic equation, which can be approximated to facilitate practical applications in the derivatives markets. Our research also explores the implications of our model for specific market scenarios and highlights the importance of the break-even point where the cost of delta hedging equals the interest earned on collateral. Ultimately, our study provides a theoretical framework for examining the interplay between the costs of delta hedging and the volatility of underlying assets and provides the foundation for exploring more complex scenarios in the derivatives markets. Additionally, we have made available pre-print versions of our earlier and later research on this topic. Our research was supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation. A dynamic model of social mobility is proposed, with multiple generations, where individuals move up or down a hierarchical ladder based on their relative position and a random shock. The model allows for reverse mobility and showcases how opportunities are distributed equally among all generations. The probability of reaching the topmost position varies significantly, with a majority of people failing to achieve it. The model's simplicity enables the derivation of analytical results, which demonstrate the importance of inclusive opportunity distribution, demands little in terms of data for parameter estimation, and offers a genuine approach to comparing the equality of opportunity in different societies. The model's robustness is demonstrated by applying it to real-world data, with the analysis yielding comparable estimates of the distribution of opportunities across all generations and providing a quantifiable measure of the equality of these opportunities. The model's ability to capture the complexity of real-world data is further validated by conducting a sensitivity analysis. The proposed method for measuring equality of opportunity in the model relies on the application of a convex combination of its various forms, which includes the minimal degree of opportunity, the maximum degree of opportunity, the equal opportunity line, and the minimum loss of information line. The model's insight into the dynamics of social mobility is also explored through policy interventions in the form of hierarchical promotion or demotion, which yields valuable knowledge on the subject. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of these transactions, it has been challenging to gather comprehensive data on a large scale. We selected the Forsage scheme, a high-profile operation from 2020 that utilized blockchain technology, to examine this phenomenon. By analyzing over 87,000 participant contracts, we uncovered the intricate structure of Forsage, revealing how the scheme's designers manipulated the terms to maintain a pseudo-decentralized appearance while preventing participants from withdrawing funds. This allowed the scammers to accumulate nearly $300 million in 6 months with minimal expenses. By tracking the origin of Forsage and analyzing the contracts, we were able to identify the key individuals behind the scheme, including the chief architect, a Russian national named Vladimir. The success of Forsage highlights the growing need to regulate the use of smart contracts in the context of scams. The Forsage case also illustrates the importance of examining the underlying code and network behavior in addition to the public promises made by scammers. The data and contract code for Forsage have been made available to the public in the hope that it may serve as a teaching tool or real-world example for various blockchain and cryptography-related courses. The pecuniary gains made by the Forsage scammers have been reported to the tax authorities in Russia. The Forsage scheme has continued to operate and evolve, with the participants adapting new strategies to bypass the laws and regulations put in place to stop the scheme. The Forsage website remains active, although it now operates under a different domain. The blockchain data used in this research is publicly available, and the analysis has been limited to a specific time frame that allows for the accurate tracking of the Forsage transactions. The study of Forsage can be seen as a broader examination of the interplay between technology, finance, and law in action. Unlike traditional statistical techniques, these techniques can account for process intricacies, including non-linear relationships and multiple interactions, without making assumptions about their form. However, without prior knowledge of how business processes operate, it can be challenging to determine whether processes are linear or non-linear, making it difficult to decide between deep and linear techniques without conducting the necessary analysis. Moreover, our findings were corroborated by a backwards analysis of the process, which revealed non-linearity in the sales data. Moreover, they underscore the significance of conducting backwards analysis to gain insight into processes and validate the assumptions made by the models. Lastly, our findings highlight the potential of deep learning in forecasting at the horizon, although further research is needed to fully explore this aspect. The rarefaction front of the 1983 March 31 stellar flare from AD Leo was likely responsible for creating a significant amount of UV and X-ray spectral lines resulting from the interaction between the front and the upper atmosphere of the star. Since the 1985 great eruption of AD Leo occurred two years after the flare, it is plausible that a similar interaction could produce observable signatures in the form of [Fe XVI] and [Si XIV] spectral lines in the UV range. To test this hypothesis, we performed a theoretical analysis of the plasma conditions required to produce these lines, finding they could be reached within a year or less after the flare, although permanent lines like these are uncommon in flare and superflare stellar massessions. If widespread and lasting, such phenomena could serve as indicators of flare-related precipitation of plasma on low mass stars. Based on this hypothesis, we searched for [Fe XVI] and [Si XIV] lines in the spectrum of AD Leo two years after the flare, and although finding them too weak in the near-UV range, we did discover a temporary and narrow band of [Si XIV] lines around 258 nm and [Fe XVI] lines around 281 nm in the spectrum from 1985 April 12, with the strength of these lines decreasing over the next year. To explain the temporary and narrow band of [Si XIV] and [Fe XVI] lines, we developed a semi-analytical model of the interaction between the front and the upper atmosphere of the star, and through this model were able to reproduce the spectrum of AD Leo two years after the flare, with the assumption that mass motions during this eruption were minor. On the other hand, with the assumption that mass motions during this eruption were significant, we were able to reproduce the spectrum of AD Leo five years after the flare, with the disappearance of [Si XIV] and [Fe XVI] lines around 2000 AD, with which the observational data conformed. With this analysis, we were able to estimate the frequency of flare-related precipitation of plasma on low mass stars, with the further consequence that such precipitation may explain the occurrence of white light supernovae from non-ejecta explosions, with the additional requirement that such explosions occur in the presence of a circumstellar gas formed by a previous and weaker stellar flare. A key step in achieving this is defeating opposing agents in a generative adversarial training process, typically considered difficult when training models of substantial size. In response, we propose the SparseGAN architecture, designed to efficiently create massive datasets by having a small neural network compete against a more advanced model. This architecture allows smaller models to generate diverse data while the opposing model, being more sophisticated, generates more precise and varied information. We have tested the SparseGAN on popular datasets for creating synthetic data and found it outperforms existing methods in terms of diversity and label accuracy. Furthermore, with a significant reduction in required memory, it successfully generated larger datasets. The code for SparseGAN has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/SparseGAN.

The precise evaluation of programming languages is a complex task that is heavily influenced by the underlying geometry of the environments in which they operate. This project establishes a foundation for program evaluation that is based on geometric principles and utilizes the concept of a "valuation." Within this framework, we define a range of mathematical objects, each representing a distinct type of programming environment. We then establish a sequence of abstract and concrete program evaluation processes, tied to the specific environments, that serve as the foundation for the concept of "environmental evaluation." This concept in turn is linked to the concept of "environmental entailment" which is, in turn, connected to the concept of "truth" within a given environment. Ultimately, this framework allows us to recover the concept of truth as it was originally defined by Algebratic Geometry. Additionally, we demonstrate that the concept of program evaluation can be realized within the framework of symmetric monoidal category theory. Furthermore, we establish that the category of the algebraic geometry related to the Kleene algebra at hand is equational, i.e., it is a category that is capable of distinguishing between elements based on their algebraic properties. Lastly, we provide an interpretation of the principles of Birkhoff's Halmos theorem within the context of algebraic geometry.

Leveraging the distinct physical properties of biological movement, our approach utilizes both spatial and temporal features, incorporating a novel descriptor called the "motion skeleton." This descriptor, derived from 3D tracklets, provides crucial insights into the self-propelled direction of motion. Our detection algorithm, comprising a weakly supervised deep learning approach and a posteriori probability estimation, ensures high precision and effectiveness. We consider a contextual linear gambit model, where agents make independent decisions based on their private contexts and a shared parameter vector, without knowing the distribution of contexts. We show that, without assuming knowledge of this distribution, cooperative learning leads to a computationally efficient and statistically optimal estimate of the parameter vector. Additionally, a decreased rate of learning is observable as cooperation progresses. We also establish a lower bound on the rate of learning that is free from any contextual distribution assumption and thus serves as a computationally unsolved problem. Moreover, this problem extends to estimating the unique equilibrium of a first-price contextual auction. Our results build upon the earlier findings from Doikov, Dvurecenskij, and Pap, "Cooperative Learning in Distributed Linear Contextual Auctions" (2021). By applying QAI, we find it can be more effective in high-dimensional settings and potentially handle real-world noise more gracefully. We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and shifted number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and shift are identified that meet the criteria for minimizing the variance of small shifts, while other scenarios are associated with non-poisonous state characteristics, enabling them to maintain Heisenberg limited estimation capabilities even in the presence of small noises. Additionally, conditions are determined under which these states ensure the minimum variance of up to three small shifts, thereby providing a basis for optimal preparation protocols. Furthermore, an analysis is provided of how the phase space structure changes over time for these states, along with an examination of their quantum coherence and quanta distribution. Lastly, the implications for implementing these states in metrology devices are discussed.

VSI leads to the development of oscillating waves and possibly even turbulence and particle transport in the outer regions of the disks. However, the impact of dust particles on VSI, particularly their influence on the VSI's growth rate, has not been thoroughly examined until now. In this study, we explored the effects of varying dust particle concentrations on VSI by incorporating dust particles into the model and accounting for their influence on the disks' opaqueness. Our results indicate that VSI's growth rate slows with increasing dust concentration, but only in the outer regions of the disks where VSI tends to dominate. Nevertheless, dust particles have a minimal impact on the VSI's overall stability, and our research suggests that VSI's persistence in the disks' outer regions could be attributed to other factors rather than low rotation rates. Additionally, our findings show that the disks' temperature structure also has a negligible influence on the VSI's growth rate. Finally, and most importantly, we discovered that the effects of particles on the VSI's growth rate could be misinterpreted as the disks' reduced opacity exerting an analogous influence on the VSI's growth rate. Consequently, this study highlights the significance of distinguishing between the disks' reduced opacity and particle influence on the VSI's growth rate. Our proposed network, DEGP-Net, incorporates a unique entrance structure where information from external sources is combined with internal data via a dynamic routing mechanism. This approach differs from conventional methods where external and internal representations are fused through weighted sums. External information is processed through separate channels that output a set of entrance probabilities and representations. These probabilities and representations are then employed to determine the entrance weights, allowing us to select the internal and external representations accordingly. We employ a global mean pooling module to calculate the entrance weights, which enables us to incorporate the mean of all entrances instead of fixing them as individual channels. This allows our model to handle problems with an unknown number of entrances. Experimental results on our specially designed datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our model, and by adapting it to incorporate spatial external information as channel weights, we obtain a simplified version that is comparable to state-of-the-art methods. This version is particularly efficient as it reduces the model to a single channel. Our model also demonstrates superior performance on popular datasets in comparison to leading methods. The code for our model is available at https://github.com/ghulam-sabih/DEGP-Net.

To enhance the performance of open-domain Commonsense Question Answering, we introduce a novel approach that bridges the gap between laymen's comprehension and in-depth knowledge. Our method, known as Coarse-to-Precise, leverages a user-friendly description to guide a more detailed explanation with greater depth, drawing on a rich knowledge base. We argue that incorporating a simpler description with a richer one can lead to a more authentic and in-depth response, mirroring how real-life conversations unfold. To accomplish this, we design a specific strategy that employs a contrastive learning technique to fuse the two descriptions and integrate a decoder to generate the response. Our approach boasts a number of innovative features, including a novel description pair construction method, a distinctive token filtering technique, and a customized evaluation metric that accounts for the relationship between the descriptions. We also build a bespoke dataset comprising conversational pairs, accessible to the public for the first time. In our experiments, we conduct thorough comparisons with cutting-edge models and demonstrate the superiority of our approach. Furthermore, we analyze the findings to gain valuable insights into the task and the newly developed dataset. Lastly, we outline potential applications and extensions of our model. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/ghruan/C2P.

Federated learning allows models to be trained on data without being physically moved, posing challenges for data sharing. Focusing on diverse data sets complicates optimization even further. We developed a new, effortless method called "stroll" to address these challenges. It combines data sets simply by taking a random step in model space without requiring the creation of centralized datasets. Training occurs locally, adding little overhead. Our research showed that this straightforward method can compete with more complex algorithms when there are many diverse data sets. It also discovered that this approach can excel when there are many diverse data sets and learning is difficult. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  Within the US, approximately two-thirds of prisoners require some form of mental health services, with half being severe enough to cause significant functional impairment.  Despite the prevalence of mental health issues, parolees with mental health conditions often struggle to access necessary post-release treatment, leading to high recidivism rates and decreased chances of successful rehabilitation.  This study examines how mandatory mental health treatment during the parole period affects reoffending behavior and mental health among released prisoners with mental health disorders.  Utilizing a difference-in-differences analysis and data from the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) and the California Board of State and Federal Affairs, we found that mental health treatment during the parole period reduces the likelihood of reoffending and improves mental health outcomes among released prisoners with mental health disorders.  Specifically, we discovered a 12-14 percent decrease in reoffending rates and improved ratings for both general and mental health functioning.  The protective effects of treatment were found to be more pronounced among individuals serving shorter sentences and those convicted of violent crimes.  Notably, the benefits of treatment were also observed among released prisoners without mental health diagnoses, suggesting that treatment may have broader societal benefits.  Finally, we identified potential avenues for improving the effectiveness of mental health treatment within the criminal justice system, including reducing the duration of which parolees are subject to mental health treatment and increasing access to treatment for released prisoners with substance use disorders.  These findings have implications for the design of rehabilitation programs and highlight the importance of providing accessible mental health treatment within the criminal justice system in order to reduce recidivism rates and improve long-term outcomes among released prisoners with mental health disorders.  System-wide adoption of such programs could also yield significant societal cost-savings.  Additionally, given the universal application of treatment to parolees, any positive effects would be realized by both high and low-risk offenders, suggesting that this approach could be an efficient means of providing community-based mental health services.  Future research opportunities are also discussed, including the potential for machine learning models and detailed program cost analyses.  Lastly, as a historical note, this research predates the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent prison reforms in California.  Future research could explore the impact of these events on the findings presented. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based approaches, and these models have demonstrated high levels of accuracy in predicting students' knowledge. However, the field has largely been observational, with little emphasis on experimental methodology. As a result, evaluating and comparing these models has become a complicated task. To address this challenge, we present PyKT, a Python-based framework designed to facilitate the evaluation and comparison of deep learning knowledge tracing models. This framework provides pre-written functions for implementing intervention studies using knowledge tracing data, as well as tools for plotting and comparing model performance. PyKT supports the evaluation of both non-personalized and personalized models, with features for plotting heatmaps based on intervention study results. With PyKT, researchers can easily replicate the methods used in our previous study, providing a straightforward framework for evaluating and comparing deep learning-based knowledge tracing models. This framework is available online at https://github.com/AmnonOverners/PyKT.

Constructing efficient proof libraries for various decision procedures and their combinations in SMT solvers poses a significant challenge, as it requires accounting for multiple proof representations and formats used across different solvers and their individual components. This task is further complicated by the need to balance the size of these proof libraries against their performance in subsequent verification tasks. We introduce a novel concept, "a blank slate" for creating and utilizing SMT proofs, which bypasses the constraint of adhering to a predetermined proof format until it's necessary to translate them for use with a particular verification tool. We've developed a prototype, the Alethe system, which demonstrates this approach and showcases our method for selectively applying a format to a subset of the proofs, thus minimizing unnecessary size expansion. By leveraging this approach, we've created a compact proof library that efficiently supports a wide range of applications, including but not limited to CVC4 and Z3 with various strategies and verifiers like KISS and Provenance. We're open sourcing the Alethe system in the hope it will contribute to resolving the challenge of constructing efficient proof libraries.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The asynchronous approach to learning, which distributes updates to devices at any time, can provide a faster training process but may lead to difficulties in scaling to large numbers of participants due to the fluctuation of gradients caused by delayed updates. The buffered asynchronous accumulation approach, which allows the server to accumulate updates from devices within a specified timeframe before applying them, can mitigate this issue but requires constrained gradients to prevent biased updates. We propose a new algorithm that overcomes this limitation by allowing unconstrained gradients and has the same positive convergence rate as the batch version of stochastic gradient descent. Furthermore, we compare our algorithm with the asynchronous approach and demonstrate that it results in a lower overall training time when the dataset is balanced but may be outperformed by the asynchronous approach when the dataset is highly imbalanced. We also explore a variant of the algorithm designed to reduce the inequality among devices and demonstrate the efficacy of our method in training models on large public datasets. Leveraging advanced neural network-based end-to-end ASR models has led to a significant performance boost when transferring knowledge between languages. Nonetheless, initiating this chain often hinges on possessing a well-performing mother-tongue ASR model. This challenge is particularly pronounced in situations like multilingual mobile applications, where the primary ASR system is frequently a monolingual one. A crucial obstacle here is obtaining a well-trained mother-tongue ASR model, which, as noted earlier, proves difficult. This paper seeks to address this issue by proposing a novel ASR knowledge transfer framework, aptly named R2F, designed to forge a working ASR model for a target speaker even when the training data comprises only the foreign language. Moreover, R2F is capable of handling situations with limited paired data, thereby successfully applying to cross-language ASR transfer. Experimental evaluations conducted on the Switchboard and Fisher datasets demonstrate R2F's efficacy, with results showing a notable performance improvement over existing state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, the introduction of a novel frequency-based mask initialization technique, coupled with a gentle refinement process, is found to enhance the model's accuracy significantly. As for cross-language ASR knowledge transfer, R2F achieves a word error rate of 24.4% on the test set, a notable reduction of 9% in comparison to the current baseline. As an additional exploration, a trial was conducted to extend R2F to the realm of multilingual mobile applications, with the outcome revealing a 10% WER improvement when utilizing a foreign language ASR model. The proposed R2F model's simplicity, coupled with its superior performance, makes it an appealing solution for real-world ASR applications. The code for the R2F model is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/RFASR. Moreover, pre-trained R2F models for the LibriSpeech and Google's Common Voice datasets, alongside additional results, are available online at https://ghru.github.io/RFASR/.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with non-isotropic pressures, leading to a well-defined four-metric that meets the physical requirements and allows for a direct link to the semi-tetrad metric. By utilizing this approach, we are able to determine the total and bound energy of the dual-fluid star within the framework of General Relativity and Einstein's mass-energy equivalence principle. Moreover, we derive an expression for the conserved mass in terms of the four-metric, and demonstrate how the semi-tetrad method facilitates the computation of the mass and energy of each individual fluid component. Finally, we provide explicit formulas for the pressures and densities of each fluid in their respective comoving frames. The aforementioned analysis serves as a starting point for exploring the dynamics of dual-fluid stars within the context of General Relativity. The associated Python code for calculating the pressures and densities of each fluid is made publicly available. The research reported herein was supported by the National Science Foundation.
