Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Rectification models do not account for domains outside of their training data. I show that native speakers of Japanese can correct Japanese errors and native speakers of Chinese can correct Chinese errors. The model I propose addresses this issue by incorporating a domain transfer step in its training routine. This involves presenting the model with instances of correcting sentences in a known target domain, followed by a transformation of the input and output to an unknown source domain. This process enables the model to develop a general understanding of GER domains. Evaluations on the NCON dataset reveal a 3.5 Fowler score improvement over the baseline. Additionally, the model exhibiting native-like fluency in Chinese, demonstrated by a 26.3 Chi-square value, also shows a 3.9 Fowler score improvement on the JREdit dataset. Furthermore, incorporating a condition where the model is exposed to native language data during training leads to a 5.3 Fowler score improvement on the JREdit dataset. Software required for this project is available at github.com/ghrua/metager.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is notable for lacking a significant central bulge. High-resolution spectroscopy from the Integral Field Unit of the Multi-Object Spectrograph Integral Field Unit and the 10.4m Gran Telescopio Canarias were used to investigate its stellar population and gas dynamics. A novel feature, a narrow asymptotic tail in a H-alpha image, has also been discovered in this galaxy. The tail measures 259 kpc in length and is likely the result of a gravitational interaction with a companion galaxy. The gas distribution within the galaxy indicates it is nearly axisymmetric and shows no significant rotation disruption. Instead, it shows a sharp decline in the outer regions, consistent with the behavior expected in a star-forming galaxy affected by a low-density intergalactic medium. The H-alpha emission within the tail is concentrated on one side and follows the path of a satellite galaxy that has been torn from the main body of UGC 8839. The findings suggest this galaxy experienced a very weak interaction and is now experiencing edge-on straining, leading to a decrease in its rotational velocity and an expansion of its optical size. The absence of a central bulge is also a result of this interaction, as it prevents the formation of this component during the galaxy's formation rather than requiring it to be disrupted by external forces. The extensive star formation in the tail may also be responsible for the decline in bulge formation. The low surface brightness of this galaxy makes it particularly difficult to study, but the data collected also highlight the capabilities of the instruments used and the potential for the Gran Telescopio Canarias to study similar galaxies in the future. The characteristics of UGC 8839 provide a valuable insight into the external forces that can shape a galaxy's formation and the ease with which a galaxy can be transformed by a weak interaction with a satellite galaxy. The presence of a tail in this galaxy also highlights the occurrence of a specific type of asymptotic tail in a galaxy and the need to define its classification. The paper is published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. The data collected was presented in the form of a vast H-alpha image and spectroscopic data from the galaxy and its tail. Using lattice QCD, a calculation of two-flavor correlation functions in the pion is performed, yielding the distribution of charge density within the pion and its associated momentum. These findings are compared to the predictions of chiral perturbation theory, demonstrating overall consistency while also identifying discrepancies, particularly in the momentum distribution. A discrepancy in the magnitude of the root-mean-square charge radius of ~10% is observed, with contributions also coming from terms involving heavier kaon correlations. A notable difference in momentum distribution is seen, with corrections arising from kaon correlations that could be attributed to the inclusion of next-order terms in chiral perturbation theory. A notable exception to overall agreement with chiral perturbation theory emerges in the limit of vanishing momentum, where the prediction of universal, flavor-independent behavior is contradicted by the data. This result, which holds for all quark mass configurations examined, may have implications for low-energy strong interaction theory. A quantitative assessment of lattice errors is challenging due to the complex nature of the correlation functions but indicates that discrepancies with chiral perturbation theory likely exceed those associated with lattice discretization and quark mass truncation. A comparison with the predictions of Symanzik's effective field theory in the form of the "chiral Fock space" expansion is also presented, offering insights into the composition of the pion and demonstrating agreement with its established characteristics while also providing a precise calculation of the charge radius and the coefficient of the $\bar{u}u$ correlation term. This coefficient, equal to 0.483 ± 0.005, is distinct from its value in the limit described by low-energy strong interaction theory and may reflect the effects of hadron dressing and the complexity of its internal structure. A similar analysis of the neutron yields a similar charge distribution, with a charge radius that is 3.5% larger, and a different coefficient for the $\bar{d}d$ correlation term, with a magnitude 1.74 times greater, indicating that the neutron contains more than two times as much of this $\bar{q}\bar{q}$ correlation compared to the pion. This distinction may be attributed to the differing ways in which the neutron and pion couple to the axial symmetry of the strong interaction or, alternatively, could reflect the distinct internal structures of these hadrons. A calculation of the probability of finding a $\bar{u}\bar{u}$ correlation within the pion also provides a hadronic perspective on the origin of the anomaly in the neutron-proton mass difference. Despite tremendous progress in reinforcement learning, training safe and robust policies for a wide range of collaborative tasks has remained a challenging problem. In many real-world scenarios, valuable training data often contains undesirable actions performed by individual agents, making their utility questionable. In this paper, we focus on a critical aspect - involving multiple agents in a collaborative project - and aim to extract beneficial information from existing data, specifically trajectories that result in successful outcomes. The key challenge lies in differentiating between successful experiences and those that would be detrimental with a different set of actions. To tackle this issue, we design a framework that leverages an action-based representation to distinguish between effective and ineffectual actions, and employs a combination of adversarial training and policy optimization to extract valuable information from successful experiences. The resulting policy is not only superior to policies trained on failing experiences but also demonstrates substantial improvement when comparing its performance in simulated environments. The proposed framework's effectiveness is further validated through the implementation of a realistic scenario involving multiple agents in a logistics project. The achieved results also align with those obtained using a simpler, alternative version of the multi-agent four-rooms problem. We developed a novel approach for aligning MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. This method compares aligned and random megavoltage image sets and uses this information to train a Convolutional Neural Network. Once trained, the network can correctly align megavoltage images with an automatically determined optimal projection angle in both 2D and 3D. Our results showed that the 2D aligned images closely matched actual clinical images, with an HU value mean difference of 3HU and a standard deviation of 161HU. Furthermore, our 3D aligned images closely resembled actual clinical images used in treatment planning, with an HU value mean difference of 3HU and a standard deviation of 156HU. Our data also indicated that the standard deviation of 3D HU values is significantly reduced with our method, from 187HU to 156HU. Our approach was implemented using TensorFlow, with training occurring on a supercomputer and image analysis performed on a standard workstation. Our code is available on GitHub at the specified URL. This project was supported by the National Cancer Institute.

The notion that entanglement between two particles is necessary for genuine nonlocal effects to occur is being challenged. Here, we demonstrate that single-particle states with specific properties can generate genuine nonlocal effects, surpassing the limitations of which can be achieved through classical means. These unique single-particle states, with both positive Wigner function and a non-zero overlap with the squeezed state, when prepared in one region and measured in another, exhibit a non-local, genuine entanglement-like phenomenon called single-particle steering. The condition under which this phenomenon occurs is defined, along with the amount of single-particle entanglement present, serving as a indicator for different preparation methods. This study also created a statistical profile for such events and may help interpret similar signals detected by the Virgo gravitational wave detector. Additionally, it highlights the superiority of gravitational wave data over electronic observations in detecting such events.

The efficiency of lasers is likely to reach levels where they can efficiently generate nuclear stages in heavy elements by hitting them with high-powered x-rays, followed by an intense laser. This approach, known as the "nuclear light sail," could potentially propel a spacecraft at high speeds. To achieve this, it's essential to understand the dynamics of nuclear stages and how they respond to high-powered lasers. Our research presents a non-equilibrium and non-thermal x-ray denisty calculation model, capable of accurately predicting the temperature and density of nuclear stages. This model was successfully applied to calculate the temperature and density of stages made from different heavy elements, including lead and mercury, and can be used to retrieve information about these stages through x-ray diffusion measurements. This processing model works even when x-ray densities are high and can be used to extract precise temperature and density readings from calculated models. By refining this model, it's possible to retrieve detailed information about heavy elements' stages and use that information to drive laser and x-ray simulations that can efficiently propel a spacecraft. We developed a novel mixed finite element method to simulate single-phase Darcy flow within porous media containing fractures. We modeled the fractures as thin layers with a distinct, high-permeability compared to the surrounding porous media. The method employs two types of elements: (1) standard triangular cells with a consistent, predetermined fluid flow rate throughout each cell, and (2) thin, linear elements representing fractures with a linear flow gradient within them. The method also employs a mixed finite element approach to better capture the fluid flow gradient within the fracture elements. The development of this method is based on the use of the hybrid Darcy mixed finite element approach, combined with the use of compatible triangulations to represent the fractures. The method accounts for fractures of varying thickness, and includes a non-fracture mesh generation tool to generate suitable triangulations. The method was implemented in the open-source finite element solver, Dune, and tested against existing numerical and analytical solutions, as well as against physical experiments involving single-phase flow within fractured media. The results showed that the method accurately represents the high-permeability fractures, and provides a good estimate of the overall flow rate within each cell. The method is particularly well-suited for modeling large numbers of thin fractures, and can be improved by optimizing the available mesh generation tools. Hypothesis testing with Bayes Factors has gained popularity, offering a direct alternative to p-values. However, criticisms of p-values, such as ignoring prior knowledge and treating the null hypothesis with equal weight, have led some to Bayes Factors. Yet, both researchers and statisticians often select Bayes Factors without a second thought. In response to this, we explore various approaches for utilizing Bayes Factors effectively. We examine the benefits and drawbacks of four distinct methods for interpreting Bayes Factors: the "default" approach based on uniform priors, the "cautious" approach with Caution Factors, the "conservative" approach with posterior predictive distributions, the "optimistic" approach with posterior predictive distributions, and the "Bayes Factor Grid" method. For each, we discuss potential pitfalls and offer guidance on how to incorporate Bayes Factors into analyses responsibly. By doing so, we provide researchers with a toolkit for making the most of Bayes Factors in their daily work. We also address frequently asked questions about incorporating prior knowledge, the relationship between Bayes Factors and p-values, and the use of Bayes Factors with continuous outcomes. In conclusion, Bayes Factors are more than just a statistical test; they require a thoughtful and data-driven approach to yield true advantages over p-values. With this paper, we aim to make Bayes Factors more accessible to a broader audience and to encourage a critical examination of the methods used with them. With over 180 figures and tables, this paper includes an extensive appendix detailing the R code and raw data for reproducibility. We hope this paper will serve as a starting point for discussions on the use of Bayes Factors and will contribute to the ongoing development of statistical practices. With time, Bayes Factors will become a household term in statistics, and with this paper, we will take a significant step towards that goal. Finally, we envision this paper as the foundation for an interactive website allowing users to customize their Bayes Factor workflows. Discourse indicators such as "however" and "in addition" facilitate the coordination of sentences with distinct topics. Nonetheless, these indicators often go unannotated in publicly available text datasets. This paper introduces a novel method for automatically identifying and categorizing the semantic content of discourse indicators within sentences. Our approach utilizes a combination of supervised learning to establish the inherent meaning of discourse indicators and neural networks to determine their significance in designated datasets. We have created a large-scale dataset comprising 30 diverse discourse indicators with associated semantic labels, known as DiscSense. This dataset, coupled with our detection model, has the potential to enhance current natural language processing systems by promoting the utilization of informed discourse indicator annotations. We have undertaken a series of experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and discovered that our detection model excels in particular datasets, such as the Wikipedia RealPost dataset. Our detection model, along with the DiscSense dataset, is available for public use at the specified URL. This has the potential to benefit researchers working on informed annotation systems for discourse indicators within sentences. We investigate the underlying geometry of a specific matrix optimization problem, focusing on the decomposition of matrices under non-convex constraints. This problem, which aims to minimize the rank of a matrix while enforcing equality constraints and bounded norms, has an associated landscape that we examine using a riemannian geometry framework. Our study reveals the presence of convexity within this geometric framework, specifically geodesic convexity, which provides a more precise understanding of the problem's geometry compared to previous analyses. The presence of geodesic convexity is further confirmed to hold true for specific optimization problems, including the non-convex matrix factorization and the trace ratio maximization problem. Our results also address the uniqueness of the solution and the structure of the solution space. The optimization problem along with associated algorithms are formulated as Riemannian stochastic gradient descent and Riemannian quasi-Newton methods, which are shown to converge under unique conditions. Our analysis of the optimization algorithms' convergence rates provides explicit bounds on the convergence rate. The results presented in this paper extend and improve previous findings, which were limited to the convex matrix optimization problem, by showing that geodesic convexity holds true even when the matrix is subject to non-convex constraints. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have gained widespread acceptance in various safety-sensitive imaging applications like in autonomous driving. Despite their success, CNNs can be vulnerable to deployment on cameras with faulty analog-to-digital conversion units, which convert image data into digital form. Such conversion errors can introduce consistent, image-dependent distortions in input data. We examine whether training CNNs with a generated dataset that accounts for typical ADC faults would provide a robust defense against these deployment-related faults. Our research involves creating a suitable training dataset with normal distribution labels to represent distorted features, and incorporating a new regularization technique called activation interval supervision to prevent cluster overlap and improve performance. We evaluate this model on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets and find improved accuracy with a normal distribution label assumption. Additionally, we apply this model to the ImageNet dataset used in a self-driving camera application, and demonstrate its efficacy in providing robust performance against real-world ADC faults. Our findings are validated through comparative analysis with baseline models. We open-source our activation interval supervision code to facilitate further research on this topic.

Constructing a unified semantic space that spans multiple languages is a key objective in multilingual applications. This space enables tasks like cross-lingual classification, where a model trained on data in one language can utilize information from another language without a word. Current methods focus primarily on preserving the intra-lingual similarities between words, but often neglect the inter-lingual relationships in favor of simpler projection techniques. This leads to a less optimal, fragmented space with poor performance in cross-lingual settings. In contrast, our proposed Cluster-consistent Word Representation (CWR) aims to create a cohesive, unified space that captures both intra- and inter-lingual similarities. CWR employs a novel cluster-aware loss function, ensuring that the word representations conform to the same semantic clusters across languages. This is achieved through a dual-learned process, where both the word clustering and the representation model are optimized in a mutually beneficial, cluster-consistent representation. Experimentation across multiple multilingual classification tasks demonstrates the superiority of CWR over baseline methods, with a particular advantage seen in scenarios with limited resource languages. The space constructed by CWR is also remarkably durable, with only a minor decline in performance after adding a million parameters. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/zwang95/CWR.

This project aims to model this outbreak of civil disorder using an epidemiological non-local simulation, drawing on the $SEI$ framework which accounts for different susceptibility and infectivity levels among individuals and varying connectivity between geographic regions. By adjusting key parameters, such as regional connectivity and immune recovery rates, this model successfully replicates the spatiotemporal progression observed during the Chilean protests. Furthermore, the simulations provide insights into the role of key factors contributing to the protests' rapid spread and duration. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the equivalence problem in extended regular expressions, resolving the issue for a subset that goes beyond standard regular expressions. The proposed technique employs a combination of rewriting rules and a decision procedure to evaluate the solvability of inequalities, ultimately leveraging the concept of recognizable sequences to underpin the strategy. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the efficient solution of various inequality problems, and the approach is specifically shown to accurately determine the distinctness of regular expression congruences. The paper's contribution is further highlighted by the discovery that first-order logic over read-only counters cannot effectively distinguish between some regular expression congruences, thereby establishing a significant inclusion within the set of problems decidably addressed by FO(RC). The associated algorithmic decision procedure, coupled with the underlying theory, offers an intriguing blend of theoretical and practical insights. The associated implementation, a tool named rexine, is made available to the public. The research underlying rexine has been the subject of a prior publication, but the tool itself has evolved substantially since then. The approach underlying the tool, when applied to the native inequality resolution problem, yields an EXPTIME decision boundary, and the associated recognition algorithm is efficient enough to support the graphical visualization of regular expression congruences. The tool further supports the conversion of regular expression congruences to recognizable transducers, and the associated documentation is provided to facilitate this process. The development of rexine has been influenced by the desire to support the teaching of the monadic logic over finite structures through the use of regular expression congruences as educational examples. The tool has been successfully utilized in this capacity and has been found suitable for a wide range of courses, extending from introductory levels to more advanced topics. The tool is available for download and can be used for the conversion of regular expression congruences to recognizable transducers, as well as for the determination of the distinctness of regular expression congruences, and further provides a graphical visualization of regular expression congruences. The development of rexine has also led to the creation of a large dataset of regular expression congruences, and the tool has been utilized in a successful attempt to prove the EXPTIME decidability of the inequality resolution problem for regular expression over finite strings. The associated results, as well as the tool and the associated documentation, are available to the public. Mobile navigation agents require orientation, position, and velocity information to navigate effectively. Inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide orientation at all times and have no occlusion issues, while being lightweight and power-efficient. However, their position and velocity estimation capabilities are limited due to drifting and limited field-of-view. To mitigate this, previous works relied heavily on vision systems with a wide field-of-view but are hampered by occlusions and high power consumption. This paper proposes a novel external memory attention model, EMA-VIO, that efficiently processes and utilizes INERTIAL and VISIONAL data equally. Integrating an external memory structure with a graph attention network, EMA-VIO dynamically allocates attention to balance the influence of vision and inertial data based on their credibility. This crediblity is determined by assessing the variability of feature representations. Our model demonstrates superior performance in navigation estimation and reduces the reliance on either sensor alone. Furthermore, introducing an online teacher-student mechanism enhances the efficiency of large-scale deployments. Evaluations on two datasets showcase the efficacy of our model, with a notable 60% reduction in the angular displacement error when relying solely on vision. Moreover, EMA-VIO's capability to adapt from a trained model results in a 70% and 30% decrease in the power consumption and size of the model, respectively. The code for EMA-VIO is available at: https://github.com/kuangruwen/EMA-VIO.

This paper proposes a novel federated selective integration framework, dubbed FedSI-KF, which enables the secure and efficient sharing and integration of data across multiple, geographically dispersed networks. FedSI-KF comprises three key components: (1) a client-level database selection mechanism, allowing for the secure transfer of chosen data samples while protecting sensitive information; (2) a server-level incremental learning framework, which facilitates the secure update of local models through selected, rather than aggregated, data; and (3) a robust evaluation protocol, comprising both theoretical privacy assurances and real-world experimentation. Our findings, obtained through realistic case studies, demonstrate the FedSI-KF framework to be highly effective in addressing several key challenges in knowledge fusion. Furthermore, FedSI-KF has been found to outperform alternative, non-selective data sharing approaches in various scenarios. The proposed framework, along with associated evaluation tools and experimental data, has been made publicly accessible. This problem is equivalent to determining the minimum time to distinguish two points on the surface of a sphere (3D sphere) with a particular sensing method. Then, we examine the asymmetry of the problem, its relationship with the spherical curvature, and its impact on the minimum time to distinguish two points. Finally, we apply and generalize these findings to the context of a 2D sphere (a ball), specifically the Bloch ball, to derive a more robust standard of distinguishability (Cramér-Rao) and a quantum speed limit (Trotter). These results are valid for any two non-equilibrated states and provide a specific test for the validity of some previously proposed quantum speed limit and asymmetry measures. Additionally, we demonstrate that the curvature-based standard of distinguishability is a more precise indicator of the identifiability of two points on a sphere when compared to the standard approach. A common technique used to achieve this involves employing LiNbO3 optoelectrical circuits, which convert terahertz radiation into optical signals that can be detected through spectroscopy. However, optoelectrical circuits operate in a parallel detection mode and require expensive equipment for access. In contrast, Josephson junction-based terahertz detectors offer a more accessible and serial detection solution. Herein, the operation of Josephson terahertz detectors is demonstrated through real-valued demodulation of 40-mV oscillations within a microwave resonator tuned to 5.9 GHz, with a detection threshold as low as 0.5 GHz in root mean square. The extremely low noise floor of these detectors also enables reliable detection of a microwave resonator's fundamental tone within a Q-factor of approximately 200. The slow development of Venus contrasts with Earth and Mars in the solar system, presenting scientists with a fascinating puzzle. One leading hypothesis proposes that asuppression of atmospheric savitation driven by sulfuric acid clouds hindered photochemical nitrogen loss and thus atmospheric escape, in turn slowing planetary differentiation and geologic activity. This hypothesis is supported by computational models showing that atmospheric escape on Venus was indeed reduced due to its distinct atmospheric chemistry. However, the mechanisms underlying the development of Venus's atmosphere remain complex and multifaceted, involving interrelated processes that feedback on one another across various timescales. The slow release of volatile compounds from the planet's core, degassing rates, and the extent of atmospheric sputtering all played crucial roles in shaping Venus's distinctive atmosphere. They, in turn, were influenced by factors such as the reflectivity of clouds, surface temperature, and atmospheric escape, each exerting its own particular pace of change. As a result, any attempt to analyze the planet's development must consider these processes and their intricate temporal relationships. Based on the current understanding, we outline the atmosphere's development as a function of four key variables, each governed by its unique dynamics from rapid degassing to slow tectonic activity. This approach enables us to gain a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between processes that have guided the development of Venus's atmosphere across its history. Additionally, by applying the principle of dimensional analysis, we can also obtain approximate numerical values for the timescales of various processes influencing the planet's evolution. These estimates break down into three main categories: (1) timescales related to the chemistry, magnetism, and geophysics of the planet, (2) timescales associated with the solar and external components affecting its evolution, and (3) timescales linked to the electromagnetic and gravitational forces governing its movement within the Milky Way. By further examining the planet's movement within the galaxy and its impact on its evolution, as well as the inherent characteristics that define it as a distinct planet, we can gain a richer appreciation for the complex interplay between the variables that have shaped its development. Ultimately, this analysis provides a foundation for exploring the planet's future evolution and offers insights into the broader principles governing the development of planets in general.

We establish a nonlinear Hawkes model based on point process theory, which enables us to model non-mixing, self-reinforcing, and inhibitory phenomena in various fields. We then develop a Bayesian estimation method for the model's parameters, which are necessary to understand these dynamics. Our algorithm uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample the posterior distribution efficiently. We prove that this algorithm converges and that the posterior distribution asymptotically satisfies strong regularity conditions, effectively making the posterior distribution approximately regular for large enough data sets. We also demonstrate that the posterior estimates converge at a rate of at least $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ as the data set size T grows. Notably, this result improves upon the previous rate of $O(1/T)$ found in a related study. We further validate our method by applying it to synthetic data sets and real-world examples from finance and neuroscience. These applications illustrate the model's capacity to extract meaningful dynamics from complex data sets. The code associated with this project is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/Alessio-Becciu/BNH. The code includes the Bayesian estimation algorithm, as well as sample data sets used in the paper. The code is written in Python and employs the Numpy, Scipy, and PyMC3 libraries. The results presented in the paper were obtained using MacPro computers with an Intel Core i9 processor and 64 GB of RAM. The estimated computational time for the Bayesian estimation algorithm is roughly 1-3 days for real-world data sets, depending on the specific data and the desired burn-in period. The code also includes the data sets used in the neuroscience applications, which were obtained from the Neurotechnik website. The license associated with the code is the MIT License. The estimated parameters and the estimated dynamics extracted from the data sets are included in the results section of the paper. The code and the results section provide a clear blueprint for replicating the paper's results. The paper concludes by outlining two potential directions for further development: the application of the nonlinear Hawkes model to modeling hierarchical phenomena and the development of a Hamiltonian Hamiltonian Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm for the model. In magnetized plasmas, the interaction between intense laser pulses and free electrons can result in the modulation of laser polarization due to the deflection of electrons by an imposed magnetic field. As a consequence, the laser's polarization alternates in a pattern that depends on the number of cycles and the magnitude of the magnetic field. However, a specific scenario, in which the magnetic field is aligned with the laser's polarization axis, instead leads to the polarization becoming circular instead of elliptical. This transformation can either amplify the laser's intensity or lead to the mitigation of its spatial instability. The degree to which the polarization changes, from either alternation to modulation or circular conversion, depends on the level of the laser's nonlinear interaction with the plasma. As such, this interplay highlights the complex nature of the interrelated effects and their potential applications. Moreover, the influence of the plasma's length and the laser's duration on this interplay demands further investigation. The theoretical model presented in this work is also validated through numerical simulations conducted using the semi-analytical "full-wave" model. The predictions made by this model identify the onset of the plasma's breakdown as well as the point at which the interaction becomes fully nonlinear, thereby providing the parameters for the numerical simulations. The simulation results include the formation of the laser's shockwave, the redistribution of the electron distribution function, the curvature of the electron trajectory, the corresponding changes in the laser's spectrum, the electron distribution, as well as the point at which the interaction becomes fully nonlinear. The validation of the model is also visually confirmed through the comparison of the numerical simulations with the corresponding movie files. The potential for the experimental verification of these predictions is also discussed, along with the possible extensions of this model to other intense laser-plasma interactions. The associated movie files depict the spatio-temporal evolution of the electron distribution function, the curvature of the electron trajectory, the corresponding changes in the laser's spectrum, along with the electron and plasma profiles during the interaction. The numerical data presented in this work can be reused for the further analysis of the corresponding movie files. The results presented in this work can be utilized for the better understanding of the interactions between intense laser pulses and plasmas, along with the possible applications in the study of astrophysical phenomena, as well as in the development of intense laser technology. Rank metric coding theory, which is pertinent to data storage systems employing optical or magnetic memory, involves investigating errors that occur in code words resulting from non-coherent optical or magnetic readings of storage devices. In contrast to binary coding theory, where decoding of rank metric errors is straightforward and identical to decoding of additive errors, determining coherent storage channels requires a more in-depth analysis. This paper examines Gaussian coherent storage channels and identifies a novel decoding technique for decoding Gaussian coherent storage channels, thereby classifying a special type of rank metric errors as additive errors. This previously unrecognized inclusion enables a reduction in the number of storage devices needed in rank metric coding schemes. In particular, it is demonstrated that any (k,r)-rank metric code can be reconfigured into an (r,k)-additive code, thereby establishing a direct relationship between codes of these two distinct types. This relationship also takes the form of an inverse image operation, making it possible to examine additive codes from the perspective of rank metric codes. This in turn leads to the discovery of a new additive code inclusion, as well as the resolution of a previous open problem posed by Gabidulin. This paper also presents several additional examples of rank metric codes. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the decoding technique mentioned above is more efficient than the conventional method of solving the rank metric problem, although it is more complex. This technique, however, is straightforward for certain codes, as illustrated in the paper. This paper and its findings are a direct continuation of the research presented in the paper titled "New Decoding Technique for Rank Metric Codes". Building upon the fundamental understanding of operator product expansion (OPE) structures in CFT, a specific set of operators in CFT$_2$ is identified that possess spinning conformal properties when situated within a specific radial range in AdS$_3$. It is demonstrated that these operators, referred to as spinning OPE segments, exhibit conformal covariance when subjected to specific transformations in AdS$_3$. Furthermore, it is shown that the spinning OPE segments can be represented as non-local operators in CFT$_2$, with implications for their operator product expansion structures also determined. A comparison with the previously established results for local AdS fields in AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ reveals that the spinning OPE segments comprise both local and semi-local fields, with additional components that are distinct in nature. Lastly, the spinning OPE segments can be represented in terms of semi-local fields when situated within a specific radial range in AdS$_3$, with this scenario sharing analogies with the Maldacena-Swansen duality. A potential application of these findings in the study of spinning semi-local fields through CFT$_2$ is also proposed. A supplementary analysis is conducted to explore spinning OPE segments at the boundary of AdS$_3$, with this specific case found to be equivalent to the semi-local fields in the Maldacena-Swansen duality. A comprehensive field operator product expansion map for AdS$_3$ is introduced, with this map capable of converting the spinning OPE segments back into the corresponding local and semi-local fields in CFT$_2$. A final interpretation of this map in the context of the CFT$_2$ operator product expansion is also provided. Our method leverages a generative adversarial technique in the training process to greatly reduce the amount of labeled documents required for effective extraction models. In this study, we analyzed the effects of COVID-19 on urban mobility patterns in Los Angeles, by comparing traffic flow data before and during the pandemic. Our findings reveal a significant reduction (38-67%) in daily traffic activity in Los Angeles during the pandemic, with the impact varying by time of day and season. We also discovered a notable decrease (10-17%) in average traffic speeds. To understand the societal implications of these changes, we used a mathematical model that simulates the movement of individuals in an overcrowded environment. Our data showed that in Los Angeles, there was a notable increase (15-20%) in the number of people avoiding crowded areas during the pandemic, with this trend being more pronounced in lower-income communities. As a result, we found that the income-based disparity in urban interactions increased by 8% during the pandemic. This shift towards less crowded behavior was found to persist even after the pandemic, with a 5% long-term rise in the income-based disparity in urban interactions. This research suggests that the pandemic accelerated the long-term trend of income-based isolation in Los Angeles, with implications for managing future crowds and preventing similar disparities from forming in other populations. To this end, we propose a data-driven approach to tracking the distribution of crowds and incentivizing more equitable movement patterns. This initiative could be applied broadly, with Los Angeles serving as a prototype with which to test and refine this method before its wider adoption. This research investigates how a uniform initial vorticity affects the behavior of water waves propelled by a moving plate in an infinitely extended, shallow body of water. We identify a specific condition under the influence of a rotating plate, which causes vorticity to emerge from nowhere. By comparing the results with those obtained using the standard Hamiltonian Dysthe formula, we establish that the waves become disordered more quickly when there is initial vorticity present. Additionally, we observe that the Hamiltonian Dysthe formula fails to accurately predict the development of the long-wave component when there is an initial vorticity present. Finally, we analyze the energy dynamics of the system, revealing that the energy associated with vorticity plays a crucial role in the Hamiltonian Dysthe formulation. This is achieved by modifying the Hamiltonian Dysthe formula, which now includes a term related to vorticity. This new formula is subsequently verified through direct integration of the Hamiltonian dynamics equations. Autonomous navigation in unfamiliar indoor spaces with limited outdoor areas is a challenging problem for drones. In such environments, a suitable navigation approach would utilize a mix of outdoor and indoor pathways, including corridors and rooms, without a comprehensive map. This research introduces a novel method, called Layered Navigation Manager (LNM), which is specifically designed for drones to fly within these types of indoor spaces without a pre-existing map. LNM incorporates two primary layers to guide the navigation: one focuses on obstacle avoidance using a 3D surroundings map, while the other deals with path planning based on a 2D floor map. The two layers are integrated through a control system that ensures safe and efficient navigation. Although the approach is generally applicable, our research was particularly focused on navigating office-style environments. In these settings, we successfully tested the LNM protocol to a distance of 220 meters without a prior map. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the protocol can be modified to accommodate larger outdoor areas, provided it has sufficient mapping data. This research introduces a novel approach that extends the traditional bending explanation beyond its limited scope within the Poisson model. Building on this foundation, we develop a general theory to describe the bending phenomenon within Gaussian random fields, even in the absence of the Poisson condition. This general framework enables us to create a parameter that characterizes the bending effect and can be employed in models and algorithms. Additionally, we establish the relationship between the bending effect and the spectrum of the underlying random field, thereby providing insights into the structure of the field. Furthermore, we identify the conditions under which the field exhibits independent blocks of varying sizes, and in the process, we develop an efficient algorithm to simulate such fields. This algorithm, known as the "cut-and-paste" method, is capable of accurately simulating independent blocks of differing scales by utilizing a range of models, including the Poisson model, Gaussian random fields, and combinations of the two, each tailored to specific scale ranges. This method allows for a controlled and deliberate creation of the bending phenomenon. Our research also explores the possibility of treating the index of the random field as a hidden variable, a configuration that enables us to apply common hidden Markov model techniques. Our research provides a novel understanding of the bending phenomenon, an insight that is further illustrated through an application to the simulation of images. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar environments, having an effective mapping technique is crucial. In the absence of a global map, local topological maps can efficiently guide the robot through the space by defining connections between different locations. Current methods represent these connections using simple symbols without considering the actual spatial configuration of the environment. As a result, they may lead to navigation errors when the map is incomplete or inaccurate. To address this issue, a new representation called HiTMap introduces a hierarchical layout that includes both a global structure and a set of local grid maps depicting the spatial relationships between different map regions. Each grid map can be individually learned using a probabilistic spatial representation, and HiTMap learns to navigate by aggregating these local maps. We demonstrate the superiority of HiTMap over traditional methods by showing it can handle complex, partially unknown environments and seamlessly adapt to map updates without compromising its efficiency. Furthermore, with its hierarchical design, HiTMap can efficiently navigate large scales by prioritizing the global map pathways. We also explore the integration of HiTMap with SLAM, enabling the direct learning of spatial representations from raw sensor data. With its innovative design and versatility, HiTMap offers a cutting-edge solution for various mobile robot navigation tasks. We have made the code available at: https://github.com/PRM-Group/HiTMap. Moreover, the code for learning individual grid maps and HiTMap without prior knowledge is also publicly available at: https://github.com/PRM-Group/HiTMap-SLAM. System HiTMap details are as follows: HiTMap has 3 main components: (1) Grid Map Learning: This component is responsible for individually learning local grid maps using a spatial representation. We used a probabilistic spatial representation, specifically a spatial Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), to model these local maps. The model comprises mixtures of spatially constrained Gaussian distributions that can be efficiently learned and efficiently navigate even in the presence of obstacles. (2) HiTMap Learning: This component combines the local grid maps to create a global topological layout. We used a spatial GMM as the base map representation, enabling the efficient learning and navigation of large scales with HiTMap. The model includes a set of local grid maps along with their corresponding spatial relationships, which can be learned and used for navigation in the absence of a prior map. (3) HiTMap Control: This component is responsible for controlling the HiTMap by determining the next map region to visit based on the perceived sensor

We propose a method that leverages the precise control of magnetic fields through the Meissner effect in superconducting materials to literally "carpet" interferometry systems, eliminating the need to measure each individual gradient and ensuring the detection of even minute magnetic changes. Based on this design, we could detect a change in magnetic field strength as minute as 10.7 nano-tesla, and a change in gradient as small as 30.5 nano-tesla per meter, both within a second. If scaled up, this design could also detect a change in magnetic field strength as small as 2.5 nano-tesla in a 1-meter interferometer. This achievement opens the door for atomic interferometry to detect local magnetic alterations and demonstrates a precise method for measuring low-frequency magnetic fluctuations. Additionally, this design has applications in quantifying the magnetic interference generated by quantum computing devices and other complex electronics. With the ability to measure fluctuations in magnetic fields as low as 1.7 x 10^-14 Tesla per second, this method surpasses the sensitivity of other measurement techniques used for this purpose. Our proposed memory allocator, DynaSOAr, is specifically designed to meet the needs of Object-oriented Programming on GPU architectures. In contrast to traditional Object-oriented Programming, Object-oriented Programming on GPUs prioritizes efficient memory access by aligning objects with a fixed block size, leaving no gap between them. This alignment leads to better memory utilization but makes memory allocation more complicated. DynaSOAr addresses this challenge by developing a state-of-the-art, concurrent memory allocator that seamlessly handles allocations of different sizes within these aligned memory blocks. Our innovative allocator employs a unique approach that combines both free-list and binary search techniques to quickly locate free memory blocks. Furthermore, DynaSOAr features a sophisticated strategy to minimize fragmentation and efficiently manages a pool of small memory blocks. In addition to its core functionality, DynaSOAr includes a feature to allocate memory from multiple pools, each with its own set of small memory blocks, as well as a pool for allocating memory for arrays. Our experiments demonstrate that DynaSOAr outperforms other memory allocators in various object-oriented applications running on GPU architectures. In particular, DynaSOAr delivers a notable improvement of 2.4 times in memory allocation speed and reduces total memory allocation time by 1.5 times when compared to other leading memory allocators. Our findings also highlight the optimal block size and pool sizes that yield the best performance in GPU Object-oriented Programming. Consequently, DynaSOAr serves as an ideal memory allocator for a wide range of Object-oriented applications running on GPU architectures, including real-world industrial cases like NVIDIA's CUDA and OpenACC. Moreover, DynaSOAr's innovative approach to memory allocation is valuable to the broader computing community and can be applied to other memory management scenarios. Our memory allocator is publicly available at https://github.com/CompArchLab/DynaSOAr.

The formation of massive young stellar objects is thought to occur primarily in molecular infrared dark cores, specifically those with mass-to-lineratio (MR) values indicative of advanced progression. We conducted a morphological and spectral analysis of the "Dragon" infrared dark nebula and discovered two core components within it: a prominent, linear core and a second, more compact, core shaped by outflow. By examining spectral lines, we determined the cores' masses, velocities, and temperatures, and found the linear core to have a higher velocity dispersion. However, the compact core exhibits brighter emission in the [CII] line and a higher mass-to-luminosity ratio, suggesting it has a hotter and brighter outershell. The Mr values for both cores fall into the massive range, implying both have the potential to form massive stars. The compact core's [SII]/[CII] line ratio indicates it has a higher gas density than the linear core, and the absence of a bright outflow peak suggests it has not yet formed a massive young stellar object. Understanding the intricacies of nuclei in histopathology images is crucial for diagnosing and predicting cancer patient outcomes. Accurate classification of images as containing tumor or normal tissue also relies on effectively analyzing these nuclei structures. To this end, a key step in this process is the segmentation of individual nuclei within these images. We propose an end-to-end approach, referred to as W-Net, which consists of two consecutive convolutional networks for performing this task. The first network, responsible for preliminary nucleus segmentation, generates an initial estimate of individual nuclei based on simple post-processing techniques. This crude representation serves as a starting point for the second network, which refines this prediction by removing unwanted nucleus remnants and combining separated nuclei structures. Evaluations conducted on public datasets have shown our method to outperform existing approaches in terms of evaluation metrics. Code available at: https://github.com/ghru/W-Net. GCNNs have gained popularity in recent years, yielding notable performance improvements in graph-based data analysis. Despite their efficacy, the underlying workings of GCNNs remain poorly understood, which is largely attributed to their treatment as "black boxes." Our research seeks to address this knowledge gap by developing a practical and interpretable GCNN called DeepMatchFilter, powered by a matched filtering framework. This method enables a deeper insight into how GCNNs function and why they are effective, also providing a means to adjust the network for enhanced interpretability. Furthermore, our findings suggest that current GCNN training objectives may be improved by incorporating a matched filtering match metric, which aligns with the principle of finding optimal hyperparameter configurations that minimize cross-validation error. DeepMatchFilter and the matched filtering method were both demonstrated to be superior to the conventional GCNN approach in experiments conducted on synthetic data, genetic association analysis, and the MNIST classification task. Lastly, an adjustment we made to DeepMatchFilter was found to be particularly effective for resolving overfitting in models trained on small datasets. In summary, our matched filtering GCNN, along with the analysis of its workings, presents a substantial advancement over existing GCNNs. Our research involves creating artificial environments that mimic predator-prey interactions with multiple areas, including both safe zones and contested spaces. We designed two types of environments: linear arrangements and divided areas with distinct regions. Our primary focus is on analyzing how complex hierarchical structures made up of multiple areas at different scales affect the behavior of prey entities evading their predators. We observed that in linear settings, prey that are faster than their predators can succeed in evading them, especially in longer arrangements. In contrast, circular environments with diverse layouts favor faster prey in most cases. However, even in these circular environments, there are exceptions, like the scenario with a small central zone. Interestingly, in circular environments, a speed difference of 1 unit is the minimum required for the faster prey to prevail. Moreover, when there are multiple predators, the environment's scale becomes even less critical, and the primary factor influencing success is the speed disparity between prey and predators. Finally, we explored how complex circular environments with multiple areas influence the behavior of both prey and predators, and surprisingly, we found that the optimal circular designs preferred by both sides are those with a central metropolis surrounded by outer suburbs. This preferred design occurs because it offers both hiding spaces for the prey to evade predators and multiple opportunities for predators to ambush their prey. In conclusion, the intricate circular designs we tested revealed both expected and more surprising outcomes, highlighting the complex and dynamic nature of pursuit-evasion interactions within hierarchical divisions of different areas. This study is relevant to a broad range of fields, including artificial intelligence, robotics, game theory, biology, and even urban planning. From an artificial intelligence perspective, our findings on preferred circular designs could guide the development of more sophisticated algorithms for creating complex environments. In biology, our discovery of preferred circular designs may provide insights into the natural habitats preferred by certain predator-prey populations. And in urban planning, our research on preferred circular designs could inform the creation of more efficient and safer public spaces. This study offers a versatile and open platform for other researchers to experiment with diverse modifications and applications. This research was conducted using Stadium, a public library of reusable Python tools for simulating and visualizing complex systems, and it is available for download on GitHub. This project was supported by Google's AI Education Grant.

Our proposed method, the Modular Systems for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning (MSMT-RL), tackles overlapping sets of relevant state observations in multi-task RL problems. By focusing on discrete, independent sets of state observations, MSMT-RL prevents destructive interference when tasks share the same relevant state observations. This is because the system's modular structure allows for distinct observation policies that prevent outputs from different modules from cancelling each other out. In contrast, existing approaches combine policies directly, which can lead to destructive interference when tasks share the same relevant state observations. Our results show that MSMT-RL reduces destructive interference and yields better performance in problem instances where tasks share the same relevant state observations. We break down the process of verifying their affiliation with Berkeley in two parts: first, we establish the fact that each of them worked at Berkeley within the "mathlib" library, and second, we provide a formal proof for this fact. The interstellar medium is home to a vast network of scatters that interfere with pulsar signals as they travel to Earth, and these interferometric patterns can provide valuable insights into the medium itself. In this study, we employed a new statistical approach to investigate the interstellar interference affecting the pulsar B1133+16 at 300.04 MHz, and our findings suggest that the scattering patterns are consistent with being produced by interstellar plasma filaments within a specific region of space that is causing the pulsar's light to be diverted from its course. If this interpretation is correct, it would make B1133+16 the second known pulsar with a designated "birthplace" in the interstellar environment, similar to PRS J0300+19. Furthermore, we estimate that the total "mass" of the filaments responsible for the scattering patterns could be roughly 10 to the power of 11 solar masses, and our results also provide an estimate for the distance to which the scattering patterns are visible, ranging from approximately 8 to 10 parsecs. Lastly, our analysis indicates that the scale of the filaments responsible for the scattering patterns is comparable to that of the Sun, and the distribution of the filaments appears random rather than structured along the line of sight. The development of our statistical approach, known as the "caustic builder," allowed us to simulate the scattering patterns caused by the filaments and compare them to the observed data, and it provides a valuable tool for interpreting similar data from other pulsars. The data used in this study were collected over a period of nearly 10 years with the LOFAR radio telescope, and the findings highlight the capabilities of scintillometry with LOFAR for conducting low-frequency pulsar studies and the importance of directed surveys for identifying specific pulsars that exhibit interference patterns with particular characteristics. In order to enhance speech generative models, particularly those handling multi-pitch speech, this paper proposes a novel architecture called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet). This model builds on the WaveNet structure while providing two significant innovations. Firstly, a new convolutional neural network (CNN) is introduced with a frequency-aggressive dilation approach, capable of capturing local and long-range period dependencies. Secondly, a modified convolutional neural network is introduced with a frame-shift property, enabling the model to effectively process multi-pitch speech even with a fixed frame length. Empirical evaluations conducted on multi-pitch speech demonstrate the efficacy of the frequency-aggressive dilated convolution, coupled with the frame-shift property, leading to a 3.5 dB improvement in the mean opinion score (MOS) and a 25.6% reduction in the mean squared error (MSE) compared to the WaveNet reference model. Moreover, QPNet outperforms BNE-WaveNet, a previously proposed model tailored for single-pitch speech, in both subjective and objective evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the model's efficiency, with a 50% compression in parameters compared to WaveNet, without compromising performance, is also demonstrated. Moreover, the model exhibits superior speech quality in both single-pitch and multi-pitch speech scenarios. Enhancing video content with realistic auditory effects that are precisely localized is a challenging task. Despite the significance of sound source localization in creating immersive experiences and the advancement of deep learning technology, this problem remains difficult to solve, especially when working with low-fidelity audio. Previous approaches relying on end-to-end learning have limitations, mainly due to their inability to effectively utilize supplementary information, such as the video's acoustical environment, to inform the audio synthesis process. This paper introduces a novel multiregion approach, comprised of multiple separate tasks that collectively achieve accurate and natural-sounding audio synthesis. By leveraging multiple regions within the frequency spectrum and utilizing deep learning models in a collaborative manner, our method effectively utilizes available information to enhance the quality of the audio. The resulting model is capable of correctly positioning the sound sources within the video's acoustical environment. Our evaluation, conducted with an openly available dataset, demonstrates the multiregion approach's superiority over prior work in terms of both the objective and subjective assessment of the audio content. Furthermore, this approach has been successfully applied to the difficult problem of sound source localization from low-quality audio. The code for this project is available at this link: https://github.com/ghr95/localize-audio.

Our proposed LGNN model leverages a novel geometric framework, utilizing edges with positive lengths to represent distances between nodes, rather than binary connections. This innovative edge representation enables our model to effectively capture complex, nonlinear relationships between inputs. Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate significant performance enhancements compared to traditional GNNs and competing metric learning models, indicating the benefits of this new geometric framework. Additionally, our model achieves state-of-the-art results in real-world classification tasks, thanks to the presence of a nonlinear projection layer that facilitates efficient feature transformations. We also introduce a novel technique for training LGNNs with high efficiency, by applying the negative sampling loss only to incorrect predictions. We explore various harmonic gauge choices in gravity, examining how different variants affect the well-posedness of the hyperbolic Einstein equations and their link to the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner parametrization. A range of well-known and lesser-known variants of the harmonic gauge are discussed, with a focus on their relationships and the underlying geometric principles that govern them. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these variants for the Cauchy problem posed by the Einstein equations and the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner parametrization. A notable aspect of our discussion involves the introduction of a novel variant of the harmonic gauge, defined by the trace-free part of the Debnath-Nair gauge. This new variant demonstrates compatibility with the conformally flat family of geometries. All of the discussed harmonic gauge choices can be viewed as projections onto the space of valid harmonic gauge vectors, with the trace-free variants forming a subset of these. This is particularly relevant as the use of the full harmonic gauge choices introduces difficulties related to the gauge's failure to completely determine a solution to the Einstein equations, as it fails to account for the trace component. We have a set of fundamental fields that make up the most elementary scoto-seesaw framework, which includes two types of scalar fields with a phase rotation symmetry and two Higgs doublets. In this study, we incorporate the most basic form of the framework and conduct an in-depth analysis of its Dark Matter characteristics when incorporating Weakly-Interactive Massive Particles. Additionally, we examine the vacuum stability of the Electroweak sector within this framework, prompted by concerns about the Higgs vacuum instability. Our results indicate that, to prevent the vacuum from becoming unstable and to accurately describe Dark Matter interactions, the most basic form of the scoto-seesaw framework requires at least four generations of fermions. Furthermore, we compare our findings to similar previous studies on the same topic. The scoto-seesaw framework's potential in explaining the mass disparities between Higgs and fermions is also explored in this research. The framework's capability to naturally generate the Dark Matter mass range is demonstrated in our analysis, and we outline the mechanism by which the mass disparities between standard model and extra scalar fermions can be created. The most basic form of the scoto-seesaw framework also includes a specific doublet-phase coefficient that characterizes Dark Matter's doublet nature, and it varies significantly depending on the Dark Matter mass. By numerically solving the Heisenberg and Hubbard models derived from the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ Hamiltonian, we analyze the magnetic properties and electronic spectra of various compounds with different orbital occupancies. The results are compared to existing research on 3d and 2d compounds, expanding the scope of these studies to 4d and 5d compounds with strong correlation and $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital mixing. The comprehensive picture obtained can be useful for understanding the physics of 4d and 5d transition metal compounds with strong interactions and $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital mixing. We establish that two algebraic structures related to knot polynomials, known as colored oriented link (CO) Frobenius algebras, are equivalent when based on an integral base field, specifically under the condition that a set of generators has a maximal length. Additionally, this equivalence holds when it is refined to Hecke operators. In order to establish this equivalence, we compare the two algebras using two methods: the first method utilizes the quantum group construction and its properties, specifically its behavior with respect to alterations; the second method, which is more explicit, involves constructing one algebra from the mirror image of a bichromatic link and determining the resulting CO Frobenius algebra explicitly. The two methods are demonstrated to yield the same algebras when applied. The (refined) equivalence of the CO Frobenius algebras is further demonstrated to extend from a specific set of generators to an arbitrary set when it is shown that the dimension of the CO Frobenius algebra is equal to the square of the number of generators, which in turn implies the equivalence holds for the dimension $n^2$ when based on an integral base field. The algebras are also shown to be isomorphic when the condition $n$ is odd is satisfied. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization. It takes in vector-based data, either individually or in groups, and represents the information in up to four dimensions using various nonlinear techniques. The program enables side-by-side comparisons of different data sets, includes features for automatic group formation, and permits the creation of custom groups for in-depth analysis. With an intuitive interface, users can interact with the visualizations, applying different techniques to further examine the data. ViDaExpert is designed specifically for the analysis of high-dimensional text-based data, featuring an integrated implementation of the widely used topic modeling technique known as Latent Dirichlet Allocation. The application is platform-independent and may be accessed via any Java-enabled browser. ViDaExpert is an expansion of earlier work presented at the 2008 IEEE Workshop on Advances in Memory, Processing, and Approximation Techniques in Data Processing. The application is now rebranded from its former name, ViDaExplorer. The program is available for download at https://cs.gmu.edu/~pcskoe/ViDaExpert.html. The underlying code for ViDaExpert is composed of approximately 7,000 lines of code, primarily written in Java with some employs of Apache Commons Mathematics Library. The application incorporates multiple visualization techniques, including t-SNE, LEAR, t-Kernel, and LLE, in addition to LDA for text-based data analysis. ViDaExpert generates interactive.swf files that may be accessed via any Java-enabled browser, and it also offers command-line functionality for the creation of standalone.swf files. The application is compatible with a range of operating systems, including but not limited to Windows, Mac OS, and Linux.
